-- Harbourline Recon: starter migration 0000 (provided by the course)
-- Run ONCE in the Supabase project harbourline-recon (SQL Editor), never in sql-course.
-- Creates the three business tables and loads a frozen copy of Harbourline v1.
BEGIN;
CREATE TABLE insurers (
    insurer_id        integer GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    code              text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    name              text NOT NULL,
    country           char(2) NOT NULL,
    time_zone         text NOT NULL,            -- IANA zone name, e.g. Europe/Amsterdam
    statement_cycle   text NOT NULL             -- how often they send a statement
);

CREATE TABLE policies (
    policy_id         integer GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    policy_number     text NOT NULL UNIQUE,    -- our format: ABC-123456
    customer_id       integer NOT NULL,           -- customer lives in the CRM, not in this app
    insurer_id        integer NOT NULL REFERENCES insurers (insurer_id),
    product           text NOT NULL,
    start_date        date NOT NULL,
    end_date          date,                    -- NULL = no end date yet
    annual_premium    numeric(12,2) NOT NULL,  -- current yearly premium in EUR
    payment_frequency text NOT NULL CHECK (payment_frequency IN ('monthly', 'quarterly', 'annual')),
    status            text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('active', 'cancelled', 'suspended')),
    notes             text
);

CREATE TABLE premium_invoices (
    invoice_id        integer GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    invoice_number    text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    policy_id         integer NOT NULL REFERENCES policies (policy_id),
    invoice_date      date NOT NULL,
    due_date          date NOT NULL,
    period_start      date NOT NULL,
    period_end        date NOT NULL,
    amount            numeric(12,2) NOT NULL,  -- premium the customer must pay
    commission        numeric(12,2) NOT NULL,  -- our share, kept from the premium
    status            text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('open', 'paid', 'partially_paid', 'overdue', 'cancelled'))
);

st-m00-run.title: What happens when you press Check

steps.caption: Every exercise starts from the same database: the lesson's setup plus the examples before it.
Your SQL runs inside a transaction, so nothing you try can break the practice data.
The course rolls everything back, then runs the model answer on the same state.
It compares the two results row by row. Same rows (and order, when the question asks for one) means **Correct**.
Different queries can be correct: only the result counts, not the exact text you wrote.

cards.back: Run it and read the output. Most examples change the practice database; later exercises build on them.
You write the SQL. **Check** compares your result with the model answer's result.
A step in your own Supabase project `harbourline-recon`. You check it yourself.
End of a module: a quiz without notes (pass at 70%) and a timed practical task.

dl-m00-ai.scenario: Exercise 4 has you stuck for ten minutes. An AI chat would give you a working query in seconds.
dl-m00-ai.question: What do you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Paste the AI's query, see it pass, move on.
options.outcome: The check turns green, but you learned nothing you can use at the checkpoint, where AI isn't allowed.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the hint, run smaller parts of your query, then look at the model answer and retype it from memory.
options.outcome: Slower today, but you find exactly which step you didn't know. That step is what sticks.

options.label: C
options.text: Skip the exercise and come back to it never.
options.outcome: Fine once. Skipped exercises tend to be the ones the checkpoint asks about.

dl-m00-ai.advice: Struggle for a few minutes, then use the hint, then the model answer. Type the answer yourself; don't copy it.

cards.back: A set of rows that all describe the same kind of thing, such as `policies`.
One thing: one policy, one invoice, one statement line.
The column (or columns) that identify each row uniquely, such as `policy_id`.
A column that points to another table's primary key, such as `premium_invoices.policy_id`.

steps.caption: An invoice doesn't repeat the policy's details. It stores only the policy's id.
That id is a **foreign key**: it points at exactly one row in `policies`.
The policy, in turn, points at its insurer.
Two invoices can point at different policies of the same insurer. The insurer is stored once.

so-m01-types.intro: Which type fits each column? Select a card, then choose its box.
so-m01-types.why: Money is numeric (exact decimals), days are date, identifiers are text even when they contain digits.

st-m02-where.title: How WHERE filters, row by row

steps.caption: PostgreSQL reads the rows of the table in `FROM`.
For each row it evaluates the condition. Row 1: open is not paid, so **true**.
Row 2: the condition is **false**. The row is dropped.
Row 3: **true**, so it's kept.
Only rows where the condition is true survive. False and NULL both drop the row (lesson 2.5).

bd-m02-order.task: Put the clauses in the order PostgreSQL requires.
bd-m02-order.success: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT: that order never changes.

pr-m02-null.question: What does PostgreSQL return?
pr-m02-null.why: Comparing with NULL gives NULL (unknown), even NULL with NULL. Use `IS NULL` to test for it.

pr-m03-key.question: What is the normalized key?
pr-m03-key.why: `regexp_replace` removes everything that isn't a letter or digit, then `upper` makes it uppercase.

st-m03-tz.title: From a moment to an Amsterdam month

steps.caption: A `timestamptz` is a moment. PostgreSQL shows it in the session time zone, here UTC.
In Amsterdam that moment is already half past midnight on 1 February.
Truncating the Amsterdam time to the month gives **February**.
Truncating in UTC would give January: one payment in the wrong month.

so-m03-cast.intro: Does the conversion work, or fail?
so-m03-cast.why: A decimal comma isn't a number for PostgreSQL, and 31 February doesn't exist. '01-03-2026' does parse, but as January 3 under MDY: it works and is wrong, which is why the course uses to_date with an explicit format.

st-m04-group.title: GROUP BY: rows into groups, groups into one row each

steps.caption: `GROUP BY insurer` sorts the rows into one group per insurer.
Every row lands in exactly one group.
The aggregate turns each group into one value.
One output row per group. A column that is neither grouped nor aggregated has no single value, so PostgreSQL refuses it.

so-m04-having.why: Conditions on single rows go in WHERE; conditions on a group's aggregate go in HAVING.

se-m05-left.intro: This query should list every policy with its number of overdue invoices, including policies with none. Click the line with the mistake, then Check.

lines.text: LEFT JOIN premium_invoices i ON i.policy_id = p.policy_id

lines.error: A condition on the right table in WHERE removes the NULL rows, so the LEFT JOIN acts like an INNER JOIN. Move it into ON: … AND i.status = 'overdue'.

st-m05-fanout.title: Fan-out: how a second join doubles a total

steps.caption: One policy with two invoices: joining them gives two rows. Correct.
Now also join the policy's two payments, on the policy.
Every invoice row meets every payment row: 2 × 2 = 4 rows.
`sum(amount)` now counts each invoice twice: 43.52 instead of 21.76. No error, just a wrong number.
Fix: aggregate each side first (in a subquery or CTE), then join the totals.

dl-m05-double.scenario: Your report says the open premium is € 41,200. Last month it was € 20,600. Nothing unusual happened in the business. The meeting starts in 20 minutes.
dl-m05-double.question: What do you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Send it. The query ran without errors.
options.outcome: Exactly double is the signature of a fan-out. 'No error' doesn't mean 'correct'.

options.label: B
options.text: Count rows after each join, find the duplicating join, fix it, then send.
options.outcome: You find that the payments join doubled every invoice, and the corrected total matches last month.

options.label: C
options.outcome: Safe for today, but the report is still wrong next month. Say so, and fix the cause.

dl-m05-double.advice: When a total suddenly doubles or triples, suspect the joins first: count rows after each one.

pr-m06-notin.question: The subquery returns one NULL. How many rows does the outer query return?
pr-m06-notin.sql: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM (VALUES (1), (2)) AS v (x) WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT NULL::int);
pr-m06-notin.why: `x NOT IN (NULL)` is NULL for every x, never true. Use NOT EXISTS, which isn't fooled by NULLs.
pr-m06-notin.code: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM (VALUES (1), (2)) AS v (x) WHERE x NOT IN (SELECT NULL::int);

st-m06-cte.title: A CTE: named steps, read top to bottom

steps.caption: Each CTE is a named step: a small query with a clear job.
A later step can use an earlier one by name, like a table.
The main query combines the steps.
To debug, end the query after any step and look at it on its own.

so-m06-sets.intro: Which set operation answers the question?

items.text: All invoice numbers from two years, duplicates kept
Our invoice numbers that aren't on any statement
Policy keys that appear on both sides

so-m06-sets.why: UNION ALL stacks, EXCEPT subtracts, INTERSECT keeps what both have.

items.text: Every line must have a booking date
A file may be imported only once
A line must belong to an existing batch
line_type is premium, correction or cancellation_refund

so-m07-constraints.why: Each rule lives in the database, so no import script can forget it.

st-m07-tx.title: A transaction you can take back

steps.caption: BEGIN starts a transaction. Nothing is permanent until COMMIT.
You run an UPDATE and forget the WHERE.
Your check shows 399 rows changed instead of 1. Others don't see your changes yet.
ROLLBACK undoes everything since BEGIN. Nobody ever saw the mistake.

dl-m07-reimport.scenario: NHV sends the February statement again, 'with corrections'. Twelve lines are the same, two amounts changed.
dl-m07-reimport.question: How do you load it?

options.label: A
options.text: Import it as a new batch next to the old one.
options.outcome: Twelve lines are now in the books twice: the reconciliation reports them as suspected duplicates and the totals are wrong.

options.label: B
options.text: Import it as a new batch, then mark the first batch as replaced and reconcile only the newest version per month.
options.outcome: Both files stay as evidence, and the numbers come from one version. The content hash tells you it's a different file.

options.label: C
options.text: UPDATE the two changed amounts in the old batch by hand.
options.outcome: The numbers are right, but the database no longer matches any file the insurer sent. An auditor can't trace the change.

dl-m07-reimport.advice: Never edit imported facts in place. Keep every file as received, and decide in SQL which version counts.

steps.caption: Pass 1: a line that names our invoice is matched by **reference**, whatever the month.
Booked in February for a January invoice: a match with a **timing difference**.
Pass 2: a line without reference looks for invoices of the same policy, in its month or the month before.
Two invoices fit. The report says **ambiguous** and lists both. A person decides.

so-m08-kinds.intro: A unique pair differs. Which kind is it? (theirs − ours)

items.text: Same amount, booked one month later

so-m08-kinds.why: Rounding is at most 0.01; anything larger is an amount difference. Remember that one pair can have two kinds.

tabs.label: Team lead
tabs.text: Wants the status per insurer and month, and what needs a person.

tabs.label: Reconciler
tabs.text: Works through the list, one exception at a time.

tabs.label: Auditor
tabs.text: Wants to see that nothing was forced or lost.
points: Every row lands in exactly one bucket

then.title: The review spreadsheet
items: Reviewer name and email typed on every row
No rule for which decision counts

now.title: Tables
items: `exception_reviews`: one row per decision, with time

st-m09-append.title: Append-only history: the newest row is the current state

steps.caption: Bas records the first decision on `missing:82:-`.
A week later he records a new one. Nothing is updated: a row is added.
Anna adds her decision. The view picks the newest row with `row_number()`.
The full history stays: who decided what, when and why.

items.text: The raw CSV row, kept as evidence

so-m09-json.why: Facts you check, join or sum get types and constraints; flexible, non-financial settings and raw evidence fit JSONB.

mc-m10-abort.question: In a transaction, your third statement fails. What happens to the fourth?

options.why: No: after an error the transaction is aborted and refuses every further statement.

options.text: It's refused until you ROLLBACK (or roll back to a savepoint).
options.why: Right: nothing half-done can be committed.

options.text: The first two statements are committed automatically.
options.why: No: nothing is committed until COMMIT, and an aborted transaction can't commit.

st-m10-lost.title: A lost update, step by step

steps.caption: Both read the same version of the view.
Each changes their own copy in the browser.
Anna saves first. The row now has her change.
Bas saves the document he read **before** Anna's change. Her change is overwritten, without any error.
With `WHERE version = 1`, Bas's save would change 0 rows, and the app would tell him to reload.
The call sends a request and returns a **promise**: a result that comes later.
`await` pauses your function until the result arrives.
The result is `{ data, error }`. Check `error` first.
Only then use `data`. Without `await`, `r.data` would be undefined.

pr-m10b-float.question: What does `console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3)` print?
pr-m10b-float.why: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in binary floating point. That's why totals come from SQL, or from cents.

bd-m10b-routine.task: Put the routine for changing unfamiliar code in order.
pieces: Read it top to bottom once
Run it unchanged and look at the output
Explain why the output is now right
bd-m10b-routine.success: One change at a time, run between changes, and stop only when you can explain it.

so-m11-keys.intro: Where may each key or value go?

items.text: A VITE_ variable holding the secret key

so-m11-keys.why: Everything in the browser is public. The publishable key is designed for that; grants and RLS protect the data. The secret key and the password bypass them.

steps.caption: The browser only reads the file into text fields. No conversions here.
One request: the function runs inside one transaction.
It checks every row first and names the first bad one.
The content hash makes a repeated file a harmless 'duplicate'.
Any error rolls back the whole call. The app shows a clear result either way.

se-m12-inject.intro: This function lets the app search by kind. Click every line that makes it vulnerable to SQL injection, then Check.

lines.text: CREATE FUNCTION search(p_kind text, p_sort text) RETURNS SETOF text LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
RETURN QUERY EXECUTE 'SELECT exception_key FROM recon_exceptions WHERE kind = ''' || p_kind || ''''
lines.error: The value is glued into the SQL text. Use `WHERE kind = $1` with `USING p_kind`.
A column name from the user, unquoted and unchecked. Use `format('%I', p_sort)` and an allow-list.

st-m12-rls.title: How a policy filters Bas's query

steps.caption: Bas runs an ordinary query. He doesn't add any condition himself.
RLS adds the policy's USING condition to every row, with `auth.uid()` = Bas.
Rows where it's false are invisible: no error, they're just not there.
He sees only his own view. WITH CHECK does the same for rows he tries to write.

tabs.label: Anna
tabs.text: Team lead. Reads everything the team reads, records her own decisions, imports.

tabs.label: Bas
tabs.text: Reconciler. Same as Anna for the work itself.

tabs.label: Dana
tabs.text: Has a login but is not on the team.

tabs.label: anon
points: No grants: every request is refused

st-m13-plan.title: Reading a plan from the inside out

steps.caption: Start at the most indented line: that step runs first.
A **Filter** is checked row by row, after reading. Every row is read.
Its rows go up to the Sort.
And then to the Limit, which takes one. An index on (exception_key, reviewed_at DESC) would replace the scan, filter and sort with one index step.

so-m13-index.intro: An index exists on `big_lines (policy_key)`. Can each WHERE clause use it?
so-m13-index.why: A function on the column or a leading wildcard hides the column from the index. Equality, IN and a prefix LIKE can use it. (A prefix LIKE needs the C collation, which this course database uses, or a text_pattern_ops index.)

dl-m13-matview.scenario: The summary screen takes 4 seconds. A colleague suggests a materialized view refreshed every night.
dl-m13-matview.question: What do you do?

options.label: A
options.text: Refresh it every night, as suggested.
options.outcome: Fast, but an import at 10:00 doesn't show until tomorrow. Reconcilers decide on stale numbers.

options.label: B
options.text: Measure with EXPLAIN ANALYZE first; add the missing indexes; only then, if still slow, refresh a materialized view at the end of every import.
options.outcome: The indexes bring it to 0.3 seconds. No staleness, and no extra moving part.

options.label: C
options.text: Cache the summary in the browser for a day.
options.outcome: Every user now sees a different, possibly day-old reconciliation.

dl-m13-matview.advice: Measure, then fix the plan. Trade freshness for speed only with a refresh tied to the data changing.

modules.title: Setup and study system
modules.summary: Get a working PostgreSQL, load the Harbourline data, set up your files and learn how this course checks your work.
objectives: Run a query in the built-in editor and in the Supabase SQL editor.
Load the Harbourline dataset and confirm the 7 row counts.
Set up the course folder and save your first query in it.
Explain the course's AI rules and when you may use AI.

lessons.title: Your practice databases
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can run SQL here and in Supabase, and you know which to use when.
lessons.explain:
A database is an organised store of data. A DBMS (database management system) is the program that stores the data, answers questions about it and keeps it safe. PostgreSQL ("Postgres") is the DBMS in this course. SQL is the language you use to talk to it, and a query is one SQL statement, such as a question.

You will use three places to run SQL, one after another:

From Where What for
Now The editor in this page. PostgreSQL 18 compiled to run in a browser (PGlite) All lessons and exercises. Nothing to install
This week Supabase project sql-course (free) A persistent copy of the dataset, CSV import (Module 7)
Module 2 Supabase project harbourline-recon Your app. Never reset with the practice script
Module 10 PostgreSQL 18 on your computer + psql Two sessions at once, backups, larger data

The editor here starts empty every time you open the page. Your answers are saved in this browser, but the database itself is rebuilt from the dataset script, so you never lose anything that matters.

Set up Supabase now (10 minutes):

  1. Go to supabase.com, sign up, and create a project named sql-course in an EU region. Save the database password in a password manager.
  2. Open SQL Editor → New query. Click Copy dataset script at the top of this page, paste it in and click Run. Confirm the warning about destructive operations: the script drops and recreates only its own 7 tables.
  3. The last result shows 7 row counts. They must match the table in the example below.

Free projects pause after a week with little activity. Resume from the dashboard; your data stays.

examples.note: Run this here. It shows which PostgreSQL you are talking to. In Supabase the answer starts with PostgreSQL 17; here it says 18.7. The course marks the few features that need 18 with PG18+.
examples.sql: SELECT version();

rows: PostgreSQL 18.7 (PGlite 0.5.17) on wasm32-unknown-emscripten, compiled by emcc (Emscripten gcc/clang-like replacement + linker emulating GNU ld) 6.0.13 (e13ee988ce3d87a738dd8f3661d02223308c412a), 32-bit

lessons.title: How to study this course
lessons.goal: Afterwards you have your course folder set up and know how checkpoints and AI use work.
lessons.explain:
Your course folder. Create a folder sql-course on your computer with two subfolders:

sql-course/
  practice/   your exercise answers, one file per module: m02.sql, m03.sql ...
  app/        only for the Harbourline Recon app (from Module 2)

Copy each answer you're proud of into the module's file with a comment line above it, such as -- 2.1 exercise 3. Two dashes start a comment: text PostgreSQL ignores. This page also remembers your answers, but only in this browser.

How each lesson works. Read, run the examples, then do the exercises. Predict first: before you run a query, guess roughly what it returns. Wrong guesses teach the most. Check compares your result with the model answer, so a query that runs but returns the wrong rows is caught. Show solution only after a real attempt.

Checkpoints. Each module ends with a 10-minute quiz (no notes) and a 35-minute practical (documentation allowed). You pass a practical when its check is green and you can explain your approach in three sentences. Otherwise redo it after 2–3 days.

AI rules.

  • AI may explain concepts and error messages at any time.
  • During checkpoints, diagnostics and the final practical: documentation and your own notes only.
  • Each module contains one "review the AI" exercise: generated SQL that looks right and isn't.
  • Explaining AI-written code does not prove you can do it. Proof is a cold change: making a similar change yourself, without AI, in limited time.

modules.title: Data, tables and keys
modules.summary: What a relational database is, what one row of each table means, and how keys connect the tables.
objectives: State in one sentence what one row of each Harbourline table represents.
Identify the primary key and the business key of a table, and explain the difference.
Name the foreign keys that connect policies, customers, insurers and invoices.
Choose a data type for a new column, including numeric for money and timestamptz for moments.

lessons.title: Databases and the relational model
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can explain what a relational database is and why it beats a folder of spreadsheets for reconciliation.
lessons.explain:
A spreadsheet is one grid that anyone can type anything into. A relational database stores data in several tables, each about one kind of thing, and enforces rules on them. The relational model (Edgar Codd, 1970) says: data lives in tables of rows and columns; each column has one data type; rows are found by their values, never by position; tables are connected by matching values.

Three consequences matter for your work:

  • One fact, one place. An insurer's name is stored once in insurers; policies only store the insurer's id. Rename the insurer once and every policy shows the new name.
  • Rules are enforced. A policy can't point at an insurer that doesn't exist; an amount column can't contain the word "TBD".
  • Many people, one truth. The DBMS lets many users read and write at the same time without corrupting the data (Module 10 shows how).

Harbourline is a fictional insurance broker: it advises customers, places their policies with insurers, sends premium invoices, receives payments, and gets monthly statements from each insurer that should match its own invoices. They often don't, and that is what this course trains you to find.

examples.note: The information_schema is a built-in set of tables that describe your tables. This lists Harbourline's tables and how many columns each has. You'll learn GROUP BY in Module 4; for now just read the result.
examples.sql:
SELECT table_name, count(*) AS columns
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_schema = 'public'
GROUP BY table_name
ORDER BY table_name;

examples.note: A first look at real rows. LIMIT 5 shows only the first five.
examples.sql: SELECT * FROM policies LIMIT 5;

mistakes.text: Table and column names are case-insensitive unless quoted. "Policies" with quotes asks for a table whose name has a capital P, which doesn't exist.
mistakes.sql: SELECT * FROM "Policies";
mistakes.error: relation "Policies" does not exist

exercises.prompt: Show the first 3 rows of customers.
exercises.solution: SELECT * FROM customers LIMIT 3;

exercises.prompt: List every column of the premium_invoices table with its data type, using information_schema.columns. Show column_name and data_type, ordered by ordinal_position.
exercises.solution:
SELECT column_name, data_type
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_name = 'premium_invoices'
ORDER BY ordinal_position;

exercises.prompt: Show all rows of insurers. Which insurer sends statements quarterly instead of monthly? (Look at the result; the check only tests the query.)
exercises.solution: SELECT * FROM insurers;

exercises.prompt: Spreadsheet or database? A colleague keeps insurer names typed in every row of a policy spreadsheet. Write a query that returns the 6 insurer names exactly once each, to show why a separate table helps.
exercises.solution: SELECT name FROM insurers;

lessons.project: Read the Harbourline Recon app description in Module 2's intro. Write in app/notes.md which Harbourline tables the app reuses (insurers, policies, premium_invoices, insurer_statements) and which it leaves out (customers, payments, renewals), with one reason each.
recap: A relational database keeps each kind of thing in its own table and enforces rules.
Tables connect through matching values, so each fact is stored once.
information_schema lets you inspect any database's structure with SQL.

lessons.title: Grain and keys
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can say what one row of a table means and tell an internal id from a business key.
lessons.explain:
The grain of a table is what exactly one row represents. Get it wrong and every count and total after it is wrong. Write it as a sentence:

Table One row is…
insurers one insurance company
customers one customer record. Not always one person: duplicates exist
policies one insurance contract, with one customer and one insurer
renewals one yearly renewal of one policy
premium_invoices one invoice for one policy and one period (a month, quarter or year)
payments one money transfer received. One invoice can have several
insurer_statements one line on an insurer's monthly statement, as the insurer wrote it

A primary key (PK) is a column whose value is unique and never empty, so it identifies exactly one row. Harbourline uses internal ids: numbers like policy_id = 17 that the database invents and that mean nothing outside it.

A business key is how people outside the database identify the thing: policy_number = 'NHV-123456', invoice_number = 'INV-2025-00001'. Business keys are what you match on when comparing with another system, because the insurer has never heard of your policy_id.

A foreign key (FK) is a column that points at another table's primary key: policies.insurer_id points at insurers.insurer_id. The database refuses a value that has no match. The insurer statements have no foreign key to your policies: they come from outside, with the insurer's own spelling of the policy number. That is why reconciliation is hard.

examples.note: One policy, with its internal id and business key side by side.
The insurer writes policy numbers its own way. These statement lines all belong to policies in your table, but none would match a plain equality test.
examples.sql:
SELECT policy_number
FROM insurer_statements
WHERE policy_number NOT LIKE '___-______'
LIMIT 8;

mistakes.text: A foreign key protects you: the database refuses a policy for insurer 99, which doesn't exist. This statement fails, and nothing is saved.
mistakes.sql:
INSERT INTO policies (policy_number, customer_id, insurer_id, product, start_date, annual_premium, payment_frequency, status)
VALUES ('XXX-000001', 1, 99, 'car', '2026-01-01', 500, 'monthly', 'active');
mistakes.error: insert or update on table "policies" violates foreign key constraint "policies_insurer_id_fkey"

mistakes.text: A primary key must be unique. Inserting a second insurer with insurer_id = 1 fails.
mistakes.sql:
INSERT INTO insurers (insurer_id, code, name, country, time_zone, statement_cycle)
VALUES (1, 'DUP', 'Duplicate Ltd', 'NL', 'Europe/Amsterdam', 'monthly');
mistakes.error: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "insurers_pkey"

exercises.prompt: Show the invoice_id, invoice_number and policy_id of the invoice with invoice_id = 10. Which column is the business key?
exercises.solution: SELECT invoice_id, invoice_number, policy_id FROM premium_invoices WHERE invoice_id = 10;

exercises.prompt: Show the statement lines (line_id, policy_number, amount) whose invoice_reference is empty (IS NULL). These lines can only be matched on policy number and month. Show the first 10 by line_id.
exercises.hint: WHERE invoice_reference IS NULL ORDER BY line_id LIMIT 10
exercises.solution:
SELECT line_id, policy_number, amount
FROM insurer_statements
WHERE invoice_reference IS NULL
ORDER BY line_id
LIMIT 10;

exercises.prompt: Find the customers named Daan Vos, however the name is capitalised. Use lower(full_name) = 'daan vos'. Show customer_id, full_name, email, birth_date. Are they the same person?
Review the AI. Asked "how many policies does Harbourline have?", an AI counted rows in premium_invoices. Write the right query.

lessons.project: In app/notes.md, write the grain sentence for each table the app reuses, plus its primary key and business key.
recap: Grain: say what one row means before counting or summing anything.
Internal ids identify rows inside the database; business keys identify things in the real world and are what you match on.
Foreign keys stop rows from pointing at nothing; outside data such as statements has none.

lessons.title: Data types
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can choose the right type for a column and explain why money is never a float.
lessons.explain:
Every column has one data type, which decides what values it accepts and how they compare and calculate.

Type Use for Harbourline example
integer whole numbers, counts, ids policy_id
numeric(12,2) money: exact decimals, 2 digits after the point amount, annual_premium
text any text policy_number, notes
date a calendar day, no time due_date, period_start
timestamptz an exact moment in time paid_at, created_at
uuid a random 128-bit id, safe to show in URLs customers.public_id
boolean true / false none yet

Money is never real/double precision. Those are binary floating-point types: they store 0.1 approximately, and errors add up over thousands of rows. numeric stores the decimal digits exactly.

timestamptz stores a moment, not a time zone. PostgreSQL converts the input to UTC and forgets the original offset; it shows the value in your session's TimeZone setting. A payment made at 23:30 in Amsterdam on 31 January is 22:30 UTC on 31 January, but 06:30 on 1 February in Singapore. Module 3 deals with this properly.

uuid: PostgreSQL 13+ generates random ones with gen_random_uuid(). PG18+ adds uuidv7(), time-ordered UUIDs that index better; it does not exist on Supabase's PostgreSQL 17.

examples.note: Floating point drifts; numeric doesn't. Ten times 0.1 should be exactly 1.
examples.sql:
SELECT sum(0.1::double precision) AS float_sum,
       sum(0.1::numeric)          AS numeric_sum,
       sum(0.1::double precision) = 1 AS float_is_one
FROM generate_series(1, 10);

examples.note: The same moment shown in three time zones. The stored value doesn't change; only the display does.
examples.sql:
SELECT ts AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'              AS utc,
       ts AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam' AS amsterdam,
       ts AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Singapore'   AS singapore
FROM (SELECT timestamptz '2026-01-31 23:30:00+01' AS ts) AS t;

mistakes.text: A type protects the column: text that isn't a number can't go into a numeric. The error names the bad value.
mistakes.sql: SELECT 'TBD'::numeric;
mistakes.error: invalid input syntax for type numeric: "TBD"

mistakes.text: numeric(12,2) rounds extra decimals instead of failing, so 12.345 becomes 12.35. Know when your input carries more precision than the column. This one works, which is the trap.
mistakes.sql: SELECT 12.345::numeric(12,2);

exercises.prompt: Show amount and commission of invoice 1, and their sum as total. Because both are numeric, the sum is exact.
exercises.solution: SELECT amount, commission, amount + commission AS total FROM premium_invoices WHERE invoice_id = 1;

exercises.prompt: Show the data_type of paid_at in payments and of due_date in premium_invoices, using information_schema.columns.
exercises.solution:
SELECT table_name, column_name, data_type
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE (table_name = 'payments' AND column_name = 'paid_at')
   OR (table_name = 'premium_invoices' AND column_name = 'due_date');

exercises.prompt: Generate one random UUID with gen_random_uuid() in a column named new_id. (Your value will differ from the solution; the check looks at the shape only.)
exercises.solution: SELECT gen_random_uuid() AS new_id;

exercises.prompt: Show payment 1's paid_at as it would appear in Amsterdam, in a column paid_at_amsterdam.
exercises.solution: SELECT paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam' AS paid_at_amsterdam FROM payments WHERE payment_id = 1;

recap: The data type decides what a column accepts and how it calculates.
Money is numeric; moments are timestamptz, which stores the instant, not the zone.
uuidv7() is PG18+; gen_random_uuid() works everywhere.

modules.intro: Before writing queries you need a picture of the data. This module is about reading a database, not yet about clever SQL.

modules.title: Querying one table
modules.summary: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, DISTINCT, LIKE/ILIKE, CASE, NULL and COALESCE on one table, plus your app project starts.
objectives: Write a query that returns exactly the rows and columns a business question asks for.
Write a query that sorts and limits results, such as the 10 largest open invoices.
Write a case-insensitive pattern search with ILIKE.
Predict the result of a WHERE condition on a column that contains NULL.
Label rows with a CASE expression and replace missing values with COALESCE.

lessons.title: SELECT, columns and expressions
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can choose columns, rename them and calculate new ones.
lessons.explain:
SELECT is the question; FROM names the table it asks. The shape is always:

SELECT column1, column2, expression AS new_name
FROM table_name;
  • * means all columns. Fine for exploring, but name your columns in anything you keep: queries with * break or change when someone adds a column.
  • An expression calculates a value per row: amount - commission, annual_premium / 12.
  • AS gives a column an alias, a name for the result. Use lowercase with underscores; if you need spaces or capitals, use double quotes: AS "Net amount".
  • SQL keywords are case-insensitive. This course writes them in capitals so you can see the structure.

The order of the result rows is not guaranteed without ORDER BY (lesson 2.3). Two runs can return the same rows in different orders.

examples.note: Invoice amounts with the part Harbourline keeps (commission) and the part it passes to the insurer (net).
A monthly equivalent of each yearly premium, rounded to cents with round(value, 2).

mistakes.text: An alias with a space needs double quotes. Without them PostgreSQL reads net as the alias and amount as an unexpected word.
mistakes.sql: SELECT amount - commission AS net amount FROM premium_invoices;
mistakes.error: syntax error at or near "amount"

mistakes.text: Single quotes make text, double quotes make names. 'amount' is the literal word "amount", repeated on every row. This runs, which is the danger; the result is useless.
mistakes.sql: SELECT 'amount' FROM premium_invoices WHERE invoice_id <= 3;

exercises.prompt: Show policy_number, product and annual_premium for all policies.
exercises.solution: SELECT policy_number, product, annual_premium FROM policies;

exercises.prompt: For every invoice show invoice_number, amount and the commission as a percentage of the amount, rounded to 1 decimal, in a column called commission_pct.
exercises.solution:
SELECT invoice_number, amount, round(commission / amount * 100, 1) AS commission_pct
FROM premium_invoices;

exercises.prompt: Show each policy's policy_number and its premium after a 3% increase, rounded to cents, as premium_next_year.
exercises.solution: SELECT policy_number, round(annual_premium * 1.03, 2) AS premium_next_year FROM policies;

exercises.prompt: Show each statement line's line_id and amount, plus the insurer's commission as a share of the amount (commission / amount) named share, rounded to 3 decimals. Only lines with line_type = 'premium'.
Review the AI. Asked for "invoice numbers with the amount after commission", an AI wrote this. It runs. What's wrong? Fix it.
exercises.solution: SELECT invoice_number, amount - commission AS net FROM premium_invoices;
exercises.starter: SELECT invoice_number, 'amount - commission' AS net FROM premium_invoices;

lessons.project: App screen Browse invoices needs: invoice number, policy id, period start and end, amount and status. Write that query (all invoices) and save it as app/queries/browse_invoices.sql. Test it here, then run it in harbourline-recon: it must return 399 rows there too.
recap: SELECT columns FROM table; name your columns instead of * in anything you keep.
Expressions calculate per row; AS names the result.
Single quotes are text, double quotes are names.

lessons.title: Filtering with WHERE
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can select exactly the rows a question asks for.
lessons.explain:
WHERE keeps only the rows for which a condition is true.

Operator Meaning Example
=, <> equal, not equal status = 'open'
<, <=, >, >= compare numbers, dates, text amount > 500
BETWEEN a AND b from a to b, both included period_start BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-03-31'
IN (…) equals one of a list status IN ('open', 'overdue')
AND, OR, NOT combine conditions insurer_id = 1 AND amount > 100

AND binds more tightly than OR, just like × before + in arithmetic. a OR b AND c means a OR (b AND c). Use brackets whenever you mix them.

Text comparisons are exact: 'NL' is not 'nl' and not 'NL ' (trailing space). Dates are written as text in ISO format 'YYYY-MM-DD' and PostgreSQL converts them.

examples.note: Overdue invoices above €200.
Invoices for periods starting in the first quarter of 2026. BETWEEN includes both ends.
Why brackets matter: these two look alike and return different counts.

mistakes.text: Text values need single quotes. Without them PostgreSQL thinks open is a column name.
mistakes.sql: SELECT * FROM premium_invoices WHERE status = open;
mistakes.error: column "open" does not exist

mistakes.text: Exact comparison misses messy data. This finds customers whose country is exactly NL, silently skipping nl, NL and Netherlands. No error: compare the count with the total later in Module 3.
mistakes.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM customers WHERE country = 'NL';

exercises.prompt: Show invoice_number, amount and status of all invoices with status partially_paid.
exercises.solution: SELECT invoice_number, amount, status FROM premium_invoices WHERE status = 'partially_paid';

exercises.prompt: Show the policy_number and annual_premium of active car policies with an annual premium of at least €1,000.
exercises.solution:
SELECT policy_number, annual_premium FROM policies
WHERE status = 'active' AND product = 'car' AND annual_premium >= 1000;

exercises.prompt: Count the statement lines of insurers 1, 3 and 5 (use IN), in a column named lines.
exercises.solution: SELECT count(*) AS lines FROM insurer_statements WHERE insurer_id IN (1, 3, 5);

exercises.prompt: Show all payments (payment_id, amount, method) that were not made by sepa_direct_debit and are larger than €300.
exercises.solution: SELECT payment_id, amount, method FROM payments WHERE method <> 'sepa_direct_debit' AND amount > 300;

exercises.prompt: Show statement lines (line_id, amount, line_type) that are either corrections or cancellation refunds, booked in 2026. Watch the brackets.
exercises.solution:
SELECT line_id, amount, line_type FROM insurer_statements
WHERE (line_type = 'correction' OR line_type = 'cancellation_refund') AND booking_date >= '2026-01-01';

exercises.prompt: Review the AI. "Open or overdue invoices above €500" became the query below. It runs, but returns the wrong rows. Fix the logic so the €500 limit applies to both statuses.
exercises.solution:
SELECT invoice_number, amount, status FROM premium_invoices
WHERE (status = 'open' OR status = 'overdue') AND amount > 500;
exercises.starter:
SELECT invoice_number, amount, status FROM premium_invoices
WHERE status = 'open' OR status = 'overdue' AND amount > 500;

lessons.project: Extend browse_invoices.sql into browse_invoices_filtered.sql: same columns, only invoices of policy 12 with status open or overdue. Later the app will pass the policy and statuses in as parameters.
recap: WHERE keeps rows where the condition is true.
BETWEEN includes both ends; IN tests a list.
Brackets whenever you mix AND and OR.

lessons.title: Sorting, limiting, DISTINCT
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can sort results, take the top N and list unique values.
lessons.explain:
• ORDER BY col sorts ascending; add DESC for descending. Several columns: ORDER BY insurer_id, amount DESC sorts by insurer, then by amount within each insurer.
  • LIMIT n keeps the first n rows after sorting. Without ORDER BY, "the first 10" means "any 10".
  • OFFSET n skips n rows: page 2 of 20 rows is LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20. This is how app screens page through long lists.
  • DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows. SELECT DISTINCT a, b is distinct on the combination of a and b.
  • When sort values tie, the order among the tied rows is not guaranteed. Add a unique column as the last sort key (ORDER BY amount DESC, invoice_id) to make results stable, which matters for paging.

examples.note: The five largest open invoices.
examples.sql:
SELECT invoice_number, amount, due_date
FROM premium_invoices
WHERE status = 'open'
ORDER BY amount DESC, invoice_id
LIMIT 5;

examples.note: Which payment methods exist? DISTINCT lists each once.
examples.sql: SELECT DISTINCT method FROM payments ORDER BY method;

examples.note: Page 2 of the browse screen, 10 rows per page.
examples.sql:
SELECT invoice_id, invoice_number, amount
FROM premium_invoices
ORDER BY invoice_id
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10;

mistakes.text: ORDER BY comes after WHERE. Clauses have a fixed order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
mistakes.sql: SELECT invoice_number FROM premium_invoices ORDER BY amount WHERE status = 'open';
mistakes.error: syntax error at or near "WHERE"

exercises.prompt: Show the 10 most expensive policies (policy_number, annual_premium), highest first. Break ties with policy_id.
exercises.solution: SELECT policy_number, annual_premium FROM policies ORDER BY annual_premium DESC, policy_id LIMIT 10;

exercises.prompt: List each distinct product in policies, alphabetically.
exercises.solution: SELECT DISTINCT product FROM policies ORDER BY product;

exercises.prompt: List the distinct combinations of insurer_id and line_type in the statements, ordered by insurer then line type.
exercises.solution: SELECT DISTINCT insurer_id, line_type FROM insurer_statements ORDER BY insurer_id, line_type;

exercises.prompt: Show the 3 earliest payments (payment_id, paid_at, amount).
exercises.solution: SELECT payment_id, paid_at, amount FROM payments ORDER BY paid_at, payment_id LIMIT 3;

exercises.prompt: Page 3 of the statement lines of insurer 2, 15 per page, ordered by line_id. Show line_id, policy_number, amount.
exercises.solution:
SELECT line_id, policy_number, amount FROM insurer_statements
WHERE insurer_id = 2 ORDER BY line_id LIMIT 15 OFFSET 30;

lessons.project: Add stable sorting and paging to browse_invoices.sql: newest period_start first, then invoice_id, 25 rows per page. Write page 1 and page 2.
recap: ORDER BY sorts; add a unique last key for stable results.
LIMIT/OFFSET give top-N and paging, only meaningful after sorting.
DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows.

lessons.title: Patterns and CASE
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can search text by pattern and label rows with CASE.
lessons.explain:
LIKE matches text against a pattern: % is "any number of characters", _ is "exactly one character". LIKE is case-sensitive; ILIKE (a PostgreSQL extra) ignores case.

Pattern Matches
'NHV-%' starts with NHV-
'%vries%' contains vries
'___-______' exactly 3 characters, a dash, 6 characters

CASE gives a value depending on conditions, checked top to bottom; the first true one wins:

CASE WHEN amount >= 1000 THEN 'large'
     WHEN amount >= 100  THEN 'medium'
     ELSE 'small' END

Without ELSE, rows that match nothing get NULL.

examples.note: Customers whose name contains "vries" in any capitalisation.
examples.sql: SELECT customer_id, full_name FROM customers WHERE full_name ILIKE '%vries%';

examples.note: Statement lines whose policy number is not in Harbourline's own format: lower case, no dash, spaces. These are why reconciliation needs cleaning (Module 3).
examples.sql:
SELECT line_id, policy_number
FROM insurer_statements
WHERE policy_number NOT LIKE '___-______'
ORDER BY line_id
LIMIT 10;

examples.note: Size labels for invoices.
examples.sql:
SELECT invoice_number, amount,
       CASE WHEN amount >= 1000 THEN 'large'
            WHEN amount >= 100  THEN 'medium'
            ELSE 'small' END AS size
FROM premium_invoices
ORDER BY invoice_id
LIMIT 8;

mistakes.text: CASE checks top to bottom. Here the first condition catches everything above 100, so "large" never appears. No error, just wrong labels.
mistakes.sql:
SELECT amount, CASE WHEN amount >= 100 THEN 'medium' WHEN amount >= 1000 THEN 'large' ELSE 'small' END
FROM premium_invoices;

mistakes.text: LIKE is case-sensitive, so this misses NHV… written in capitals.
mistakes.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM insurer_statements WHERE policy_number LIKE 'nhv%';

exercises.prompt: Find all customers whose email ends with @gmail.com, ignoring case. Show customer_id and email.
exercises.solution: SELECT customer_id, email FROM customers WHERE email ILIKE '%@gmail.com';

exercises.prompt: Find policies whose notes mention "premium" in any capitalisation. Show policy_number and notes.
exercises.solution: SELECT policy_number, notes FROM policies WHERE notes ILIKE '%premium%';

exercises.prompt: Label each policy by payment frequency: monthly → 12 invoices, quarterly → 4 invoices, annual → 1 invoice. Show policy_number, payment_frequency and the label as invoices_per_year.
Count statement lines whose policy number contains a space, in a column with_space.
exercises.solution: SELECT count(*) AS with_space FROM insurer_statements WHERE policy_number LIKE '% %';

exercises.prompt: Show each invoice's invoice_number, status and a column needs_action that is yes for open, overdue and partially_paid, otherwise no.

lessons.project: For the app's statement-lines screen, write browse_statement_lines.sql: line id, insurer id, statement month, policy number as written, amount, line type, and a format_ok column that is yes when the policy number matches '___-______', else no. Test here on insurer_statements.
recap: % any characters, _ one character; ILIKE ignores case.
CASE checks conditions top to bottom; first match wins; add ELSE.
Pattern checks reveal messy keys before you try to match on them.

lessons.title: NULL, three-valued logic and COALESCE
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can predict what NULL does to conditions and totals, and handle it deliberately.
lessons.explain:
NULL means unknown or missing. It is not zero and not empty text. Any comparison with NULL gives NULL (unknown), not true or false. That is three-valued logic: true, false, unknown. WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true, so unknown rows silently disappear.

  • email = NULL is never true. Use email IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.
  • email <> 'x@y.nl' skips rows where email is NULL: unknown is not true.
  • NOT IN (…) with a NULL inside the list returns no rows at all. One of the most common silent bugs.
  • count(*) counts rows; count(email) counts non-NULL emails.
  • COALESCE(a, b, …) returns the first non-NULL argument: COALESCE(email, 'no email').
  • IS DISTINCT FROM is a NULL-safe "not equal": NULL vs NULL counts as equal, NULL vs a value counts as different. You will use it to compare two sources.

examples.note: Count customers with and without an email. Notice count(email) skips NULLs.
examples.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS customers, count(email) AS with_email, count(*) - count(email) AS without_email
FROM customers;

examples.note: NULL comparisons in action: the second and third columns are NULL (unknown), not true or false.
examples.sql: SELECT 1 = 1 AS a, NULL = NULL AS b, NULL <> 1 AS c, NULL IS NULL AS d, NULL IS DISTINCT FROM 1 AS e;

examples.note: Show a readable reference for statement lines whose invoice reference is missing.
examples.sql:
SELECT line_id, COALESCE(invoice_reference, '(no reference)') AS reference
FROM insurer_statements
ORDER BY line_id
LIMIT 6;

mistakes.text: = NULL is never true, so this returns 0 rows without any error. Use IS NULL.
mistakes.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM customers WHERE email = NULL;

mistakes.text: The NOT IN trap: because the subquery list contains a NULL invoice id, "not in the list" is unknown for every invoice, and the result is empty.
mistakes.sql:
SELECT count(*) FROM premium_invoices
WHERE invoice_id NOT IN (SELECT invoice_id FROM payments);

exercises.prompt: Show customer_id and full_name of customers without a phone number.
exercises.solution: SELECT customer_id, full_name FROM customers WHERE phone IS NULL;

exercises.prompt: Show every policy's policy_number and end_date, with 'open-ended' instead of NULL in a column named ends. Hint: cast the date to text first: end_date::text.
exercises.solution: SELECT policy_number, end_date, COALESCE(end_date::text, 'open-ended') AS ends FROM policies;

exercises.prompt: How many payments are not linked to an invoice? Column name unlinked.
exercises.solution: SELECT count(*) AS unlinked FROM payments WHERE invoice_id IS NULL;

exercises.prompt: Predict, then write: how many customers do not have the email info@bakkerijhetgou.nl, counting customers without an email as "not having it"? Use IS DISTINCT FROM. Column others.
exercises.solution: SELECT count(*) AS others FROM customers WHERE email IS DISTINCT FROM 'info@bakkerijhetgou.nl';

exercises.prompt: Count customers with a birth date, without one, and in total, in one row: columns with_bd, without_bd, total.
exercises.solution: SELECT count(birth_date) AS with_bd, count(*) - count(birth_date) AS without_bd, count(*) AS total FROM customers;

exercises.prompt: Review the AI. "Invoices with no payment at all" was written as below and returns 0. Rewrite it so NULL payment rows are excluded from the list: add WHERE invoice_id IS NOT NULL inside the subquery.
exercises.solution: SELECT count(*) FROM premium_invoices WHERE invoice_id NOT IN (SELECT invoice_id FROM payments WHERE invoice_id IS NOT NULL);
exercises.starter: SELECT count(*) FROM premium_invoices WHERE invoice_id NOT IN (SELECT invoice_id FROM payments);

lessons.project: In browse_statement_lines.sql, show COALESCE(invoice_reference, '—') so the screen never shows an empty cell, and add a filter for lines without a reference. Note in app/notes.md why the app must never treat a missing reference as "no match".
recap: NULL is unknown; comparisons with it are unknown, and WHERE drops unknown rows.
IS NULL, IS DISTINCT FROM and COALESCE handle it deliberately.
count(column) skips NULLs; NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns nothing.

quiz.text: Which query returns the 10 largest invoices reliably?

options.text: SELECT * FROM premium_invoices LIMIT 10 ORDER BY amount DESC;
SELECT * FROM premium_invoices ORDER BY amount DESC, invoice_id LIMIT 10;

quiz.explain: LIMIT needs ORDER BY first; the extra key makes ties stable. Option 2 is a syntax error.

quiz.text:
Predict the result.

SELECT count(*) FROM customers WHERE email <> 'nobody@example.com';
quiz.answer: The number of customers **with** an email (88), not all 102. Rows with NULL email give "unknown" and are dropped.
quiz.explain: Use IS DISTINCT FROM when NULLs should count as "different".
quiz.predictSql: SELECT count(*) FROM customers WHERE email <> 'nobody@example.com';

quiz.text: WHERE status = 'open' OR status = 'overdue' AND amount > 500 means:
quiz.explain: AND binds before OR.

quiz.text: What does COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 'x', 'y') return?
quiz.explain: The first non-NULL argument.

quiz.text:
Predict the number of rows.

SELECT DISTINCT payment_frequency FROM policies;
quiz.explain: DISTINCT lists each value once.

quiz.text: Show the invoice_number and amount of the 5 smallest overdue invoices, smallest first, ties broken by invoice_id.
quiz.solution: SELECT invoice_number, amount FROM premium_invoices WHERE status = 'overdue' ORDER BY amount, invoice_id LIMIT 5;

quiz.text: Count customers whose country is written in any form of the Netherlands that starts with nl ignoring case and spaces at the end: use ILIKE 'nl%'. Column nl_like.
quiz.solution: SELECT count(*) AS nl_like FROM customers WHERE country ILIKE 'nl%';

practical.prompt: Harbourline's team lead asks: "Which active policies with insurer 1 or 3 have a premium of at least €500 and no notes? Show the policy number, product, premium, and a column band that says top for premiums of €1,500 or more and standard otherwise. Most expensive first." Write the query. Then explain in three sentences how you checked it returns the right rows.
practical.solution:
SELECT policy_number, product, annual_premium,
       CASE WHEN annual_premium >= 1500 THEN 'top' ELSE 'standard' END AS band
FROM policies
WHERE status = 'active' AND insurer_id IN (1, 3) AND annual_premium >= 500 AND notes IS NULL
ORDER BY annual_premium DESC, policy_id;

modules.intro:
Your app project starts here: Harbourline Recon

From this module on you also build a small internal app for Harbourline's reconciliation team. It lets staff browse invoices and insurer statement lines, see exceptions (missing rows, amount differences, suspected duplicates, timing differences, ambiguous matches), record a review decision against an exception, and summarize by insurer and month. Review decisions never change the financial facts.

The app lives in its own Supabase project, so resetting practice data can never touch it. Do this once now (10 minutes):

  1. In Supabase, create a second project named harbourline-recon (EU region). The free plan allows two active projects.
  2. Open its SQL Editor, click the button below, paste and run. You get the app's first three tables (insurers, policies, premium_invoices) with a frozen copy of the Harbourline data: 6, 172 and 399 rows.
  3. Save the same script as app/migrations/0000_starter.sql in your course folder.

Those three tables are identical to the practice tables here, so the app queries you write in this module can be tested in this page and then saved for the app.

modules.title: Functions, dates and time zones
modules.summary: Clean messy text, calculate with dates and intervals, place moments in the right month and time zone, and convert between types.
objectives: Write a query that normalizes policy numbers like 'nhv 123456' to one comparable key.
Calculate due-date gaps, ages and month starts with date functions.
Assign each payment to a month in a stated time zone and explain why the month can differ.
Convert text to numbers and dates, and read the error when a conversion fails.

lessons.title: Text and number functions
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can clean text and round numbers so that values from two sources become comparable.
lessons.explain:
A function takes values and returns a new one: upper('nhv') returns 'NHV'. Functions never change the stored data; they change what the query returns.

Function Does Example → result
trim(s) removes spaces at both ends trim(' NL ') → 'NL'
upper(s), lower(s) change case upper('nhv-1') → 'NHV-1'
replace(s, from, to) replaces every occurrence replace('NHV 1', ' ', '-') → 'NHV-1'
regexp_replace(s, pattern, to, 'g') replaces by regular expression (a pattern language) regexp_replace('nh v-1', '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g') → 'nhv1'
length(s) number of characters length('NL ') → 3
a || b joins text 'INV' || '-1' → 'INV-1'
split_part(s, sep, n) n-th piece split_part('INV-2025-00001', '-', 2) → '2025'
round(x, 2), abs(x) rounding, absolute value abs(-2.25) → 2.25

[^A-Za-z0-9] means "any character that is not a letter or digit"; the 'g' flag means "every occurrence", not just the first.

A normalized key is a cleaned version of a business key, used only for matching: remove everything that isn't a letter or digit, then upper-case. NHV-123456, nhv-123456, NHV 123456 and NHV-123456 all become NHV123456. Keep the original column too: you need it as evidence.

examples.note: Four spellings, one key.
examples.sql:
SELECT raw, upper(regexp_replace(raw, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) AS policy_key
FROM (VALUES ('NHV-123456'), ('nhv-123456'), ('NHV 123456'), (' NHV-123456 ')) AS t(raw);

examples.note: The country column cleaned: trim + upper, then a CASE for the long names.
examples.sql:
SELECT country AS raw,
       CASE upper(trim(country)) WHEN 'NETHERLANDS' THEN 'NL' WHEN 'BELGIUM' THEN 'BE' WHEN 'UK' THEN 'GB' WHEN 'USA' THEN 'US'
            ELSE upper(trim(country)) END AS country_code
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id <= 8;

examples.note: Amount differences as absolute values: a difference of −2.25 and +2.25 are equally large.
examples.sql:
SELECT line_id, amount, abs(amount - round(amount)) AS cents_part
FROM insurer_statements
ORDER BY line_id
LIMIT 5;

mistakes.text: Cleaning only one side doesn't help: here the statement side is cleaned but the comparison value isn't, so nothing matches.
mistakes.sql:
SELECT count(*) FROM insurer_statements
WHERE upper(regexp_replace(policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) = 'NHV-152244';

mistakes.text: replace is literal and case-sensitive: removing '-' leaves spaces and lowercase. Regular expressions handle all variants in one go.

exercises.prompt: Show each customer's customer_id, full_name and a cleaned name clean_name: spaces trimmed and in lower case.
exercises.solution: SELECT customer_id, full_name, lower(trim(full_name)) AS clean_name FROM customers;

exercises.prompt: Show every statement line's line_id, policy_number and its normalized key as policy_key.
exercises.solution:
SELECT line_id, policy_number, upper(regexp_replace(policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) AS policy_key
FROM insurer_statements;

exercises.prompt: Show the year part of every invoice_number (the piece between the first and second dash) as invoice_year, with the invoice number. Use split_part.
exercises.solution: SELECT invoice_number, split_part(invoice_number, '-', 2) AS invoice_year FROM premium_invoices;

exercises.prompt: How many distinct normalized countries are there after upper(trim(country))? Column countries. (The long names still count separately.)
exercises.solution: SELECT count(DISTINCT upper(trim(country))) AS countries FROM customers;

exercises.prompt: Payment references are typed by people: INV-2025-00012, inv-2025-00012, INV-2025-00012, Invoice INV-2025-00012. Show payment_id, reference and a cleaned ref_key: upper-cased, with the word INVOICE and all spaces removed. Only payments with a reference.
exercises.solution:
SELECT payment_id, reference, replace(replace(upper(reference), 'INVOICE', ''), ' ', '') AS ref_key
FROM payments WHERE reference IS NOT NULL;

lessons.project: Save app/queries/policy_key.sql: the normalized-key expression applied to policies.policy_number. In Module 7 it becomes a stored column on imported statement lines.
recap: Functions change what a query returns, never the stored data.
A normalized key (letters and digits only, upper case) makes differently written keys comparable.
Keep the original value next to the cleaned one as evidence.

lessons.title: Dates, intervals and time zones
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can calculate with dates and decide which month a moment belongs to.
lessons.explain:
Dates (date) subtract to a number of days: due_date - invoice_date → 14. Add an interval (a length of time) to move them: date '2026-01-31' + interval '1 month' → 2026-02-28.

Function Does Example → result
date_trunc('month', x) first moment of x's month 2026-02-14 → 2026-02-01 00:00
extract(year FROM x) one part as a number extract(month FROM date '2026-02-14') → 2
age(a, b) years-months-days between age('2026-03-31', '1990-05-10') → 35 years 10 mons 21 days
x AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam' the local clock time of a timestamptz in that zone see below

The dataset's "today" is 31 March 2026. Use date '2026-03-31' instead of current_date so your answers match the model answers.

Which month is a payment in? A timestamptz is a moment. Its month depends on the clock you read it from. Harbourline books in Amsterdam time, so always convert first:

date_trunc('month', paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam')

A payment at 2025-12-31 23:30 UTC is 2026-01-01 00:30 in Amsterdam: January, not December. This page and Supabase both run in UTC by default, so without the conversion you'd book it in the wrong month. Always state the time zone of a monthly report.

examples.note: Days between invoice date and due date, and how many days each due date is before "today".
examples.sql:
SELECT invoice_number, due_date - invoice_date AS payment_term_days,
       date '2026-03-31' - due_date AS days_since_due
FROM premium_invoices
WHERE status = 'overdue'
ORDER BY days_since_due DESC
LIMIT 5;

examples.note: Payments whose month is different in UTC and in Amsterdam: the time-zone trap, in the data.
examples.sql:
SELECT payment_id, paid_at,
       date_trunc('month', paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS month_utc,
       date_trunc('month', paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam')::date AS month_amsterdam
FROM payments
WHERE date_trunc('month', paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') <> date_trunc('month', paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam');

examples.note: Month arithmetic is calendar-aware: one month after 31 January is the last day of February.

mistakes.text: Comparing a timestamptz to a date treats the date as midnight in the session time zone (UTC here). A payment at 23:30 Amsterdam time on 31 December is counted in January's UTC range, or the other way round. Always convert explicitly.
mistakes.sql: SELECT count(*) AS dec_by_utc FROM payments WHERE paid_at >= '2025-12-01' AND paid_at < '2026-01-01';

mistakes.text: extract returns a number, so comparing with text needs care; and BETWEEN on timestamps misses the last day's afternoon: paid_at BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-01-31' stops at 31 January 00:00. Use >= start AND < next start.

exercises.prompt: Show each customer's customer_id, birth_date and their age in whole years on 31 March 2026 as age_years. Only customers with a birth date. Use extract(year FROM age(date '2026-03-31', birth_date)).
exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id, birth_date, extract(year FROM age(date '2026-03-31', birth_date)) AS age_years
FROM customers WHERE birth_date IS NOT NULL;

exercises.prompt: For every payment show payment_id and the month it belongs to in Amsterdam time as a date, named booking_month.
exercises.solution: SELECT payment_id, date_trunc('month', paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam')::date AS booking_month FROM payments;

exercises.prompt: Count payments made in January 2026, Amsterdam time, in a column jan_2026. Use a half-open range on the converted time.
exercises.solution:
SELECT count(*) AS jan_2026 FROM payments
WHERE paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam' >= '2026-01-01' AND paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam' < '2026-02-01';

exercises.prompt: Show the invoices that were paid late: compare the Amsterdam date of each linked payment with the invoice's due_date. Show payment_id, invoice_id, due_date, the payment date as paid_on and days_late, only where days_late > 0. You need both tables; use the starter, which joins them (joins come in Module 5).
exercises.solution:
SELECT p.payment_id, i.invoice_id, i.due_date,
       (p.paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam')::date AS paid_on,
       (p.paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam')::date - i.due_date AS days_late
FROM payments p JOIN premium_invoices i ON i.invoice_id = p.invoice_id
WHERE (p.paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam')::date - i.due_date > 0;
exercises.starter:
SELECT p.payment_id, i.invoice_id, i.due_date
FROM payments p JOIN premium_invoices i ON i.invoice_id = p.invoice_id;

exercises.prompt: Review the AI. A monthly payments report for December 2025 used the query below. Explain what's wrong (time zone and range), then fix it to count Amsterdam-time December payments.
exercises.solution:
SELECT count(*) FROM payments
WHERE paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam' >= '2025-12-01' AND paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam' < '2026-01-01';
exercises.starter: SELECT count(*) FROM payments WHERE paid_at BETWEEN '2025-12-01' AND '2025-12-31';

lessons.project: Write in app/notes.md: "All monthly figures in Harbourline Recon are in Europe/Amsterdam time." Then save app/queries/booking_month.sql with the month expression for a timestamptz column.
recap: Dates subtract to days; intervals move dates by calendar months.
A timestamptz belongs to a month only once you choose a time zone: convert with AT TIME ZONE.
Use half-open ranges (>= start AND < next start) for periods.

lessons.title: Casting and formatting
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can convert values between types and format them for reports.
lessons.explain:
Casting converts a value to another type: '12.50'::numeric or CAST('12.50' AS numeric). Imported data often arrives as text, so you cast it before calculating. A failed cast stops the whole query with an error naming the bad value; that's good, because a silent wrong number is worse.

Need Use Example → result
text → number ::numeric '1250.00'::numeric → 1250.00
text → date ::date or to_date(s, 'DD-MM-YYYY') to_date('31-03-2026', 'DD-MM-YYYY') → 2026-03-31
Dutch amount → number replace(replace(s, '.', ''), ',', '.')::numeric '1.250,00' → 1250.00
number → formatted text to_char(x, 'FM999G990D00') to_char(1250, 'FM999G990D00') → 1,250.00
empty text → NULL NULLIF(s, '') NULLIF('', '') → NULL

to_char formatting is for display only: never calculate with formatted text.

examples.note: Converting messy imported values.
examples.sql:
SELECT '1250.00'::numeric AS plain,
       replace(replace('1.250,00', '.', ''), ',', '.')::numeric AS dutch,
       to_date('31-03-2026', 'DD-MM-YYYY') AS dmy_date,
       NULLIF('', '')::numeric AS empty_becomes_null;

examples.note: A readable invoice line for a letter.

mistakes.text: A cast fails on the first bad value and the whole query stops. The message names the value: find it in the source.
mistakes.sql: SELECT ('1.250,00')::numeric;
mistakes.error: invalid input syntax for type numeric: "1.250,00"

mistakes.text: Text sorts character by character, so '1000' comes before '200'. Cast before sorting numbers stored as text.
mistakes.sql: SELECT v FROM (VALUES ('200'), ('1000'), ('30')) AS t(v) ORDER BY v;

exercises.prompt: Convert the text '2026-04-15' to a date and add 14 days, in a column due.
exercises.solution: SELECT '2026-04-15'::date + 14 AS due;

exercises.prompt: Convert these Dutch-formatted amounts to numbers: '12,50', '1.034,99', '0,01'. Show the original raw and amount.
exercises.solution:
SELECT raw, replace(replace(raw, '.', ''), ',', '.')::numeric AS amount
FROM (VALUES ('12,50'), ('1.034,99'), ('0,01')) AS t(raw);

exercises.prompt: Show each policy's policy_number and start_date formatted as March 2024 style text (to_char(start_date, 'FMMonth YYYY')) in a column started.
exercises.solution: SELECT policy_number, to_char(start_date, 'FMMonth YYYY') AS started FROM policies;

exercises.prompt: Sort these text values numerically, largest first: '200', '1000', '30'. Show the column v (as text).
exercises.solution: SELECT v FROM (VALUES ('200'), ('1000'), ('30')) AS t(v) ORDER BY v::numeric DESC;

exercises.prompt: For each statement line show line_id and the amount as text with exactly 2 decimals and a sign, like +17.98 or -35.40, named signed. Use to_char(amount, 'FMSG990D00'): FM removes padding, SG adds the sign.
exercises.solution: SELECT line_id, to_char(amount, 'FMSG990D00') AS signed FROM insurer_statements;

lessons.project: The app's CSV import (Module 7) receives amounts as text. In app/notes.md, write the cast you will use for an amount column and what should happen when a line can't be converted (hint: reject the whole file, not just the line).
recap: Cast text to numbers and dates before calculating; failed casts stop with a useful error.
Convert local formats (Dutch decimal commas) explicitly.
Format with to_char only for display.

quiz.text: What does upper(regexp_replace(' nhv 12-34 ', '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) return?
quiz.explain: Every non-letter, non-digit character is removed, then upper case.

quiz.text:
Predict the result.

SELECT date '2026-01-31' + interval '1 month' AS d;
quiz.explain: Interval arithmetic clamps to the last day of the month.
quiz.predictSql: SELECT date '2026-01-31' + interval '1 month' AS d;

quiz.text: A payment is stored as 2025-12-31 23:30:00+00. In which month is it booked by Harbourline (Amsterdam time)?
quiz.explain: 23:30 UTC is 00:30 on 1 January in Amsterdam (UTC+1 in winter).

options.text: BETWEEN stops at 31 January 00:00 and misses the rest of that day

quiz.explain: The half-open range includes every moment of January and nothing of February.

quiz.text: Show the number of distinct normalized policy keys in insurer_statements, in a column keys.
quiz.solution: SELECT count(DISTINCT upper(regexp_replace(policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g'))) AS keys FROM insurer_statements;

quiz.text: Show payment_id and paid_at for payments made on 31 December 2025 Amsterdam time.
quiz.solution: SELECT payment_id, paid_at FROM payments WHERE (paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam')::date = date '2025-12-31';

practical.prompt: The finance team wants "payments per booking month" checked for the time-zone trap. Write one query that lists every payment whose Amsterdam booking month differs from its UTC month, with payment_id, amount, month_utc, month_amsterdam (both as dates), ordered by payment_id. Then explain in your notes which month Harbourline should use and why.
practical.solution:
SELECT payment_id, amount,
       date_trunc('month', paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS month_utc,
       date_trunc('month', paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam')::date AS month_amsterdam
FROM payments
WHERE date_trunc('month', paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') <> date_trunc('month', paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam')
ORDER BY payment_id;

modules.intro: Reconciliation fails on details: a space, a lowercase letter, a payment at 23:50. This module gives you the tools to clean them.

modules.title: Aggregation basics
modules.summary: COUNT, SUM, GROUP BY, HAVING, COUNT(DISTINCT) and FILTER on one table, and using totals to check your own work.
objectives: Write a query that totals amounts per insurer and per month.
Filter groups with HAVING and count conditional subsets with FILTER.
Find duplicate business keys with GROUP BY and HAVING count(*) > 1.
Check a result against a control total before trusting it.

lessons.title: Aggregate functions and GROUP BY
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can summarize a table per group, such as premium per insurer and month.
lessons.explain:
An aggregate function combines many rows into one value: count(*), sum(amount), avg(amount), min(x), max(x). Without GROUP BY the whole table is one group.

GROUP BY splits the rows into groups with equal values and returns one row per group:

SELECT insurer_id, count(*) AS lines, sum(amount) AS total
FROM insurer_statements
GROUP BY insurer_id;

The rule: every column in SELECT is either in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate. "Show policy_number per insurer" has no single answer per insurer, so PostgreSQL refuses.

The grain of the result is the GROUP BY columns: GROUP BY insurer_id, statement_month gives one row per insurer per month. Say it out loud before you write the query.

sum and avg ignore NULLs; sum of no rows is NULL, not 0. Wrap it in COALESCE(sum(x), 0) when you need a zero.

examples.note: Statement totals per insurer.
examples.sql:
SELECT insurer_id, count(*) AS lines, sum(amount) AS premium, sum(commission) AS commission
FROM insurer_statements
GROUP BY insurer_id
ORDER BY insurer_id;

examples.note: Invoiced premium per period month: one row per month.
examples.sql:
SELECT period_start AS month, count(*) AS invoices, sum(amount) AS invoiced
FROM premium_invoices
GROUP BY period_start
ORDER BY period_start;

examples.note: Several aggregates on the whole table at once.

mistakes.text: A column that is neither grouped nor aggregated has no single value per group.
mistakes.sql: SELECT insurer_id, policy_number, sum(amount) FROM insurer_statements GROUP BY insurer_id;
mistakes.error: column "insurer_statements.policy_number" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function

mistakes.text: WHERE can't contain aggregates: it filters rows before grouping. Use HAVING (next lesson).
mistakes.sql: SELECT insurer_id, sum(amount) FROM insurer_statements WHERE sum(amount) > 10000 GROUP BY insurer_id;
mistakes.error: aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE

exercises.prompt: Count policies per product. Columns product, policies, ordered by product.
exercises.solution: SELECT product, count(*) AS policies FROM policies GROUP BY product ORDER BY product;

exercises.prompt: Total annual premium per insurer (insurer_id, total_premium) for active policies only, largest total first.
exercises.solution: SELECT insurer_id, sum(annual_premium) AS total_premium FROM policies WHERE status = 'active' GROUP BY insurer_id ORDER BY total_premium DESC;

exercises.prompt: Statement premium per insurer and month: insurer_id, statement_month, lines, total. Only line_type = 'premium'. Order by insurer and month.
Payments per method and Amsterdam booking month: method, month (as date), payments, received. Order by month, then method.
exercises.solution:
SELECT method, date_trunc('month', paid_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/Amsterdam')::date AS month, count(*) AS payments, sum(amount) AS received
FROM payments GROUP BY method, month ORDER BY month, method;

exercises.prompt: Invoice counts per status, with the status that has most invoices first.
exercises.solution: SELECT status, count(*) AS invoices FROM premium_invoices GROUP BY status ORDER BY invoices DESC;

lessons.project: First version of the app's summary screen, invoice side: app/queries/summary_invoices.sql with insurer id, period month, number of invoices and total amount, excluding cancelled invoices. Policies tell you the insurer: for now group premium_invoices by policy_id is not enough, so keep the policy id and finish it in Module 5 with a join.
recap: Aggregates turn many rows into one value; GROUP BY makes one row per group.
Every selected column is grouped or aggregated.
State the grain of your result before writing it.

lessons.title: HAVING, FILTER and COUNT(DISTINCT)
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can filter groups and count conditional subsets in one pass.
lessons.explain:
• HAVING filters groups, after aggregation: HAVING sum(amount) > 10000. WHERE filters rows before grouping. Use WHERE for row conditions; it is clearer and faster.
  • count(DISTINCT x) counts different values: number of policies with an invoice, not number of invoices.
  • FILTER (WHERE …) restricts one aggregate: count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'overdue'). Several conditional counts side by side, in one query, is conditional aggregation: the backbone of every exception summary.

The order PostgreSQL evaluates a query in explains most errors: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. That's why an alias from SELECT works in ORDER BY but not in WHERE.

examples.note: Status counts per invoice period, side by side in one row each: conditional aggregation.
examples.sql:
SELECT period_start,
       count(*) AS invoices,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid') AS paid,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status IN ('open', 'overdue', 'partially_paid')) AS outstanding
FROM premium_invoices
GROUP BY period_start
ORDER BY period_start;

examples.note: Insurers with more than €10,000 of statement premium.
examples.sql:
SELECT insurer_id, sum(amount) AS premium
FROM insurer_statements
WHERE line_type = 'premium'
GROUP BY insurer_id
HAVING sum(amount) > 10000
ORDER BY premium DESC;

examples.note: Invoices versus distinct policies invoiced.
examples.sql: SELECT count(*) AS invoices, count(DISTINCT policy_id) AS policies_invoiced FROM premium_invoices;

mistakes.text: An alias defined in SELECT doesn't exist yet in WHERE or HAVING, which run earlier. Repeat the expression.
mistakes.sql: SELECT insurer_id, sum(amount) AS premium FROM insurer_statements GROUP BY insurer_id HAVING premium > 10000;
mistakes.error: column "premium" does not exist

exercises.prompt: Per insurer, count statement lines by type in one row: insurer_id, premium_lines, corrections, refunds. Order by insurer.
exercises.solution:
SELECT insurer_id,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE line_type = 'premium') AS premium_lines,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE line_type = 'correction') AS corrections,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE line_type = 'cancellation_refund') AS refunds
FROM insurer_statements GROUP BY insurer_id ORDER BY insurer_id;

exercises.prompt: How many distinct customers have at least one policy? Column customers_with_policy.
exercises.solution: SELECT count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers_with_policy FROM policies;

exercises.prompt: Customers with 3 or more policies: customer_id, policies. Order by customer_id.
exercises.solution: SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS policies FROM policies GROUP BY customer_id HAVING count(*) >= 3 ORDER BY customer_id;

exercises.prompt: Per statement month: statement_month, total lines, lines without_reference (invoice_reference IS NULL), and the share without reference as a percentage rounded to 1 decimal, pct_without_ref. Order by month.
exercises.solution:
SELECT statement_month, count(*) AS lines,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE invoice_reference IS NULL) AS without_reference,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE invoice_reference IS NULL) / count(*), 1) AS pct_without_ref
FROM insurer_statements GROUP BY statement_month ORDER BY statement_month;

exercises.prompt: Review the AI. "Insurers whose average statement line is above €100" was answered with the query below. It fails. Fix it.
exercises.solution: SELECT insurer_id, avg(amount) AS avg_line FROM insurer_statements GROUP BY insurer_id HAVING avg(amount) > 100;
exercises.starter: SELECT insurer_id, avg(amount) AS avg_line FROM insurer_statements WHERE avg(amount) > 100 GROUP BY insurer_id;

lessons.project: Draft app/queries/summary_counts.sql: per insurer and statement month, the number of statement lines, how many lack an invoice reference, and how many are corrections or refunds. The app's summary screen will show these next to the exception counts.
