recap: HAVING filters groups; WHERE filters rows.
count(DISTINCT x) counts different values.
FILTER (WHERE …) puts several conditional counts in one row.

lessons.title: Checking with totals and finding duplicates
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can prove a summary is complete and find duplicate keys before they spoil a match.
lessons.explain:
A control total is a number you know independently: the row count of a table, the total on the insurer's statement header. After any query that splits or summarizes data, check that the parts add up to the whole. If the monthly totals add up to less than the table total, you lost rows (often NULLs in a grouping column).

Duplicate business keys break matching: if one invoice number appears twice, every match against it doubles. Find them with:

SELECT key_column, count(*) FROM t GROUP BY key_column HAVING count(*) > 1;

Not every repeat is an error. Monthly policies legitimately have one statement line per month; a true duplicate repeats the same key, the same month and the same amount. Decide what makes a row unique for your question before you call something a duplicate, and keep "suspected" in the name until a person confirms it.

examples.note: Tie-out: the per-month totals add up to the table total.
examples.sql:
SELECT (SELECT sum(amount) FROM insurer_statements) AS table_total,
       (SELECT sum(month_total) FROM (SELECT statement_month, sum(amount) AS month_total FROM insurer_statements GROUP BY statement_month) AS m) AS sum_of_months;

examples.note: Suspected duplicate statement lines: same insurer, month, normalized policy key, amount and type.
examples.sql:
SELECT insurer_id, statement_month, upper(regexp_replace(policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) AS policy_key,
       amount, line_type, count(*) AS copies
FROM insurer_statements
GROUP BY insurer_id, statement_month, policy_key, amount, line_type
HAVING count(*) > 1
ORDER BY copies DESC, insurer_id, statement_month
LIMIT 10;

mistakes.text: Grouping by a raw messy key undercounts duplicates: NHV-123456 and nhv-123456 land in different groups. Normalize first.
mistakes.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS duplicate_groups_raw FROM (
  SELECT policy_number, statement_month, amount FROM insurer_statements GROUP BY 1, 2, 3 HAVING count(*) > 1) AS d;

exercises.prompt: Check that grouping payments by method loses nothing: one row with table_count (all payments) and sum_of_groups (sum of the per-method counts).
exercises.solution:
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM payments) AS table_count,
       (SELECT sum(n) FROM (SELECT method, count(*) AS n FROM payments GROUP BY method) AS g) AS sum_of_groups;

exercises.prompt: Are invoice numbers unique? Show any invoice_number that occurs more than once with its count (expect none). Columns invoice_number, copies.
exercises.solution: SELECT invoice_number, count(*) AS copies FROM premium_invoices GROUP BY invoice_number HAVING count(*) > 1;

exercises.prompt: Invoices with more than one linked payment: invoice_id, payments, paid_total. Order by invoice. These are double or split payments.
exercises.solution:
SELECT invoice_id, count(*) AS payments, sum(amount) AS paid_total
FROM payments WHERE invoice_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY invoice_id HAVING count(*) > 1 ORDER BY invoice_id;

exercises.prompt: Count customer records that share the same cleaned name (lower(trim(full_name))) with at least one other record: one row, column records_sharing_a_name. These are candidates, not proven duplicates.
exercises.solution:
SELECT sum(n) AS records_sharing_a_name FROM (
  SELECT lower(trim(full_name)) AS name, count(*) AS n FROM customers GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1) AS g;

exercises.prompt: For each name shared by more than one customer record, show name, records, the number of distinct non-NULL birth_date values (birth_dates) and distinct lower-cased emails (emails). Order by name. Which pairs are probably different people?

lessons.project: Add a tie-out to summary_counts.sql: a second query showing the total line count of all groups next to SELECT count(*) FROM insurer_statements. Every summary in the app gets such a check in app/checks.sql later.
recap: Check every summary against a control total.
Find duplicate keys with GROUP BY … HAVING count(*) > 1, on normalized keys.
Repeats can be legitimate; call them suspected until evidence says otherwise.

quiz.text: Which query is valid?

options.text: SELECT insurer_id, policy_number, sum(amount) FROM insurer_statements GROUP BY insurer_id;
SELECT insurer_id, count(DISTINCT policy_number) FROM insurer_statements GROUP BY insurer_id;
SELECT insurer_id, sum(amount) FROM insurer_statements WHERE sum(amount) > 0 GROUP BY insurer_id;
SELECT insurer_id, sum(amount) AS s FROM insurer_statements GROUP BY insurer_id HAVING s > 0;

quiz.explain: Only option 2 groups or aggregates every column and uses no aggregate or alias too early.

quiz.text:
Predict: is the result 0 or NULL?

SELECT sum(amount) AS total FROM payments WHERE amount < 0;
quiz.answer: NULL: there are no negative payments, and sum of no rows is NULL.
quiz.explain: Use COALESCE(sum(amount), 0) when a zero is needed.
quiz.predictSql: SELECT sum(amount) AS total FROM payments WHERE amount < 0;

quiz.text: What is the grain of SELECT insurer_id, statement_month, sum(amount) FROM insurer_statements GROUP BY insurer_id, statement_month?

options.text: One row per insurer per month

quiz.explain: The GROUP BY columns define the result's grain.

quiz.text: Two statement lines have the same insurer, month, normalized policy key and amount. What should you call them?

options.text: A suspected duplicate, until evidence (invoice reference, source file) confirms it

quiz.explain: Repeats can be real transactions; flag them, don't delete them.

quiz.text: Per insurer: insurer_id, lines, and refund_total, the sum of amount for cancellation_refund lines only (0 when none). Order by insurer.
quiz.solution:
SELECT insurer_id, count(*) AS lines, COALESCE(sum(amount) FILTER (WHERE line_type = 'cancellation_refund'), 0) AS refund_total
FROM insurer_statements GROUP BY insurer_id ORDER BY insurer_id;

quiz.text: Policies with more than 6 invoices: policy_id, invoices, ordered by policy_id.
quiz.solution: SELECT policy_id, count(*) AS invoices FROM premium_invoices GROUP BY policy_id HAVING count(*) > 6 ORDER BY policy_id;

practical.prompt: Build the statement side of Harbourline's monthly overview: one row per insurer and statement month with insurer_id, statement_month, lines, premium_total (premium lines only), adjustments_total (corrections and refunds, 0 if none) and lines_without_reference. Order by insurer and month. Then verify in your notes that premium_total plus adjustments_total, summed over all rows, equals SELECT sum(amount) FROM insurer_statements.
practical.solution:
SELECT insurer_id, statement_month,
       count(*) AS lines,
       COALESCE(sum(amount) FILTER (WHERE line_type = 'premium'), 0) AS premium_total,
       COALESCE(sum(amount) FILTER (WHERE line_type <> 'premium'), 0) AS adjustments_total,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE invoice_reference IS NULL) AS lines_without_reference
FROM insurer_statements
GROUP BY insurer_id, statement_month
ORDER BY insurer_id, statement_month;

modules.intro: Aggregation turns many rows into one summary row per group. It comes before joins in this course so that, when you join tables in Module 5, you can already count rows and check totals.

modules.title: Joins and cardinality
modules.summary: Combine tables with inner, left, full outer, self and cross joins, find rows without a match, and catch joins that silently multiply amounts.
objectives: Write a join across three tables, such as invoice, policy and insurer.
Write an anti-join that finds invoices with no payment or no statement line.
Write a full outer join that shows both sides of a comparison and flags the missing side.
Check row counts before and after a join and fix a join that doubles amounts.

lessons.title: Inner joins
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can combine related tables into one result.
lessons.explain:
JOIN … ON pairs each row of one table with the rows of another table that satisfy the condition:

SELECT i.invoice_number, p.policy_number, i.amount
FROM premium_invoices AS i
JOIN policies AS p ON p.policy_id = i.policy_id;
  • i and p are table aliases: short names. Prefix every column with its alias, so readers (and PostgreSQL) know which table it comes from.
  • JOIN means inner join: only pairs where ON is true appear. An invoice whose policy is missing would vanish silently.
  • Chain joins for more tables: invoice → policy → insurer.
  • Join on keys: usually a foreign key on one side and the primary key on the other. Here each invoice has exactly one policy, so the result has exactly as many rows as premium_invoices. Check it.

examples.note: Invoices with their policy number and insurer name.
examples.sql:
SELECT i.invoice_number, p.policy_number, ins.name AS insurer, i.amount
FROM premium_invoices AS i
JOIN policies AS p ON p.policy_id = i.policy_id
JOIN insurers AS ins ON ins.insurer_id = p.insurer_id
ORDER BY i.invoice_id
LIMIT 5;

examples.note: Row-count check: the join returns exactly as many rows as there are invoices, because each invoice has one policy.
examples.sql:
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM premium_invoices) AS invoices,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM premium_invoices i JOIN policies p ON p.policy_id = i.policy_id) AS joined;

examples.note: Invoiced amount per insurer: join first, then group.
examples.sql:
SELECT ins.code, count(*) AS invoices, sum(i.amount) AS invoiced
FROM premium_invoices i
JOIN policies p ON p.policy_id = i.policy_id
JOIN insurers ins ON ins.insurer_id = p.insurer_id
WHERE i.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY ins.code
ORDER BY ins.code;

mistakes.text: A column that exists in both tables must be prefixed. Both policies and premium_invoices have status.
mistakes.sql: SELECT invoice_number, status FROM premium_invoices i JOIN policies p ON p.policy_id = i.policy_id;
mistakes.error: column reference "status" is ambiguous

mistakes.text: A forgotten ON condition pairs every row with every row (a cross join): 399 × 172 rows. PostgreSQL refuses JOIN without ON, but a wrong condition (ON true, or the wrong columns) gives the same explosion.
mistakes.sql: SELECT count(*) AS rows_returned FROM premium_invoices i JOIN policies p ON true;

exercises.prompt: Show each policy's policy_number, product and its insurer's name as insurer.
exercises.solution: SELECT p.policy_number, p.product, ins.name AS insurer FROM policies p JOIN insurers ins ON ins.insurer_id = p.insurer_id;

exercises.prompt: Show the customer's full_name next to each policy number for policies of insurer 4. Columns policy_number, full_name.
exercises.solution: SELECT p.policy_number, c.full_name FROM policies p JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = p.customer_id WHERE p.insurer_id = 4;

exercises.prompt: Payments with their invoice number: payment_id, invoice_number, payment amount and invoice amount as invoice_amount. Inner join, so unlinked payments disappear. Then check: how many payments are left?
exercises.solution:
SELECT pay.payment_id, i.invoice_number, pay.amount, i.amount AS invoice_amount
FROM payments pay JOIN premium_invoices i ON i.invoice_id = pay.invoice_id;

exercises.prompt: Total invoiced (non-cancelled) amount per insurer and period month: insurer_id, period_start, invoices, invoiced. Order by insurer and month.
exercises.solution:
SELECT p.insurer_id, i.period_start, count(*) AS invoices, sum(i.amount) AS invoiced
FROM premium_invoices i JOIN policies p ON p.policy_id = i.policy_id
WHERE i.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY p.insurer_id, i.period_start ORDER BY p.insurer_id, i.period_start;

exercises.prompt: Review the AI. "Invoice number and policy status" gave an error. Fix the query without changing what it should show.
exercises.solution: SELECT i.invoice_number, p.status FROM premium_invoices i JOIN policies p ON p.policy_id = i.policy_id;
exercises.starter: SELECT invoice_number, status FROM premium_invoices i JOIN policies p ON p.policy_id = i.policy_id;

lessons.project: Finish app/queries/summary_invoices.sql from Module 4: invoice count and total per insurer and period month (non-cancelled), using the join to policies. Add the row-count check as a comment underneath.
recap: JOIN … ON pairs matching rows; inner joins drop rows without a match.
Use aliases and prefix every column.
Count rows before and after every join.

lessons.title: Left joins and anti-joins
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can keep rows without a match and find exactly those rows.
lessons.explain:
LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table. Where no right row matches, the right columns are NULL.

An anti-join finds rows with no match: left join, then keep only the rows where the right side's key is NULL.

SELECT i.invoice_number
FROM premium_invoices i
LEFT JOIN payments pay ON pay.invoice_id = i.invoice_id
WHERE pay.payment_id IS NULL;

Two traps:

  • A condition on the right table in WHERE turns the left join back into an inner join, because NULL rows fail it. Put such conditions in ON instead.
  • Test the right table's key (never NULL when matched) for IS NULL, not a column that may be NULL anyway.

NOT EXISTS (Module 6) is the other common way to write an anti-join, and it has no NULL traps.

examples.note: Every insurer with its number of policies, including insurers with none (there are none here, but the query is safe).
examples.sql:
SELECT ins.code, count(p.policy_id) AS policies
FROM insurers ins
LEFT JOIN policies p ON p.insurer_id = ins.insurer_id
GROUP BY ins.code
ORDER BY ins.code;

examples.note: Non-cancelled invoices with no payment at all.
examples.sql:
SELECT i.invoice_number, i.status, i.amount
FROM premium_invoices i
LEFT JOIN payments pay ON pay.invoice_id = i.invoice_id
WHERE pay.payment_id IS NULL AND i.status <> 'cancelled'
ORDER BY i.invoice_id
LIMIT 8;

examples.note: The WHERE trap: filtering the right table in WHERE removes the unmatched rows the left join was meant to keep.

mistakes.text: Counting * after a left join counts the unmatched row too, so every insurer seems to have at least one policy. Count the right table's key instead, as in example 1.
mistakes.sql: SELECT ins.code, count(*) AS looks_like_policies FROM insurers ins LEFT JOIN policies p ON p.insurer_id = ins.insurer_id AND p.product = 'travel' GROUP BY ins.code ORDER BY ins.code;

exercises.prompt: List all policies with their number of invoices, including policies with zero: policy_number, invoices. Order by invoices, then policy_number.
Policies that have no invoice: policy_number, status.
exercises.solution: SELECT p.policy_number, p.status FROM policies p LEFT JOIN premium_invoices i ON i.policy_id = p.policy_id WHERE i.invoice_id IS NULL;

exercises.prompt: Payments that are not linked to any invoice, with their payment_id, amount and reference. Use a left join from payments to invoices (not invoice_id IS NULL on its own).
exercises.solution: SELECT pay.payment_id, pay.amount, pay.reference FROM payments pay LEFT JOIN premium_invoices i ON i.invoice_id = pay.invoice_id WHERE i.invoice_id IS NULL;

exercises.prompt: For each insurer, count its policies with product legal_aid, showing 0 for insurers without any: code, legal_aid_policies. Order by code. Put the product condition in the right place.
Invoices whose invoice_number never appears as an invoice_reference on any statement line: invoice_number, status. Exclude cancelled invoices.

lessons.project: Draft app/queries/missing_on_statement_v0.sql: non-cancelled invoices whose invoice number doesn't appear as a statement reference. Note in app/notes.md why this overstates the problem (85 lines have no reference at all) and what you'll match on instead.
recap: LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows; unmatched right columns are NULL.
Anti-join: left join and test the right key for IS NULL.
Conditions on the right table belong in ON, not WHERE.

lessons.title: Full outer, self and cross joins
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can compare two sources side by side and build complete grids.
lessons.explain:
• FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides. It is the natural shape of a reconciliation: one row per key, with "ours" on the left and "theirs" on the right, NULL where a side is missing.
  • A self join joins a table to itself with two aliases, for example to put candidate duplicate customers side by side.
  • CROSS JOIN pairs every row with every row. Useful on purpose: every insurer × every month gives a complete grid, so months with zero lines still show up.

To label a full outer join result, test which side's key is NULL:

CASE WHEN o.key IS NULL THEN 'only on statement'
     WHEN s.key IS NULL THEN 'only in our books'
     ELSE 'both' END

examples.note: Our invoice months versus the insurer's statement months for one policy, side by side.
examples.sql:
SELECT COALESCE(o.month, s.month) AS month, o.amount AS ours, s.amount AS theirs,
       CASE WHEN o.month IS NULL THEN 'only on statement' WHEN s.month IS NULL THEN 'only in our books' ELSE 'both' END AS side
FROM (SELECT i.period_start AS month, i.amount FROM premium_invoices i JOIN policies p ON p.policy_id = i.policy_id WHERE p.policy_number = 'ATL-668421') AS o
FULL OUTER JOIN (SELECT statement_month AS month, amount FROM insurer_statements WHERE upper(regexp_replace(policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) = 'ATL668421' AND line_type = 'premium') AS s
  ON s.month = o.month
ORDER BY month;

examples.note: A self join: customer records sharing a cleaned name, as pairs. a.customer_id < b.customer_id shows each pair once.
examples.sql:
SELECT a.customer_id AS id_a, b.customer_id AS id_b, a.full_name AS name_a, b.full_name AS name_b,
       a.birth_date = b.birth_date AS same_birth_date
FROM customers a
JOIN customers b ON lower(trim(a.full_name)) = lower(trim(b.full_name)) AND a.customer_id < b.customer_id
ORDER BY id_a;

examples.note: A complete insurer × month grid with statement line counts, zeros included.
examples.sql:
SELECT ins.code, m.month::date, count(s.line_id) AS lines
FROM insurers ins
CROSS JOIN generate_series(date '2025-10-01', date '2026-04-01', interval '1 month') AS m(month)
LEFT JOIN insurer_statements s ON s.insurer_id = ins.insurer_id AND s.statement_month = m.month
GROUP BY ins.code, m.month
ORDER BY ins.code, m.month
LIMIT 14;

mistakes.text: Self-join without a.customer_id < b.customer_id pairs every record with itself and shows each pair twice.
mistakes.sql: SELECT count(*) AS pairs FROM customers a JOIN customers b ON lower(trim(a.full_name)) = lower(trim(b.full_name));

exercises.prompt: Full outer join of invoice periods and statement months for policy ATL-276744 (normalized key ATL276744, premium lines only): month, ours, theirs, side, ordered by month. Copy the structure of example 1.
exercises.solution:
SELECT COALESCE(o.month, s.month) AS month, o.amount AS ours, s.amount AS theirs,
       CASE WHEN o.month IS NULL THEN 'only on statement' WHEN s.month IS NULL THEN 'only in our books' ELSE 'both' END AS side
FROM (SELECT i.period_start AS month, i.amount FROM premium_invoices i JOIN policies p ON p.policy_id = i.policy_id WHERE p.policy_number = 'ATL-276744') AS o
FULL OUTER JOIN (SELECT statement_month AS month, amount FROM insurer_statements WHERE upper(regexp_replace(policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) = 'ATL276744' AND line_type = 'premium') AS s
  ON s.month = o.month
ORDER BY month;

exercises.prompt: Self join on policies: pairs of policies of the same customer with the same product (customer_id, policy_a, policy_b, product), each pair once. Possible double insurance.
exercises.solution:
SELECT a.customer_id, a.policy_number AS policy_a, b.policy_number AS policy_b, a.product
FROM policies a JOIN policies b ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id AND a.product = b.product AND a.policy_id < b.policy_id;

exercises.prompt: A grid of every insurer code × every product (from SELECT DISTINCT product FROM policies), with the number of policies, zeros included. Columns code, product, policies. Order by code and product.
exercises.solution:
SELECT ins.code, pr.product, count(p.policy_id) AS policies
FROM insurers ins CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT product FROM policies) AS pr
LEFT JOIN policies p ON p.insurer_id = ins.insurer_id AND p.product = pr.product
GROUP BY ins.code, pr.product ORDER BY ins.code, pr.product;

exercises.prompt: Count how many statement lines have a normalized policy key that matches no policy at all, using a left join to policies on the normalized key of both sides. Column unknown_policy_lines.
exercises.solution:
SELECT count(*) AS unknown_policy_lines
FROM insurer_statements s
LEFT JOIN policies p ON upper(regexp_replace(p.policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) = upper(regexp_replace(s.policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g'))
WHERE p.policy_id IS NULL;

lessons.project: Generalize example 1 into app/queries/match_v1.sql: a full outer join between all non-cancelled invoices (normalized policy key + period month) and all premium statement lines (normalized key + statement month), with the side label. You'll refine it in Modules 6 and 8.
recap: Full outer join = both sides kept: the shape of a reconciliation.
Self joins compare rows of one table; use < on the id to get each pair once.
Cross joins build complete grids, so zero rows show up.

lessons.title: Cardinality and fan-out
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can predict how many rows a join returns and fix a join that double counts.
lessons.explain:
Cardinality describes how many rows on one side match a row on the other:

  • one-to-one: each invoice ↔ at most one … (rare)
  • one-to-many: one policy → many invoices; one invoice → many payments
  • many-to-many: one statement line ↔ several possible invoices (monthly policies, ±1-month timing window)

Joining "down" a one-to-many relationship repeats the "one" side once per match. That's correct for listing, but wrong for summing the one side: join invoices to payments and sum(i.amount) counts an invoice twice when it has two payments. This is fan-out, and it runs without error.

Two fixes:

  1. Aggregate first, then join: sum payments per invoice in a subquery, then join one row per invoice.
  2. Sum only the "many" side after the join.

The check that catches it: compare a total before and after the join.

examples.note: Fan-out in action. The invoiced total jumps when payments are joined in.
examples.sql:
SELECT (SELECT sum(amount) FROM premium_invoices) AS invoiced_true,
       (SELECT sum(i.amount) FROM premium_invoices i LEFT JOIN payments pay ON pay.invoice_id = i.invoice_id) AS invoiced_after_join;

examples.note: The fix: aggregate payments per invoice first, then join one row per invoice.
How many statement lines match more than one invoice when you allow the statement to be one month late? This is many-to-many, the root of ambiguous matches.
examples.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS lines_with_several_candidates FROM (
  SELECT s.line_id
  FROM insurer_statements s
  JOIN policies p ON upper(regexp_replace(p.policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) = upper(regexp_replace(s.policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g'))
  JOIN premium_invoices i ON i.policy_id = p.policy_id AND s.statement_month IN (i.period_start, (i.period_start + interval '1 month')::date)
  WHERE s.line_type = 'premium'
  GROUP BY s.line_id HAVING count(*) > 1) AS x;

mistakes.text: Counting invoices after joining payments counts invoice–payment pairs. Use count(DISTINCT i.invoice_id), or aggregate first.
mistakes.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS looks_like_invoices, count(DISTINCT i.invoice_id) AS real_invoices
FROM premium_invoices i JOIN payments pay ON pay.invoice_id = i.invoice_id;

exercises.prompt: Per insurer: insurer_id, invoiced (sum of non-cancelled invoice amounts) and paid (sum of payments linked to those invoices). Avoid fan-out: aggregate payments per invoice first. Order by insurer.
exercises.solution:
SELECT p.insurer_id, sum(i.amount) AS invoiced, sum(COALESCE(pp.paid, 0)) AS paid
FROM premium_invoices i
JOIN policies p ON p.policy_id = i.policy_id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT invoice_id, sum(amount) AS paid FROM payments GROUP BY invoice_id) AS pp ON pp.invoice_id = i.invoice_id
WHERE i.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY p.insurer_id ORDER BY p.insurer_id;

exercises.prompt: Show the row counts at each step in one row: invoices (all), with_policy (invoices joined to policies) and with_payments (that result left-joined to payments). Explain the difference in your notes.
Invoices whose payments add up to more than the invoice amount (overpaid, often double payments): invoice_number, amount, paid. Use aggregate-first.
Review the AI. "Total invoiced per product" was written as below. It runs, and the totals are too high. Fix it.
exercises.starter:
SELECT p.product, sum(i.amount) AS invoiced
FROM policies p JOIN premium_invoices i ON i.policy_id = p.policy_id
LEFT JOIN payments pay ON pay.invoice_id = i.invoice_id
GROUP BY p.product;

lessons.project: Add a check block to match_v1.sql: count invoices, count statement premium lines, and count the joined rows. In app/notes.md, write which relationship is one-to-many and where the ambiguous (many-to-many) cases come from.
recap: One-to-many joins repeat the "one" side; summing it then double counts.
Aggregate first, then join, or sum only the "many" side.
Compare totals before and after every join.

quiz.text: An invoice has two payments. You join invoices to payments and sum i.amount. What happens?

options.text: That invoice's amount is counted twice

quiz.explain: Fan-out: the invoice row is repeated once per payment.

quiz.text: Which finds invoices with no payment?

options.text: ... JOIN payments pay ON ... WHERE pay.payment_id IS NULL
... LEFT JOIN payments pay ON pay.invoice_id = i.invoice_id WHERE pay.payment_id IS NULL
... LEFT JOIN payments pay ON ... WHERE pay.method = 'ideal'

quiz.explain: An inner join never produces NULL right sides; the third option turns into an inner join.

quiz.text:
Predict the number.

SELECT count(*) FROM insurers CROSS JOIN insurers AS b;
quiz.explain: A cross join pairs every row with every row.
quiz.predictSql: SELECT count(*) FROM insurers CROSS JOIN insurers AS b;

quiz.text: In a full outer join of our invoices (o) and statement lines (s), a row has o.key IS NULL. What does it mean?

options.text: The line is on the statement but not in our books
The invoice is missing on the statement

quiz.explain: The left side is missing, so only the statement has it.

quiz.text: Insurers with the number of their policies that have no invoices: code, policies_without_invoice, including 0. Order by code.
quiz.solution:
SELECT ins.code, count(p.policy_id) AS policies_without_invoice
FROM insurers ins
LEFT JOIN policies p ON p.insurer_id = ins.insurer_id AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM premium_invoices i WHERE i.policy_id = p.policy_id)
GROUP BY ins.code ORDER BY ins.code;

quiz.text: Per customer type (customer_type): number of policies and total annual premium, columns customer_type, policies, premium.
quiz.solution:
SELECT c.customer_type, count(*) AS policies, sum(p.annual_premium) AS premium
FROM policies p JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = p.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_type;

practical.prompt: For the reconciliation team: per insurer code, show invoices (non-cancelled), invoiced (their total), paid (payments linked to them) and open_balance (invoiced minus paid). Order by code. Prove in your notes that your invoiced column adds up to the non-cancelled invoice total of the whole table.
practical.solution:
SELECT ins.code, count(*) AS invoices, sum(i.amount) AS invoiced, sum(COALESCE(pp.paid, 0)) AS paid,
       sum(i.amount) - sum(COALESCE(pp.paid, 0)) AS open_balance
FROM premium_invoices i
JOIN policies p ON p.policy_id = i.policy_id
JOIN insurers ins ON ins.insurer_id = p.insurer_id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT invoice_id, sum(amount) AS paid FROM payments GROUP BY invoice_id) AS pp ON pp.invoice_id = i.invoice_id
WHERE i.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY ins.code ORDER BY ins.code;

modules.intro: A join combines rows from two tables where a condition matches. Most wrong reports come from joins that run fine and return too many or too few rows, so this module counts rows at every step.

modules.title: Subqueries, EXISTS, CTEs and set operations
modules.summary: Questions inside questions, NOT EXISTS without NULL traps, readable step-by-step queries with WITH, and comparing lists with EXCEPT.
objectives: Write a query with EXISTS or NOT EXISTS and explain when it beats a join.
Rewrite a long query as named steps with WITH.
Compare two lists of keys with EXCEPT and INTERSECT.
Predict the row counts of UNION versus UNION ALL.

lessons.title: Subqueries and EXISTS
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can use the result of one query inside another, and test for existence safely.
lessons.explain:
A subquery is a query inside another query, in brackets. It can return:

  • one value (a scalar subquery): WHERE amount > (SELECT avg(amount) FROM premium_invoices)
  • a list: WHERE policy_id IN (SELECT policy_id FROM policies WHERE product = 'car')
  • a table, used in FROM (you did this in Module 5: aggregate first, then join)

A correlated subquery refers to the outer row: "for this invoice, is there a payment?". EXISTS (subquery) is true when the subquery returns at least one row; it doesn't care what the row contains, so people write SELECT 1.

SELECT i.invoice_number
FROM premium_invoices i
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payments pay WHERE pay.invoice_id = i.invoice_id);

NOT EXISTS is the safest anti-join: unlike NOT IN, NULLs can't make it return nothing, and unlike LEFT JOIN … IS NULL it can never duplicate rows. Prefer it for "rows without a match".

examples.note: Invoices above the average invoice amount: a scalar subquery.
examples.sql:
SELECT invoice_number, amount
FROM premium_invoices
WHERE amount > (SELECT avg(amount) FROM premium_invoices)
ORDER BY amount DESC
LIMIT 5;

examples.note: NOT EXISTS versus the NOT IN trap from Module 2, on the same question.
A correlated subquery in SELECT: the number of payments per invoice, without a join.
examples.sql:
SELECT i.invoice_number,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM payments p WHERE p.invoice_id = i.invoice_id) AS payments
FROM premium_invoices i
ORDER BY i.invoice_id
LIMIT 5;

mistakes.text: A scalar subquery must return one row. "The insurer's policy number" returns many, so PostgreSQL stops.
mistakes.sql: SELECT code, (SELECT policy_number FROM policies p WHERE p.insurer_id = ins.insurer_id) FROM insurers ins;
mistakes.error: more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression

exercises.prompt: Policies with a premium above the average premium of their own product: policy_number, product, annual_premium. Use a correlated scalar subquery.
exercises.solution:
SELECT p.policy_number, p.product, p.annual_premium FROM policies p
WHERE p.annual_premium > (SELECT avg(p2.annual_premium) FROM policies p2 WHERE p2.product = p.product);

exercises.prompt: Customers who have at least one cancelled policy: customer_id, full_name. Use EXISTS.
exercises.solution:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM policies p WHERE p.customer_id = c.customer_id AND p.status = 'cancelled');

exercises.prompt: Non-cancelled invoices whose policy has no premium statement line at all (matched on normalized key, any month): invoice_number, policy_id. Use NOT EXISTS.
exercises.solution:
SELECT i.invoice_number, i.policy_id FROM premium_invoices i JOIN policies p ON p.policy_id = i.policy_id
WHERE i.status <> 'cancelled' AND NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM insurer_statements s
  WHERE s.line_type = 'premium'
    AND upper(regexp_replace(s.policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) = upper(regexp_replace(p.policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')));

exercises.prompt: Insurers whose largest statement line is more than 20 times their average line: insurer_id. Use a subquery in FROM that computes max and avg per insurer.
exercises.solution: SELECT insurer_id FROM (SELECT insurer_id, max(amount) AS mx, avg(amount) AS av FROM insurer_statements GROUP BY insurer_id) AS t WHERE mx > 20 * av;

exercises.prompt: Review the AI. "Policies without any invoice" was written with NOT IN against invoices. It happens to work here, but rewrite it with NOT EXISTS so it stays correct if policy_id could ever be NULL.
exercises.solution: SELECT p.policy_number FROM policies p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM premium_invoices i WHERE i.policy_id = p.policy_id);
exercises.starter: SELECT policy_number FROM policies WHERE policy_id NOT IN (SELECT policy_id FROM premium_invoices);

lessons.project: Rewrite missing_on_statement_v0.sql as missing_on_statement_v1.sql with NOT EXISTS on normalized key and period month (s.statement_month = i.period_start). Compare the row count with v0 and write the difference in app/notes.md.
recap: Subqueries return a value, a list or a table.
EXISTS tests for at least one row; NOT EXISTS is the safe anti-join.
A scalar subquery must return exactly one row.

lessons.title: Named steps with WITH
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can break a long query into readable, testable steps.
lessons.explain:
A CTE (common table expression) names a subquery and puts it first:

WITH ours AS (
  SELECT … FROM premium_invoices …
), theirs AS (
  SELECT … FROM insurer_statements …
)
SELECT … FROM ours FULL OUTER JOIN theirs ON …;

Each step reads like a sentence and can be tested on its own: replace the final SELECT with SELECT * FROM ours to check that step. Steps can use earlier steps. In PostgreSQL 12+ a CTE used once is usually optimized like a subquery, so readability costs nothing.

This is how you'll write every reconciliation from now on: one step to clean each side, one to match, one to classify.

examples.note: The matching from Module 5 rewritten in named steps.
examples.sql:
WITH ours AS (
  SELECT i.invoice_id, upper(regexp_replace(p.policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) AS policy_key, i.period_start AS month, i.amount
  FROM premium_invoices i JOIN policies p ON p.policy_id = i.policy_id
  WHERE i.status <> 'cancelled'
), theirs AS (
  SELECT line_id, upper(regexp_replace(policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) AS policy_key, statement_month AS month, amount
  FROM insurer_statements WHERE line_type = 'premium'
)
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE theirs.line_id IS NULL) AS only_ours,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE ours.invoice_id IS NULL) AS only_theirs,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE ours.invoice_id IS NOT NULL AND theirs.line_id IS NOT NULL) AS paired
FROM ours FULL OUTER JOIN theirs ON theirs.policy_key = ours.policy_key AND theirs.month = ours.month;

examples.note: Testing one step: just look at theirs.

mistakes.text: Steps are separated by commas and only the first has WITH. A second WITH is a syntax error.
mistakes.sql: WITH a AS (SELECT 1 AS x) WITH b AS (SELECT 2 AS y) SELECT * FROM a, b;
mistakes.error: syntax error at or near "WITH"

exercises.prompt: Using a CTE named per_policy (invoice count and total per policy_id), show the 5 policies with the highest invoiced total: policy_id, invoices, total, highest first, ties by policy_id.
exercises.solution:
WITH per_policy AS (SELECT policy_id, count(*) AS invoices, sum(amount) AS total FROM premium_invoices GROUP BY policy_id)
SELECT policy_id, invoices, total FROM per_policy ORDER BY total DESC, policy_id LIMIT 5;

exercises.prompt: Two steps: paid (sum of payments per invoice) and balance (invoice amount minus paid, for non-cancelled invoices). Then show invoices with a balance below zero (overpaid): invoice_id, amount, paid, balance.
exercises.solution:
WITH paid AS (SELECT invoice_id, sum(amount) AS paid FROM payments WHERE invoice_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY invoice_id),
balance AS (
  SELECT i.invoice_id, i.amount, COALESCE(paid.paid, 0) AS paid, i.amount - COALESCE(paid.paid, 0) AS balance
  FROM premium_invoices i LEFT JOIN paid ON paid.invoice_id = i.invoice_id WHERE i.status <> 'cancelled')
SELECT invoice_id, amount, paid, balance FROM balance WHERE balance < 0;

exercises.prompt: Using the ours and theirs steps from example 1, list the paired rows whose amounts differ: invoice_id, line_id, ours_amount, theirs_amount, difference (theirs − ours). Order by invoice_id, line_id.
exercises.solution:
WITH ours AS (
  SELECT i.invoice_id, upper(regexp_replace(p.policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) AS policy_key, i.period_start AS month, i.amount
  FROM premium_invoices i JOIN policies p ON p.policy_id = i.policy_id WHERE i.status <> 'cancelled'
), theirs AS (
  SELECT line_id, upper(regexp_replace(policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) AS policy_key, statement_month AS month, amount
  FROM insurer_statements WHERE line_type = 'premium'
)
SELECT ours.invoice_id, theirs.line_id, ours.amount AS ours_amount, theirs.amount AS theirs_amount, theirs.amount - ours.amount AS difference
FROM ours JOIN theirs ON theirs.policy_key = ours.policy_key AND theirs.month = ours.month
WHERE theirs.amount <> ours.amount
ORDER BY ours.invoice_id, theirs.line_id;

exercises.prompt: Rewrite this nested query as a CTE named big_payers without changing its result.
exercises.solution:
WITH big_payers AS (SELECT customer_id, sum(annual_premium) AS total FROM policies GROUP BY customer_id)
SELECT customer_id FROM big_payers WHERE total > 3000;
exercises.starter: SELECT customer_id FROM (SELECT customer_id, sum(annual_premium) AS total FROM policies GROUP BY customer_id) AS t WHERE total > 3000;

lessons.project: Rewrite match_v1.sql as match_v2.sql with three named steps: ours, theirs, matched. The final SELECT counts rows per side label. Keep each step testable.
recap: WITH names steps; only the first has WITH, the rest are separated by commas.
Test a step by selecting from it.
Clean each side, match, then classify: one step each.

lessons.title: UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can combine or compare whole lists of rows.
lessons.explain:
Set operations combine the results of two queries with the same number of columns and compatible types:

Operation Returns Duplicates
UNION rows in either removed
UNION ALL rows in either kept (faster)
INTERSECT rows in both removed
EXCEPT rows in the first, not in the second removed

EXCEPT is the quickest way to compare two lists of keys: "policy keys on the statement that we don't have". Set operations treat NULLs as equal to each other, unlike =.

Use UNION ALL to stack rows of the same shape from different sources, such as "our side" and "their side" before grouping, and UNION only when you really want duplicates removed.

examples.note: Normalized policy keys on statements that don't exist in our policies.
examples.sql:
SELECT upper(regexp_replace(policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) AS policy_key FROM insurer_statements
EXCEPT
SELECT upper(regexp_replace(policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) FROM policies
ORDER BY policy_key;

examples.note: UNION versus UNION ALL on the same input.
examples.sql:
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT product FROM policies UNION SELECT product FROM policies) AS u) AS union_rows,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT product FROM policies UNION ALL SELECT product FROM policies) AS u) AS union_all_rows;

examples.note: Stacking both sides into one list, ready to group per month.
examples.sql:
SELECT 'ours' AS side, period_start AS month, amount FROM premium_invoices WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
UNION ALL
SELECT 'theirs', statement_month, amount FROM insurer_statements WHERE line_type = 'premium'
ORDER BY month, side
LIMIT 6;

mistakes.text: Both queries need the same number of columns.
mistakes.sql: SELECT policy_number, product FROM policies EXCEPT SELECT policy_number FROM insurer_statements;
mistakes.error: each EXCEPT query must have the same number of columns

exercises.prompt: Normalized policy keys that appear both in our policies and on statements: one column policy_key, ordered.
exercises.solution:
SELECT upper(regexp_replace(policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) AS policy_key FROM policies
INTERSECT
SELECT upper(regexp_replace(policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) FROM insurer_statements
ORDER BY policy_key;

exercises.prompt: Our policy keys (active policies only) that never appear on any statement: column policy_key, ordered.
exercises.solution:
SELECT upper(regexp_replace(policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) AS policy_key FROM policies WHERE status = 'active'
EXCEPT
SELECT upper(regexp_replace(policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) FROM insurer_statements
ORDER BY policy_key;

exercises.prompt: Per month, our total and their total side by side, by stacking with UNION ALL and then grouping: month, ours, theirs. Ours = non-cancelled invoices by period_start; theirs = premium lines by statement_month. Order by month.
exercises.solution:
WITH stacked AS (
  SELECT 'ours' AS side, period_start AS month, amount FROM premium_invoices WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'theirs', statement_month, amount FROM insurer_statements WHERE line_type = 'premium')
SELECT month, COALESCE(sum(amount) FILTER (WHERE side = 'ours'), 0) AS ours, COALESCE(sum(amount) FILTER (WHERE side = 'theirs'), 0) AS theirs
FROM stacked GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;

exercises.prompt: Predict, then check: how many rows does SELECT method FROM payments UNION SELECT method FROM payments return? Write the query.
exercises.solution: SELECT method FROM payments UNION SELECT method FROM payments;

lessons.project: Add an unknown_on_statement step to match_v2.sql using EXCEPT (statement keys minus policy keys). These become the app's "unknown policy" exceptions.
recap: UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT combine whole result lists with matching columns.
EXCEPT compares key lists in one line.
UNION ALL stacks sources without removing duplicates.

quiz.text: Why is NOT EXISTS safer than NOT IN for "invoices without payment"?

options.text: A NULL in the subquery can't make it return nothing
NOT IN doesn't work with subqueries

quiz.explain: NOT IN with a NULL in the list is never true.

quiz.text:
Predict the result.

SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT 1 UNION SELECT 1) AS t;
quiz.answer: 1. UNION removes duplicates from the whole combined result so far.
quiz.explain: Set operations are evaluated left to right; the last UNION deduplicates everything before it.
quiz.predictSql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT 1 UNION SELECT 1) AS t;

quiz.text: What does SELECT a FROM t1 EXCEPT SELECT a FROM t2 return?

options.text: Distinct values of a in t1 that are not in t2
All rows of t1 and t2
Rows in t2 not in t1

quiz.explain: EXCEPT keeps the first list minus the second, without duplicates.

quiz.text: In a CTE chain, how do you test the second step?

options.text: Replace the final SELECT with SELECT * FROM the second step

quiz.explain: Each named step can be selected from directly.

quiz.text: Customers with policies at more than 2 different insurers: customer_id. Use a CTE.
quiz.solution:
WITH per_customer AS (SELECT customer_id, count(DISTINCT insurer_id) AS insurers FROM policies GROUP BY customer_id)
SELECT customer_id FROM per_customer WHERE insurers > 2;

quiz.text: How many statement lines have no invoice reference but a normalized policy key that does exist in our policies? These can only be matched by key and month. One column matchable_by_key_only. Use EXISTS.

practical.prompt: Write a CTE-based query with steps ours, theirs and per_month that shows, per insurer and month, our invoiced total (non-cancelled, by period), their premium total (by statement month), and the difference (theirs − ours). Columns insurer_id, month, ours, theirs, difference. Order by insurer and month. Include months that exist on only one side, with 0 for the missing side.

modules.intro: Reconciliation queries get long. This module gives you the tools to keep them readable and correct.

modules.title: Changing data safely
modules.summary: Create tables with constraints, insert, update and delete without surprises, upsert on business keys, and import a CSV so that importing it twice changes nothing.
objectives: Create a table with sensible types, a primary key, defaults and constraints.
Write INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements that change exactly the intended rows, previewed first and checked with RETURNING.
Wrap changes in a transaction and roll them back on purpose.
Write an upsert on a business key and explain what happens on a repeated import.
Move a CSV from a text staging table into typed tables in one transaction.

lessons.title: CREATE TABLE with constraints
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can create a table whose rules stop bad data at the door.
lessons.explain:
CREATE TABLE defines columns, types and constraints: rules the database enforces on every insert and update.

Constraint Means Example
PRIMARY KEY unique and not null; identifies the row batch_id integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY
NOT NULL a value is required file_name text NOT NULL
UNIQUE no two rows share the value (or combination) UNIQUE (batch_id, source_row)
CHECK (…) the condition must be true CHECK (line_type IN ('premium', 'correction', 'cancellation_refund'))
REFERENCES t (c) foreign key: must exist in t insurer_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES insurers (insurer_id)
DEFAULT … value when none is given imported_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()

GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY makes PostgreSQL number the rows itself; inserting your own id is refused. A generated column computes its value from other columns: policy_key text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (upper(regexp_replace(policy_number_raw, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g'))) STORED keeps the normalized key next to the raw value, always consistent. (PG18+ adds VIRTUAL generated columns; STORED works on Supabase's 17.)

Choose constraints from the business: what must be true for every row? Here: one imported file can only be imported once (unique hash), a line belongs to one batch and one source row, amounts are exact numbers.

examples.note: The two app tables for imports. Run them; the next lessons use them.
examples.sql:
CREATE TABLE import_batches (
    batch_id        integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    insurer_id      integer NOT NULL REFERENCES insurers (insurer_id),
    statement_month date NOT NULL CHECK (statement_month = date_trunc('month', statement_month)),
    file_name       text NOT NULL,
    file_sha256     text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    row_count       integer NOT NULL CHECK (row_count >= 0),
    imported_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE statement_lines (
    line_id           integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    batch_id          integer NOT NULL REFERENCES import_batches (batch_id),
    source_row        integer NOT NULL,
    policy_number_raw text NOT NULL,
    policy_key        text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (upper(regexp_replace(policy_number_raw, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g'))) STORED,
    invoice_reference text,
    booking_date      date NOT NULL,
    amount            numeric(12,2) NOT NULL,
    commission        numeric(12,2) NOT NULL,
    line_type         text NOT NULL CHECK (line_type IN ('premium', 'correction', 'cancellation_refund')),
    UNIQUE (batch_id, source_row)
);

examples.note: Check what you created: the columns of statement_lines.
examples.sql:
SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable, is_generated
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE table_name = 'statement_lines'
ORDER BY ordinal_position;

mistakes.text: A CHECK constraint refuses a value outside the list, and names the constraint so you know which rule failed.
mistakes.sql:
INSERT INTO import_batches (insurer_id, statement_month, file_name, file_sha256, row_count)
VALUES (1, '2026-02-15', 'x.csv', 'abc', 3);
mistakes.error: new row for relation "import_batches" violates check constraint "import_batches_statement_month_check"

mistakes.text: An identity column GENERATED ALWAYS refuses ids you make up. That protects the numbering.
mistakes.sql:
INSERT INTO import_batches (batch_id, insurer_id, statement_month, file_name, file_sha256, row_count)
VALUES (99, 1, '2026-02-01', 'x.csv', 'abc', 3);
mistakes.error: cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column "batch_id"

exercises.prompt: Create a table insurer_contacts with: contact_id (identity primary key), insurer_id (required, foreign key to insurers), full_name (required text), email (text, unique), is_primary (boolean, required, default false). The check looks at the columns you created.
exercises.solution:
CREATE TABLE insurer_contacts (
  contact_id integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  insurer_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES insurers (insurer_id),
  full_name text NOT NULL,
  email text UNIQUE,
  is_primary boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false
);
exercises.verify: SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'insurer_contacts' ORDER BY ordinal_position;

lessons.title: INSERT and RETURNING
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can add rows, including from another table, and see exactly what was inserted.
lessons.explain:
• INSERT INTO t (col1, col2) VALUES (…), (…); adds rows. Always list the columns: then adding a column later can't shift your values.
  • INSERT INTO t (…) SELECT … FROM …; copies rows from a query: this is how staging rows become typed rows, with casts in the SELECT.
  • RETURNING shows the inserted rows, including generated values such as ids: INSERT … RETURNING batch_id.
  • Columns you leave out get their DEFAULT, or NULL.

The import pattern: first insert the batch and get its id, then insert its lines with that id. In SQL you can do both in one statement with a CTE: WITH b AS (INSERT … RETURNING batch_id) INSERT INTO statement_lines … SELECT … FROM staging, b;.

Never hardcode an id. Identity numbers are not guaranteed to be consecutive: a failed insert or a rolled-back transaction uses up numbers, so the February batch may be number 3, not 1. Look ids up by business key: (SELECT batch_id FROM import_batches WHERE file_name = 'nhv_2026-02.csv').

The CSV uses Dutch formats: dates as dd-mm-yyyy, amounts with a decimal comma. Convert them while inserting: to_date(booking_date, 'DD-MM-YYYY'), replace(amount, ',', '.')::numeric.

examples.note: Import the February file: one batch row, then its 14 lines, in one statement. The hash is computed from the file content so the same file always gets the same hash.
examples.sql:
WITH b AS (
  INSERT INTO import_batches (insurer_id, statement_month, file_name, file_sha256, row_count)
  SELECT 1, date '2026-02-01', 'nhv_2026-02.csv',
         encode(sha256(convert_to(string_agg(concat_ws(',', policy_number, invoice_reference, booking_date, amount, commission, line_type), E'\n' ORDER BY source_row), 'UTF8')), 'hex'),
         count(*)
  FROM staging_statement_rows WHERE source_file = 'nhv_2026-02.csv'
  RETURNING batch_id
)
INSERT INTO statement_lines (batch_id, source_row, policy_number_raw, invoice_reference, booking_date, amount, commission, line_type)
SELECT b.batch_id, s.source_row, s.policy_number, NULLIF(s.invoice_reference, ''),
       to_date(s.booking_date, 'DD-MM-YYYY'), replace(s.amount, ',', '.')::numeric, replace(s.commission, ',', '.')::numeric, s.line_type
FROM staging_statement_rows s CROSS JOIN b
WHERE s.source_file = 'nhv_2026-02.csv'
RETURNING line_id, source_row, policy_key, amount;

examples.note: What's in the batch now.

lessons.title: UPDATE, DELETE and transactions
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can change or remove exactly the rows you mean, and undo a mistake before it counts.
lessons.explain:
• UPDATE t SET col = value WHERE …; changes matching rows. Without WHERE it changes every row.
  • DELETE FROM t WHERE …; removes matching rows. Without WHERE it empties the table.

The safe routine, every time:

  1. Preview: run SELECT count(*), sum(…) FROM t WHERE <same condition>. Is that the number you expect?
  2. Open a transaction: BEGIN; Changes inside are invisible to others and can be undone.
  3. Change with RETURNING: UPDATE … WHERE … RETURNING *; and compare with the preview.
  4. COMMIT; if right, ROLLBACK; if not.

A transaction is a group of statements that succeed or fail together (Module 10 goes deeper). If any statement fails, PostgreSQL refuses further commands until ROLLBACK.

Foreign keys also protect deletes: you can't delete a batch that still has lines, unless the key says ON DELETE CASCADE. For imported evidence, don't cascade: delete lines deliberately, or better, never delete evidence at all and mark a batch as withdrawn.

examples.note: Preview, then change in a transaction, then look, then undo.
examples.sql: SELECT count(*) AS to_change FROM statement_lines WHERE batch_id = (SELECT batch_id FROM import_batches WHERE file_name = 'nhv_2026-02.csv') AND line_type = 'premium' AND amount < 10;

examples.note: The change itself, with RETURNING, rolled back so the lesson data stays intact.

mistakes.text: The foreign key refuses to delete a batch that still has lines.
mistakes.sql: DELETE FROM import_batches WHERE batch_id = (SELECT batch_id FROM import_batches WHERE file_name = 'nhv_2026-02.csv');
mistakes.error: update or delete on table "import_batches" violates foreign key constraint "statement_lines_batch_id_fkey" on table "statement_lines"

Preview with SELECT, change inside BEGIN with RETURNING, then COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

lessons.title: Upserts and repeat imports
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can insert-or-update on a business key and make an import safe to run twice.
lessons.explain:
An upsert inserts a row, or does something else if a row with the same key already exists:

INSERT INTO t (key, value) VALUES (…)
ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET value = EXCLUDED.value;   -- or DO NOTHING

EXCLUDED is the row you tried to insert. ON CONFLICT needs a UNIQUE constraint or primary key on exactly those columns.

The real question is which key. An internal id (batch_id) is new on every insert, so it never conflicts: useless for detecting repeats. The business key says what makes a thing the same thing in the real world: for an imported file, its content hash; for a line, (batch, source row).

An idempotent operation gives the same result however often you run it. Your import is idempotent when importing the same file twice changes nothing the second time. With ON CONFLICT (file_sha256) DO NOTHING RETURNING batch_id, the second run returns no batch id, so no lines are inserted.

What it does not protect against: the insurer sending a corrected file for the same month. Different content, different hash, a second batch. That's correct: keep both and decide which one counts. Never silently overwrite evidence.

examples.note: Re-running the February import: the batch conflicts on its hash, so nothing is inserted. Zero rows returned.
examples.sql:
WITH b AS (
  INSERT INTO import_batches (insurer_id, statement_month, file_name, file_sha256, row_count)
  SELECT 1, date '2026-02-01', 'nhv_2026-02.csv',
         encode(sha256(convert_to(string_agg(concat_ws(',', policy_number, invoice_reference, booking_date, amount, commission, line_type), E'\n' ORDER BY source_row), 'UTF8')), 'hex'),
         count(*)
  FROM staging_statement_rows WHERE source_file = 'nhv_2026-02.csv'
  ON CONFLICT (file_sha256) DO NOTHING
  RETURNING batch_id
)
INSERT INTO statement_lines (batch_id, source_row, policy_number_raw, invoice_reference, booking_date, amount, commission, line_type)
SELECT b.batch_id, s.source_row, s.policy_number, NULLIF(s.invoice_reference, ''),
       to_date(s.booking_date, 'DD-MM-YYYY'), replace(s.amount, ',', '.')::numeric, replace(s.commission, ',', '.')::numeric, s.line_type
FROM staging_statement_rows s CROSS JOIN b
WHERE s.source_file = 'nhv_2026-02.csv'
RETURNING line_id;

examples.note: Still one batch and 14 lines.
examples.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM import_batches) AS batches, (SELECT count(*) FROM statement_lines) AS lines;

INSERT INTO insurers (insurer_id, code, name, country, time_zone, statement_cycle)
VALUES (1, 'NHV', 'Noordhaven Verzekeringen N.V.', 'NL', 'Europe/Amsterdam', 'monthly')
ON CONFLICT (insurer_id) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name
RETURNING insurer_id, name;

VALUES (1, '2026-02-01', 'nhv_2026-02.csv', 'x', 1) ON CONFLICT (file_name) DO NOTHING;
mistakes.error: there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification

Internal ids never conflict, so they can't detect repeats.
Idempotent imports: same file twice changes nothing; a corrected file is new evidence, not an overwrite.

lessons.title: CSV imports from start to finish
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can import a CSV file into Supabase, validate it and promote it in one transaction.
lessons.explain:
Getting the file in. Three routes, depending on where you work:

Where How Limits
Supabase dashboard Table Editor → table → Insert → Import data from CSV Small files (up to 100 MB); you map columns in the dialog
psql (Module 10) \copy staging FROM 'file.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true) Reads the file from your computer
SQL COPY … FROM 'file' Reads a file on the database server Needs superuser or pg_read_server_files; not available on Supabase

COPY and \copy look alike but aren't: COPY runs on the server and reads server files; \copy is a psql command that reads your local file and streams it to the server. Neither works in this page or in the Supabase SQL editor; use the dashboard importer there.

Always import into a staging table first, all columns text. Typed columns would reject or silently reinterpret bad values during the import, where you can't see them. In staging you validate with SQL.

Validate, then promote, in one transaction:

  1. Row count equals what the file header or the insurer says.
  2. Every value converts: amount ~ '^-?[0-9.]+,[0-9]{2}$' (a regular-expression match with ~) for Dutch amounts, valid dates.
  3. Totals match the statement's control total.
  4. Only then insert the batch and lines. If any check fails, insert nothing: a half-imported file is worse than none.

examples.note: Validation report for the staged file: every check in one row.
examples.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS rows_in_file,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE amount !~ '^-?[0-9]+,[0-9]{2}$') AS bad_amounts,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE booking_date !~ '^[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{4}$') AS bad_dates,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE line_type NOT IN ('premium', 'correction', 'cancellation_refund')) AS bad_types,
       sum(replace(amount, ',', '.')::numeric) AS file_total
FROM staging_statement_rows
WHERE source_file = 'nhv_2026-02.csv';

examples.note: Compare the imported batch with the old statement table for the same insurer and month: the totals must tie out.
examples.sql:
SELECT (SELECT sum(amount) FROM statement_lines WHERE batch_id = (SELECT batch_id FROM import_batches WHERE file_name = 'nhv_2026-02.csv')) AS imported,
       (SELECT sum(amount) FROM insurer_statements WHERE insurer_id = 1 AND statement_month = '2026-02-01') AS original;

mistakes.text: Casting during import stops at the first bad value. In staging you can find all bad values first; here one Dutch amount stops everything.
mistakes.sql: SELECT '147,67'::numeric;
mistakes.error: invalid input syntax for type numeric: "147,67"

exercises.prompt: List any staged rows of nhv_2026-02.csv whose amount is not a valid Dutch amount or whose date is not dd-mm-yyyy (expect none): source_row, amount, booking_date.
exercises.solution:
SELECT source_row, amount, booking_date FROM staging_statement_rows
WHERE source_file = 'nhv_2026-02.csv' AND (amount !~ '^-?[0-9]+,[0-9]{2}$' OR booking_date !~ '^[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{4}$');

exercises.prompt: Add a bad row to staging (source row 15, policy NHV-1, amount '12.50' with a dot, date '2026-02-30', type premium) and then run a validation query that returns bad_amounts and bad_dates counts for the file. Both should be 1.

Tie-out per line type: for the February batch, show line_type, lines, total from statement_lines, next to the same from insurer_statements (insurer 1, February 2026) as original_lines, original_total. One row per line type.
exercises.solution:
WITH imp AS (SELECT line_type, count(*) AS lines, sum(amount) AS total FROM statement_lines WHERE batch_id = (SELECT batch_id FROM import_batches WHERE file_name = 'nhv_2026-02.csv') GROUP BY 1),
orig AS (SELECT line_type, count(*) AS original_lines, sum(amount) AS original_total FROM insurer_statements WHERE insurer_id = 1 AND statement_month = '2026-02-01' GROUP BY 1)
SELECT COALESCE(imp.line_type, orig.line_type) AS line_type, imp.lines, imp.total, orig.original_lines, orig.original_total
FROM imp FULL OUTER JOIN orig ON orig.line_type = imp.line_type;

COPY reads server files; \copy reads yours; Supabase's dashboard importer works for small files.
Validate, then promote in one transaction; a failed check means nothing is imported.

quiz.text: Which constraint makes a repeated import of the same file detectable?
quiz.explain: The content hash is the business key of a file; ids and timestamps are new every time.

quiz.text: What does UPDATE premium_invoices SET status = 'paid'; do?

quiz.text:
Predict the result.

quiz.predictSql: SELECT count(*) FROM statement_lines WHERE policy_key <> upper(policy_key);

quiz.text: Why import a CSV into an all-text staging table first?

options.text: So you can find every bad value with SQL before anything typed is written

         count(*)
  FROM staging_statement_rows WHERE source_file = 'atl_2026-02.csv'
  ON CONFLICT (file_sha256) DO NOTHING
  RETURNING batch_id)

       replace(s.amount, ',', '.')::numeric, replace(s.commission, ',', '.')::numeric, s.line_type

modules.intro:
From here on you change data. In this page every exercise runs inside a transaction that is rolled back afterwards, so you can't break anything. In Supabase you can, which is why this module teaches habits first.

A staging table staging_statement_rows is already loaded: it is what an insurer's CSV file (nhv_2026-02.csv, 14 lines) looks like right after import, every column still text.

modules.title: Reconciliation workshop and window functions
modules.summary: Window functions, then a complete, honest reconciliation of invoices against insurer statements, saved as views with a tie-out.
objectives: Number, rank and compare rows within groups with ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG and running totals.
Match two sources on references first, then on normalized key and month, and keep ambiguous cases ambiguous.
Classify differences as timing, rounding, amount or commission, with the evidence next to each.
List candidate duplicates with evidence and a confidence level, without merging anything.
Save the exception report as a view and prove with a tie-out that nothing was lost.

lessons.title: Window functions
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can calculate per row while looking at other rows in the same group.
lessons.explain:
An aggregate with GROUP BY collapses rows. A window function keeps every row and adds a value computed over a window of related rows:

function() OVER (PARTITION BY group_columns ORDER BY sort_columns)
  • PARTITION BY sets the groups (like GROUP BY, without collapsing). Leave it out for one window over everything.
  • ORDER BY inside OVER sets the order within the group.
Function Gives Typical use
row_number() 1, 2, 3 … per group pick the first row, number copies
rank() 1, 2, 2, 4 … (ties share a rank) top-N with ties
count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY …) group size on every row "is this row one of several?"
lag(x) / lead(x) value from the previous / next row month-on-month change
sum(x) OVER (ORDER BY …) running total balance over time

Window functions run after WHERE and GROUP BY, so you can't filter on them directly. Wrap the query in a CTE and filter outside: WITH t AS (… row_number() …) SELECT … FROM t WHERE rn = 1.

examples.note: Number each policy's invoices in period order.
examples.sql:
SELECT policy_id, period_start, amount,
       row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY policy_id ORDER BY period_start) AS invoice_no
FROM premium_invoices
WHERE policy_id IN (2, 3)
ORDER BY policy_id, period_start;

examples.note: Month-on-month change in statement premium per insurer, with lag.
examples.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT insurer_id, statement_month, sum(amount) AS total
  FROM insurer_statements WHERE line_type = 'premium' GROUP BY 1, 2)
SELECT insurer_id, statement_month, total,
       total - lag(total) OVER (PARTITION BY insurer_id ORDER BY statement_month) AS change
FROM monthly
WHERE insurer_id = 1
ORDER BY statement_month;

examples.note: A running balance of payments received, in Amsterdam booking order.
examples.sql:
SELECT payment_id, paid_at, amount,
       sum(amount) OVER (ORDER BY paid_at, payment_id) AS running_total
FROM payments
ORDER BY paid_at, payment_id
LIMIT 6;

mistakes.text: Window functions can't be used in WHERE: they're computed later. Filter in an outer query.
mistakes.sql:
SELECT policy_id, period_start, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY policy_id ORDER BY period_start) AS n
FROM premium_invoices WHERE row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY policy_id ORDER BY period_start) = 1;
mistakes.error: window functions are not allowed in WHERE

exercises.prompt: Each policy's first invoice (earliest period): policy_id, invoice_number, period_start. Use row_number() in a CTE and filter on 1.
exercises.solution:
WITH ranked AS (SELECT policy_id, invoice_number, period_start, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY policy_id ORDER BY period_start, invoice_id) AS rn FROM premium_invoices)
SELECT policy_id, invoice_number, period_start FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;

exercises.prompt: The 2 most expensive policies per insurer, ties included: insurer_id, policy_number, annual_premium, rnk (rank). Order by insurer, rank, policy number.
exercises.solution:
WITH r AS (SELECT insurer_id, policy_number, annual_premium, rank() OVER (PARTITION BY insurer_id ORDER BY annual_premium DESC) AS rnk FROM policies)
SELECT insurer_id, policy_number, annual_premium, rnk FROM r WHERE rnk <= 2 ORDER BY insurer_id, rnk, policy_number;

exercises.prompt: For each payment of invoice 147 and invoice 213, show invoice_id, payment_id, amount and paid_so_far, the running total per invoice in payment order. Order by invoice, then paid_at.
exercises.solution:
SELECT invoice_id, payment_id, amount, sum(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY invoice_id ORDER BY paid_at, payment_id) AS paid_so_far
FROM payments WHERE invoice_id IN (147, 213) ORDER BY invoice_id, paid_at, payment_id;

exercises.prompt: Show every statement line of insurer 6 with line_id, statement_month, amount and lines_in_month, the number of lines of that insurer in that month (on every row).
exercises.solution: SELECT line_id, statement_month, amount, count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY statement_month) AS lines_in_month FROM insurer_statements WHERE insurer_id = 6;

exercises.prompt: Per insurer and statement month, the premium total and the cumulative premium since the first month: insurer_id, statement_month, total, cumulative. Order by insurer and month.

lessons.project: In app/notes.md, describe how the app's review history will use row_number(): reviews are never updated, so the current review of an exception is the one with row number 1 when ordered by time, newest first.
recap: Window functions add a per-row value computed over a group, without collapsing rows.
row_number, rank, lag/lead, count(*) OVER and running sums cover most needs.
Filter on a window value in an outer query.

lessons.title: Two clean sides, saved as views
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can define each side of a reconciliation once, as a view, with the copies already numbered.
lessons.explain:
A view is a saved query with a name: CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT …. It stores no data; selecting from it runs the query. Views make each reconciliation step reusable and checkable: the app will read from them, and so will your checks.

Our side (recon_ours): one row per non-cancelled invoice, with insurer, normalized policy key, period month, amount and commission.

Their side (recon_theirs): one row per premium statement line, with the same normalized key, the statement month and a copy_no: the number of the line within a group of lines that are identical in insurer, month, key, amount and invoice reference. copy_no > 1 is a suspected duplicate. Including the reference in the group matters: two lines with the same amount but different references are two real invoices, not a duplicate.

Matching only on copy_no = 1 keeps duplicates from creating extra matches.

examples.note: Our side.
examples.sql:
CREATE VIEW recon_ours AS
SELECT i.invoice_id, i.invoice_number, p.insurer_id,
       upper(regexp_replace(p.policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) AS policy_key,
       i.period_start AS month, i.amount, i.commission
FROM premium_invoices i
JOIN policies p ON p.policy_id = i.policy_id
WHERE i.status <> 'cancelled';

examples.note: Their side, with copies numbered.
examples.sql:
CREATE VIEW recon_theirs AS
SELECT line_id, insurer_id,
       upper(regexp_replace(policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')) AS policy_key,
       statement_month AS month, amount, commission, invoice_reference,
       row_number() OVER (
         PARTITION BY insurer_id, statement_month, upper(regexp_replace(policy_number, '[^A-Za-z0-9]', '', 'g')), amount, COALESCE(invoice_reference, '')
         ORDER BY line_id) AS copy_no
FROM insurer_statements
WHERE line_type = 'premium';

examples.note: Check the views against their source tables.
examples.sql:
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM recon_ours) AS ours,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM premium_invoices WHERE status <> 'cancelled') AS invoices,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM recon_theirs) AS theirs,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM recon_theirs WHERE copy_no > 1) AS suspected_copies;

mistakes.text: A view keeps the column list it was created with. Selecting a column the view doesn't have fails, even if the underlying table has it.
mistakes.sql: SELECT status FROM recon_ours LIMIT 1;
mistakes.error: column "status" does not exist

exercises.prompt: List the suspected duplicate copies from recon_theirs: line_id, insurer_id, month, policy_key, amount, copy_no. Order by line_id.
exercises.solution: SELECT line_id, insurer_id, month, policy_key, amount, copy_no FROM recon_theirs WHERE copy_no > 1 ORDER BY line_id;

exercises.prompt: Statement lines (first copies) whose policy key doesn't exist on our side at all: line_id, insurer_id, policy_key, amount. Use NOT EXISTS against recon_ours.
exercises.solution:
SELECT t.line_id, t.insurer_id, t.policy_key, t.amount FROM recon_theirs t
WHERE t.copy_no = 1 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM recon_ours o WHERE o.policy_key = t.policy_key);

exercises.prompt: Create a view recon_adjustments with the non-premium statement lines (line_id, insurer_id, month from statement_month, policy_key, amount, line_type). Then select its row count. The check counts the rows.

Review the AI. An AI's duplicate check numbered copies without the invoice reference. Run it, compare the number of "duplicates" with recon_theirs, and fix it by adding COALESCE(invoice_reference, '') to the partition. Return the count of copies with copy_no > 1 as copies.

lessons.project: In harbourline-recon, start app/migrations/0002_recon_views.sql with recon_ours (from premium_invoices and policies, as above) and recon_theirs, reading from statement_lines joined to import_batches: the batch gives insurer_id and statement_month, and statement_lines already has policy_key. Keep the same column names as here, so every later query works on both.
recap: A view is a named, saved query; it stores no data.
Clean each side once, in a view, with a normalized key.
Number identical lines (including the reference) and match only first copies.

lessons.title: Candidates, unique matches and ambiguity
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can match on the strongest evidence first and report every case you can't decide as ambiguous.
lessons.explain:
Match in order of evidence strength:

  1. By invoice reference. The line names our invoice. Strong evidence, even if the month differs.
  2. By policy key and month, for lines without a reference. A line can belong to an invoice of the same month or of the month before (insurers often book one month late). Invoices already matched by reference are excluded.

Step 2 produces candidates: possible (invoice, line) pairs. Count them per line and per invoice with window functions:

  • exactly one candidate on both sides → a unique match
  • a line with several candidate invoices, or an invoice with several candidate lines → ambiguous. Don't pick one. Report it with its candidates, so a person can decide with evidence you don't have (a phone call, the insurer's detail file).

Lines with no candidate at all are not in our books; invoices with no candidate are missing on the statement.

examples.note: All candidates with their counts, as a view.
examples.sql:
CREATE VIEW recon_candidates AS
WITH by_ref AS (
  SELECT o.invoice_id, t.line_id
  FROM recon_ours o JOIN recon_theirs t ON t.invoice_reference = o.invoice_number
  WHERE t.copy_no = 1
), by_key AS (
  SELECT o.invoice_id, t.line_id
  FROM recon_ours o JOIN recon_theirs t
    ON t.insurer_id = o.insurer_id AND t.policy_key = o.policy_key
   AND t.month IN (o.month, (o.month + interval '1 month')::date)
  WHERE t.copy_no = 1 AND t.invoice_reference IS NULL
    AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM by_ref r WHERE r.invoice_id = o.invoice_id)
)
SELECT invoice_id, line_id, 'reference' AS matched_by, 1::bigint AS candidates_for_line, 1::bigint AS candidates_for_invoice FROM by_ref
UNION ALL
SELECT invoice_id, line_id, 'policy and month', count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY line_id), count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY invoice_id) FROM by_key;

examples.note: How the candidates split.
examples.sql:
SELECT matched_by,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE candidates_for_line = 1 AND candidates_for_invoice = 1) AS unique_pairs,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE candidates_for_line > 1 OR candidates_for_invoice > 1) AS ambiguous_candidates
FROM recon_candidates
GROUP BY matched_by
ORDER BY matched_by;

examples.note: One ambiguous line with all its candidate invoices: the evidence a person needs.
examples.sql:
SELECT c.line_id, t.month AS statement_month, t.amount, string_agg(o.invoice_number || ' (' || o.month || ', ' || o.amount || ')', '; ' ORDER BY o.month) AS candidates
FROM recon_candidates c
JOIN recon_theirs t ON t.line_id = c.line_id
JOIN recon_ours o ON o.invoice_id = c.invoice_id
WHERE c.candidates_for_line > 1
GROUP BY c.line_id, t.month, t.amount
ORDER BY c.line_id
LIMIT 5;

mistakes.text: Forcing a match: taking "the first candidate" with row_number() … = 1 turns every ambiguous line into a confident pair. It runs, it looks tidy, and it's wrong half the time.

exercises.prompt: Count unique pairs, ambiguous lines (distinct line_id with more than one candidate or whose invoice has more than one), and ambiguous invoices, in one row: unique_pairs, ambiguous_lines, ambiguous_invoices.
exercises.solution:
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE candidates_for_line = 1 AND candidates_for_invoice = 1) AS unique_pairs,
       count(DISTINCT line_id) FILTER (WHERE candidates_for_line > 1 OR candidates_for_invoice > 1) AS ambiguous_lines,
       count(DISTINCT invoice_id) FILTER (WHERE candidates_for_line > 1 OR candidates_for_invoice > 1) AS ambiguous_invoices
FROM recon_candidates;

exercises.prompt: Invoices missing on the statement: in recon_ours with no candidate at all. Show invoice_id, invoice_number, insurer_id, month, amount. Order by invoice_id.
exercises.solution:
SELECT o.invoice_id, o.invoice_number, o.insurer_id, o.month, o.amount FROM recon_ours o
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM recon_candidates c WHERE c.invoice_id = o.invoice_id) ORDER BY o.invoice_id;

exercises.prompt: Lines not in our books: first copies in recon_theirs with no candidate. Show line_id, insurer_id, month, policy_key, amount. Order by line_id.
exercises.solution:
SELECT t.line_id, t.insurer_id, t.month, t.policy_key, t.amount FROM recon_theirs t
WHERE t.copy_no = 1 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM recon_candidates c WHERE c.line_id = t.line_id) ORDER BY t.line_id;

exercises.prompt: For each ambiguous invoice, list its candidate lines: invoice_id, candidate_lines (number) and line_ids (comma-separated, ascending, with string_agg(line_id::text, ',' ORDER BY line_id)). Order by invoice_id.
exercises.solution:
SELECT invoice_id, count(*) AS candidate_lines, string_agg(line_id::text, ',' ORDER BY line_id) AS line_ids
FROM recon_candidates WHERE candidates_for_invoice > 1 GROUP BY invoice_id ORDER BY invoice_id;

exercises.prompt: Review the AI. To "match everything" an AI matched unreferenced lines on policy key only, ignoring the month. Count how many (invoice, line) candidate pairs that creates versus the month-limited rule, in one row: key_only, key_and_month. Use recon_ours/recon_theirs, unreferenced first copies, invoices not matched by reference ignored for simplicity.

lessons.project: Add recon_candidates to 0002_recon_views.sql (reading the app's views). In app/notes.md, write the rule in one sentence for the team: "We never pick between candidates; ambiguous cases go to a person with the candidate list."
recap: Match on the strongest evidence first: reference, then key and month.
Count candidates per line and per invoice; only one-to-one is a match.
Ambiguous cases are reported with their candidates, never forced.

lessons.title: Differences and evidence
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can classify every difference in a matched pair and back each claim with evidence.
lessons.explain:
A unique pair can still differ. Classify, from most to least benign:

Kind Rule Evidence to show
timing_difference statement month ≠ our period month both months
rounding amounts differ by at most €0.01 both amounts
amount_difference amounts differ by more than €0.01 both amounts and the difference
commission_difference amounts equal, commission differs both commissions

A pair can have two kinds: booked a month late and with a different amount. Report both; don't let one hide the other.

Difference sign convention: theirs − ours. Positive means the insurer has more than our books. Write the convention on every report.

The same discipline applies to customers. Grouping by name gives candidate duplicates, not duplicates. Give each candidate pair a confidence from the evidence: same email or same birth date → high; same name only → low. Never delete or merge in SQL on a name match; that decision needs a person and the source documents.

examples.note: Unique pairs with both sides side by side: the base for classification.
examples.sql:
SELECT c.invoice_id, c.line_id, o.month AS our_month, t.month AS their_month,
       o.amount AS ours, t.amount AS theirs, t.amount - o.amount AS difference
FROM recon_candidates c
JOIN recon_ours o ON o.invoice_id = c.invoice_id
JOIN recon_theirs t ON t.line_id = c.line_id
WHERE c.candidates_for_line = 1 AND c.candidates_for_invoice = 1
  AND (t.month <> o.month OR t.amount <> o.amount)
ORDER BY c.invoice_id
LIMIT 8;

examples.note: Candidate duplicate customers with a confidence level, from the evidence.
examples.sql:
SELECT a.customer_id AS id_a, b.customer_id AS id_b, lower(trim(a.full_name)) AS name,
       CASE WHEN lower(a.email) = lower(b.email) OR a.birth_date = b.birth_date THEN 'high'
            ELSE 'low' END AS confidence,
       concat_ws('; ',
         CASE WHEN lower(a.email) = lower(b.email) THEN 'same email' END,
         CASE WHEN a.birth_date = b.birth_date THEN 'same birth date' END,
         CASE WHEN a.birth_date <> b.birth_date THEN 'different birth dates' END) AS evidence
FROM customers a
JOIN customers b ON lower(trim(a.full_name)) = lower(trim(b.full_name)) AND a.customer_id < b.customer_id
ORDER BY confidence, name;
