mistakes.text: CASE returns the first matching kind only. A pair that is both late and different in amount gets one label, and the amount difference disappears from the report.
mistakes.sql:
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'timing_difference') AS timing, count(*) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'amount_difference') AS amount
FROM (SELECT CASE WHEN t.month <> o.month THEN 'timing_difference' WHEN abs(t.amount - o.amount) > 0.01 THEN 'amount_difference' END AS kind
      FROM recon_candidates c JOIN recon_ours o USING (invoice_id) JOIN recon_theirs t USING (line_id)
      WHERE c.candidates_for_line = 1 AND c.candidates_for_invoice = 1) AS x;

exercises.prompt: Count the unique pairs per kind in one row: timing, rounding, amount, commission. A pair can count in several columns.
exercises.solution:
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE t.month <> o.month) AS timing,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE t.amount <> o.amount AND abs(t.amount - o.amount) <= 0.01) AS rounding,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE abs(t.amount - o.amount) > 0.01) AS amount,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE t.amount = o.amount AND t.commission <> o.commission) AS commission
FROM recon_candidates c JOIN recon_ours o ON o.invoice_id = c.invoice_id JOIN recon_theirs t ON t.line_id = c.line_id
WHERE c.candidates_for_line = 1 AND c.candidates_for_invoice = 1;

exercises.prompt: The amount differences above €0.01: invoice_id, line_id, insurer_id, ours, theirs, difference (theirs − ours), largest absolute difference first, then invoice_id.
exercises.solution:
SELECT c.invoice_id, c.line_id, o.insurer_id, o.amount AS ours, t.amount AS theirs, t.amount - o.amount AS difference
FROM recon_candidates c JOIN recon_ours o ON o.invoice_id = c.invoice_id JOIN recon_theirs t ON t.line_id = c.line_id
WHERE c.candidates_for_line = 1 AND c.candidates_for_invoice = 1 AND abs(t.amount - o.amount) > 0.01
ORDER BY abs(t.amount - o.amount) DESC, c.invoice_id;

exercises.prompt: Commission differences where the amount matches: invoice_id, our_commission, their_commission, and the insurer's effective rate their_rate (their commission / amount, rounded to 3 decimals). Order by invoice_id.
exercises.solution:
SELECT c.invoice_id, o.commission AS our_commission, t.commission AS their_commission, round(t.commission / t.amount, 3) AS their_rate
FROM recon_candidates c JOIN recon_ours o ON o.invoice_id = c.invoice_id JOIN recon_theirs t ON t.line_id = c.line_id
WHERE c.candidates_for_line = 1 AND c.candidates_for_invoice = 1 AND t.amount = o.amount AND t.commission <> o.commission
ORDER BY c.invoice_id;

exercises.prompt: Review the AI. "Remove duplicate customers" was answered with the DELETE below. Don't run it in real life. Explain in your notes what it destroys, then write instead a query listing the candidate pairs with low confidence only (same name, no matching email or birth date): id_a, id_b, name.
exercises.starter:
DELETE FROM customers c USING customers d
WHERE lower(trim(c.full_name)) = lower(trim(d.full_name)) AND c.customer_id > d.customer_id;

lessons.project: Write in app/notes.md the four difference kinds, their rule, the sign convention, and that a pair can have two kinds. These become the kind values of the app's exceptions.
recap: Classify pairs as timing, rounding, amount or commission; a pair can have more than one.
State the sign convention: theirs − ours.
Duplicates are candidates with a confidence from evidence; never merge on a name.

lessons.title: The exception report and its tie-out
lessons.goal: Afterwards you have one view with every exception, a summary per insurer and month, and proof that nothing fell through.
lessons.explain:
The exception report is a UNION ALL of every kind, all with the same columns:

Column Meaning
exception_key stable text id: kind + invoice id + line id. Reviews in the app point at this key
kind missing_on_statement, not_in_our_books, suspected_duplicate, ambiguous, timing_difference, rounding, amount_difference, commission_difference
insurer_id, month for filtering and the summary (our month where we have one)
invoice_id, line_id the evidence rows (one may be NULL)
our_amount, their_amount, difference theirs − ours
evidence a short human-readable reason

Tie-out. Every invoice in recon_ours must end up in exactly one bucket: uniquely matched, ambiguous, or missing. Every first-copy line likewise: uniquely matched, ambiguous, or not in our books; extra copies are duplicates. Count each bucket and compare with the totals. If they don't add up, a rule overlaps or leaks.

examples.note: The exception report view.
examples.sql:
CREATE VIEW recon_exceptions AS
WITH uniq AS (
  SELECT c.invoice_id, c.line_id, o.insurer_id, o.month AS our_month, t.month AS their_month,
         o.amount AS ours, t.amount AS theirs, o.commission AS our_comm, t.commission AS their_comm
  FROM recon_candidates c JOIN recon_ours o ON o.invoice_id = c.invoice_id JOIN recon_theirs t ON t.line_id = c.line_id
  WHERE c.candidates_for_line = 1 AND c.candidates_for_invoice = 1
), amb AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT line_id FROM recon_candidates WHERE candidates_for_line > 1 OR candidates_for_invoice > 1
)
SELECT 'timing:' || invoice_id || ':' || line_id AS exception_key, 'timing_difference' AS kind, insurer_id, our_month AS month,
       invoice_id, line_id, ours AS our_amount, theirs AS their_amount, theirs - ours AS difference, 'booked in ' || their_month AS evidence
FROM uniq WHERE their_month <> our_month
UNION ALL
SELECT 'rounding:' || invoice_id || ':' || line_id, 'rounding', insurer_id, our_month, invoice_id, line_id, ours, theirs, theirs - ours, 'difference of at most 0.01'
FROM uniq WHERE theirs <> ours AND abs(theirs - ours) <= 0.01
UNION ALL
SELECT 'amount:' || invoice_id || ':' || line_id, 'amount_difference', insurer_id, our_month, invoice_id, line_id, ours, theirs, theirs - ours, 'amounts differ'
FROM uniq WHERE abs(theirs - ours) > 0.01
UNION ALL
SELECT 'commission:' || invoice_id || ':' || line_id, 'commission_difference', insurer_id, our_month, invoice_id, line_id, our_comm, their_comm, their_comm - our_comm, 'commission ' || our_comm || ' vs ' || their_comm
FROM uniq WHERE theirs = ours AND their_comm <> our_comm
UNION ALL
SELECT 'missing:' || o.invoice_id || ':-', 'missing_on_statement', o.insurer_id, o.month, o.invoice_id, NULL, o.amount, NULL, -o.amount, 'no matching line'
FROM recon_ours o WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM recon_candidates c WHERE c.invoice_id = o.invoice_id)
UNION ALL
SELECT 'notours:-:' || t.line_id, 'not_in_our_books', t.insurer_id, t.month, NULL, t.line_id, NULL, t.amount, t.amount,
       CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM recon_ours o WHERE o.policy_key = t.policy_key) THEN 'policy known, no matching invoice' ELSE 'unknown policy ' || t.policy_key END
FROM recon_theirs t WHERE t.copy_no = 1 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM recon_candidates c WHERE c.line_id = t.line_id)
UNION ALL
SELECT 'duplicate:-:' || t.line_id, 'suspected_duplicate', t.insurer_id, t.month, NULL, t.line_id, NULL, t.amount, t.amount, 'copy ' || t.copy_no || ' of an identical line'
FROM recon_theirs t WHERE t.copy_no > 1
UNION ALL
SELECT 'ambiguous:-:' || t.line_id, 'ambiguous', t.insurer_id, t.month, NULL, t.line_id, NULL, t.amount, NULL,
       'candidates: ' || (SELECT string_agg(c.invoice_id::text, ',' ORDER BY c.invoice_id) FROM recon_candidates c WHERE c.line_id = t.line_id)
FROM recon_theirs t JOIN amb ON amb.line_id = t.line_id;

examples.note: Exceptions per kind.
examples.sql:
SELECT kind, count(*) AS exceptions, sum(difference) AS total_difference
FROM recon_exceptions GROUP BY kind ORDER BY exceptions DESC;

examples.note: The summary per insurer and month, as a view the app's summary screen reads.
examples.sql:
CREATE VIEW recon_summary AS
SELECT insurer_id, month,
       count(*) AS exceptions,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'missing_on_statement') AS missing,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'not_in_our_books') AS not_ours,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'ambiguous') AS ambiguous,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE kind IN ('amount_difference', 'rounding', 'commission_difference')) AS differences,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'timing_difference') AS timing,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'suspected_duplicate') AS duplicates
FROM recon_exceptions
GROUP BY insurer_id, month;

mistakes.text: UNION (without ALL) silently removes identical exception rows, for example two different missing invoices with identical columns would collapse if the key were left out. Always use UNION ALL and a unique key. Here the key keeps them apart; check uniqueness:
mistakes.sql: SELECT count(*) AS rows, count(DISTINCT exception_key) AS distinct_keys FROM recon_exceptions;

exercises.prompt: Tie-out for our side, in one row: ours_total (rows in recon_ours), matched (invoices in a unique pair), ambiguous (invoices only in ambiguous candidates), missing, and check_sum = matched + ambiguous + missing.
exercises.solution:
WITH u AS (SELECT DISTINCT invoice_id FROM recon_candidates WHERE candidates_for_line = 1 AND candidates_for_invoice = 1),
a AS (SELECT DISTINCT invoice_id FROM recon_candidates WHERE (candidates_for_line > 1 OR candidates_for_invoice > 1) AND invoice_id NOT IN (SELECT invoice_id FROM u)),
m AS (SELECT invoice_id FROM recon_ours o WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM recon_candidates c WHERE c.invoice_id = o.invoice_id))
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM recon_ours) AS ours_total, (SELECT count(*) FROM u) AS matched, (SELECT count(*) FROM a) AS ambiguous,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM m) AS missing, (SELECT count(*) FROM u) + (SELECT count(*) FROM a) + (SELECT count(*) FROM m) AS check_sum;

exercises.prompt: Tie-out for their side: theirs_total (all rows in recon_theirs), matched (lines in a unique pair), ambiguous (lines in ambiguous candidates only), not_ours, duplicates, check_sum.
exercises.solution:
WITH u AS (SELECT DISTINCT line_id FROM recon_candidates WHERE candidates_for_line = 1 AND candidates_for_invoice = 1),
a AS (SELECT DISTINCT line_id FROM recon_candidates WHERE (candidates_for_line > 1 OR candidates_for_invoice > 1) AND line_id NOT IN (SELECT line_id FROM u)),
n AS (SELECT line_id FROM recon_theirs t WHERE copy_no = 1 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM recon_candidates c WHERE c.line_id = t.line_id)),
d AS (SELECT line_id FROM recon_theirs WHERE copy_no > 1)
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM recon_theirs) AS theirs_total, (SELECT count(*) FROM u) AS matched, (SELECT count(*) FROM a) AS ambiguous,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM n) AS not_ours, (SELECT count(*) FROM d) AS duplicates,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM u) + (SELECT count(*) FROM a) + (SELECT count(*) FROM n) + (SELECT count(*) FROM d) AS check_sum;

exercises.prompt: From recon_summary, the insurer-months with the most exceptions: insurer_id, month, exceptions, top 5, ties by insurer and month.
exercises.solution: SELECT insurer_id, month, exceptions FROM recon_summary ORDER BY exceptions DESC, insurer_id, month LIMIT 5;

exercises.prompt: All exceptions for insurer 4 (Brightgate) in December 2025: kind, invoice_id, line_id, difference, evidence. Order by exception_key.
exercises.solution: SELECT kind, invoice_id, line_id, difference, evidence FROM recon_exceptions WHERE insurer_id = 4 AND month = '2025-12-01' ORDER BY exception_key;

lessons.project: Add recon_exceptions and recon_summary to 0002_recon_views.sql and run it in harbourline-recon. Save both tie-out queries in app/checks.sql; they must pass after every import.
recap: One exception view, UNION ALL of every kind, with a stable key and evidence.
The summary view groups exceptions per insurer and month.
Tie-outs prove every row landed in exactly one bucket.

quiz.text: A statement line without reference has two candidate invoices: January and February of the same policy. What does the report say?

options.text: Matched to February, the same month
Matched to January, the older one

quiz.explain: Without more evidence, picking one is a guess presented as fact.

quiz.text: Why does recon_theirs include the invoice reference in the duplicate partition?

options.text: Two identical-looking lines with different references are two real invoices, not a duplicate

quiz.explain: The reference is evidence that the lines are different transactions.

quiz.text:
Predict: is the result greater than 0?

SELECT count(*) FROM recon_exceptions WHERE kind = 'timing_difference' AND line_id IN (SELECT line_id FROM recon_theirs WHERE invoice_reference IS NOT NULL);
quiz.answer: Yes. Most timing differences come from lines matched by reference: the reference proves the pair, and the month shows it was booked late.
quiz.explain: Strong evidence (the reference) and a difference (the month) can come together.
quiz.predictSql: SELECT count(*) FROM recon_exceptions WHERE kind = 'timing_difference' AND line_id IN (SELECT line_id FROM recon_theirs WHERE invoice_reference IS NOT NULL);

quiz.text: The tie-out for our side gives check_sum 380, ours_total 381. What does it mean?

options.text: One invoice landed in no bucket, or a rule leaks; investigate before reporting

quiz.explain: Tie-outs must match exactly.

quiz.text: Exceptions per kind for insurer 2, ordered by kind: kind, exceptions.
quiz.solution: SELECT kind, count(*) AS exceptions FROM recon_exceptions WHERE insurer_id = 2 GROUP BY kind ORDER BY kind;

quiz.text: The exception_key of every ambiguous exception, ordered.
quiz.solution: SELECT exception_key FROM recon_exceptions WHERE kind = 'ambiguous' ORDER BY exception_key;

practical.prompt: The team lead asks for the January 2026 status: per insurer code, the number of exceptions, the number that need a person (ambiguous, not_in_our_books, missing_on_statement, amount_difference), and the sum of absolute differences for amount differences only (amount_gap, 0 if none). Include insurers with no exceptions, with zeros. Order by code. Use the views. Then write a three-sentence summary for the team lead, including what "ambiguous" means.
practical.solution:
SELECT ins.code,
       count(e.exception_key) AS exceptions,
       count(e.exception_key) FILTER (WHERE e.kind IN ('ambiguous', 'not_in_our_books', 'missing_on_statement', 'amount_difference')) AS needs_person,
       COALESCE(sum(abs(e.difference)) FILTER (WHERE e.kind = 'amount_difference'), 0) AS amount_gap
FROM insurers ins
LEFT JOIN recon_exceptions e ON e.insurer_id = ins.insurer_id AND e.month = '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY ins.code ORDER BY ins.code;

modules.intro: This is the module your job looks like. You build the reconciliation step by step as views, so each step can be checked on its own. The rule throughout: report what the evidence supports, nothing more. A forced match is worse than an honest "ambiguous".

modules.title: Schema design and migrations
modules.summary: Design the tables for human decisions next to the calculated facts, store flexible settings as JSONB, and change a schema safely with numbered migrations.
objectives: Spot repeated facts in a flat table and split them into related tables.
Keep calculated financial facts and human review decisions in separate structures, with history.
Use JSONB for small, flexible settings and query it, and say when a real column is better.
Write numbered, forward-only migrations that change a schema with data in it.
Design a small schema for an unfamiliar domain and defend the choices.

lessons.title: From a flat sheet to tables
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can find repeated facts in a flat table and say how to split it.
lessons.explain:
Before the app, the team tracked reviews in a shared spreadsheet: one row per review, with the reviewer's name, email and role typed on every row. That shape causes three classic problems:

  • Update anomaly. Bas changes his email; you must fix every row, and if you miss one, the sheet contradicts itself.
  • Insertion anomaly. You can't record a new colleague until they've reviewed something.
  • Deletion anomaly. Delete Chris's only review and you lose that Chris exists.

Normalization fixes this by storing each fact once. The working rule (roughly third normal form): every column in a table should describe the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key. The reviewer's email describes the reviewer, not the review, so it belongs in a staff table; the review keeps only a reference to the reviewer.

You don't normalize everything. Snapshots that must not change later (the amount as the insurer sent it) are deliberately copied. The question is always: is this the same fact, or a record of what it was at that moment?

examples.note: The old sheet, loaded as a table.
examples.sql:
CREATE TABLE review_sheet (
  row_no int PRIMARY KEY, exception_key text, reviewer text, reviewer_email text, reviewer_role text,
  decision text, note text, reviewed_on date);
INSERT INTO review_sheet VALUES
 (1, 'amount:80:287',     'Bas Vermeer', 'bas@harbourline.test',  'reconciler', 'to_insurer', 'Insurer used old premium', '2026-02-03'),
 (2, 'missing:82:-',      'Bas Vermeer', 'bas@harbourline.test',  'reconciler', 'needs_info', 'Ask account manager',     '2026-02-03'),
 (3, 'rounding:6:343',    'Anna de Wit', 'anna@harbourline.test', 'team_lead',  'accepted',   'Cent rounding',           '2026-02-04'),
 (4, 'missing:82:-',      'Bas Vermeer', 'b.vermeer@harbourline.test', 'reconciler', 'to_insurer', 'Not on statement, mailed', '2026-02-10'),
 (5, 'ambiguous:-:125',   'Anna de Wit', 'anna@harbourline.test', 'team_lead',  'needs_info', 'Two January candidates',  '2026-02-11'),
 (6, 'timing:2:2',        'Chris Bakker','chris@harbourline.test','viewer',     'accepted',   'Booked a month late',     '2026-02-12'),
 (7, 'amount:80:287',     'Anna de Wit', 'anna@harbourline.test', 'team_lead',  'accepted',   'Insurer confirmed, fixed in Feb', '2026-02-20');
SELECT reviewer, count(*) AS reviews, count(DISTINCT reviewer_email) AS emails FROM review_sheet GROUP BY reviewer ORDER BY reviewer;

examples.note: The sheet repeats the reviewer on every row and has no history rule: row 4 and row 7 are later decisions about exceptions already reviewed. Which decision counts? The latest one, so time is part of the data.
examples.sql:
SELECT exception_key, count(*) AS reviews, min(reviewed_on) AS first, max(reviewed_on) AS last
FROM review_sheet GROUP BY exception_key HAVING count(*) > 1 ORDER BY exception_key;

mistakes.text: Splitting by copying the distinct rows keeps the contradiction: Bas becomes two people, because his two emails make two "distinct" rows.
mistakes.sql: SELECT DISTINCT reviewer, reviewer_email, reviewer_role FROM review_sheet ORDER BY reviewer;

exercises.prompt: Find the reviewers whose details disagree across rows: reviewer and emails, the number of different emails, only where that's more than one.
exercises.solution: SELECT reviewer, count(DISTINCT reviewer_email) AS emails FROM review_sheet GROUP BY reviewer HAVING count(DISTINCT reviewer_email) > 1;

exercises.prompt: For each exception key in the sheet, show the latest decision: exception_key, decision, reviewed_on. Use row_number() (newest first). Order by key.
exercises.solution:
WITH r AS (SELECT exception_key, decision, reviewed_on, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY exception_key ORDER BY reviewed_on DESC, row_no DESC) AS rn FROM review_sheet)
SELECT exception_key, decision, reviewed_on FROM r WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY exception_key;

exercises.prompt: Which sheet rows point at an exception key that the current report doesn't contain (anymore)? Show row_no and exception_key. Compare with recon_exceptions.
exercises.solution: SELECT row_no, exception_key FROM review_sheet s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM recon_exceptions e WHERE e.exception_key = s.exception_key);

exercises.prompt: Design on paper. List the facts in review_sheet and name the table each belongs in: the reviewer (name, email, role), the review (exception, decision, note, moment, who), and the exception itself. Which column of the sheet should not be stored at all, because it is calculated elsewhere? Write it as SQL comments.
exercises.solution:
-- staff:      full_name, email, role               (one row per person; the email is a fact about the person)
-- reviews:    exception_key, decision, note, reviewed_at, reviewed_by -> staff
-- exceptions: not stored; recon_exceptions calculates them from the data.
--             The sheet has no amount column, which is right: amounts come from the view,
--             so a review can never disagree with the numbers.
-- reviewer_role on each row is not a review fact: it describes the person (staff.role).

lessons.project: In app/notes.md, record the rule "exceptions are calculated, decisions are recorded" and list the three tables you'll add in this module: staff, exception_reviews, saved_views.
recap: Store each fact once; repeated facts drift apart.
Ask of every column: does it describe this table's key?
Copy on purpose when you need a snapshot of what was true at a moment.

lessons.title: Staff and an append-only review history
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can model human decisions as an append-only history and derive the current state from it.
lessons.explain:
staff holds one row per person on the team, linked to their login (auth.users.id) and with a role: team_lead, reconciler or viewer. Dana has a login but is not staff: she is an outside auditor, and in Module 12 that difference decides what she may see.

exception_reviews is append-only: a new decision is a new row; nothing is updated or deleted. The current decision of an exception is its newest row. This gives you, for free:

  • the full history (who decided what, when, and why)
  • no lost updates: two people reviewing at once both get recorded (Module 10)
  • an audit trail an accountant will accept

A review points at an exception by exception_key, without a foreign key: exceptions are a view, not a table. If the data changes so that an exception disappears (the insurer's correction arrives and the amounts now match), the review stays as history. You report such reviews as resolved by data, not delete them.

The allowed decisions are a CHECK list, so the app can't invent new ones by accident.

examples.note: The staff table, linked to the logins.
The review history. The email lives in auth.users, once.
examples.sql:
CREATE TABLE exception_reviews (
  review_id     integer GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  exception_key text NOT NULL,
  decision      text NOT NULL CHECK (decision IN ('accepted', 'to_insurer', 'to_finance', 'corrected_in_books', 'needs_info')),
  note          text,
  reviewed_by   integer NOT NULL REFERENCES staff (staff_id),
  reviewed_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
INSERT INTO exception_reviews (exception_key, decision, note, reviewed_by, reviewed_at) VALUES
  ('amount:80:287',   'to_insurer', 'Insurer used old premium',        2, '2026-02-03 09:15+01'),
  ('missing:82:-',    'needs_info', 'Ask account manager',             2, '2026-02-03 09:40+01'),
  ('rounding:6:343',  'accepted',   'Cent rounding',                   1, '2026-02-04 14:02+01'),
  ('missing:82:-',    'to_insurer', 'Not on statement, mailed',        2, '2026-02-10 11:20+01'),
  ('ambiguous:-:125', 'needs_info', 'Two January candidates',          1, '2026-02-11 16:05+01'),
  ('amount:80:287',   'accepted',   'Insurer confirmed, fixed in Feb', 1, '2026-02-20 10:30+01');
SELECT count(*) AS reviews FROM exception_reviews;

examples.note: The current decision per exception, as a view: the newest review wins. (The times were entered in Amsterdam time, +01; the course session shows them in UTC.)
The work queue: exceptions joined to their current review. Calculated facts on the left, recorded decisions on the right.
examples.sql:
SELECT e.exception_key, e.kind, e.difference, cr.decision, s.full_name AS decided_by
FROM recon_exceptions e
LEFT JOIN exception_current_review cr ON cr.exception_key = e.exception_key
LEFT JOIN staff s ON s.staff_id = cr.reviewed_by
WHERE e.insurer_id = 1 AND e.kind IN ('amount_difference', 'missing_on_statement')
ORDER BY cr.decision IS NULL, e.exception_key
LIMIT 6;

mistakes.text: Only listed decisions are allowed. A typo is refused, which is exactly what you want from the database.
mistakes.sql: INSERT INTO exception_reviews (exception_key, decision, reviewed_by) VALUES ('missing:82:-', 'acepted', 2);
mistakes.error: new row for relation "exception_reviews" violates check constraint "exception_reviews_decision_check"

exercises.prompt: Bas reviews missing:89:- with decision to_insurer and note Asked for statement copy. Insert it (let reviewed_at default) and return the new row's exception_key and decision with RETURNING.
exercises.solution:
INSERT INTO exception_reviews (exception_key, decision, note, reviewed_by) VALUES ('missing:89:-', 'to_insurer', 'Asked for statement copy', 2)
RETURNING exception_key, decision;

exercises.prompt: The open work: exceptions of kinds that need a person (ambiguous, not_in_our_books, missing_on_statement, amount_difference) with no current review, or whose current decision is needs_info. Count them per kind: kind, open. Order by kind.
exercises.solution:
SELECT e.kind, count(*) AS open
FROM recon_exceptions e LEFT JOIN exception_current_review cr ON cr.exception_key = e.exception_key
WHERE e.kind IN ('ambiguous', 'not_in_our_books', 'missing_on_statement', 'amount_difference')
  AND (cr.decision IS NULL OR cr.decision = 'needs_info')
GROUP BY e.kind ORDER BY e.kind;

exercises.prompt: The full history of missing:82:-, oldest first: reviewed_at, full_name, decision, note.
exercises.solution:
SELECT r.reviewed_at, s.full_name, r.decision, r.note FROM exception_reviews r JOIN staff s ON s.staff_id = r.reviewed_by
WHERE r.exception_key = 'missing:82:-' ORDER BY r.reviewed_at, r.review_id;

exercises.prompt: Reviews resolved by data: current reviews whose exception_key is no longer in recon_exceptions. Show exception_key and decision. (In this dataset there may be none: an empty result is a valid answer, as long as the query is right.)
exercises.solution:
SELECT cr.exception_key, cr.decision FROM exception_current_review cr
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM recon_exceptions e WHERE e.exception_key = cr.exception_key);

exercises.prompt: Review the AI. To "track status", an AI suggests the migration below: a status column on statement_lines, updated by the app. Write in SQL comments three things this loses compared to exception_reviews. Think about history, missing invoices (which have no statement line), and calculated facts.
exercises.solution:
-- 1. History: an UPDATE overwrites the old status. Who decided, when and why is gone.
-- 2. Coverage: a missing_on_statement exception has no statement line, so it has nowhere to store a decision.
--    An exception is not a row of one table; it is a result of comparing two.
-- 3. Separation: statement_lines holds what the insurer sent (a financial fact). Mixing our decisions into
--    it means a re-import or correction can wipe decisions, and the import table is no longer a faithful copy.
-- (Also: two reviewers at once silently overwrite each other — a lost update, Module 10.)
exercises.starter:
ALTER TABLE statement_lines ADD COLUMN status text DEFAULT 'open';
UPDATE statement_lines SET status = 'accepted' WHERE line_id = 287;

lessons.project: Write app/migrations/0003_reviews.sql in harbourline-recon with staff, exception_reviews and the exception_current_review view, inside BEGIN; … COMMIT;. On Supabase, insert your own staff row with your own user id from Authentication → Users.
recap: Human decisions are an append-only history; the current state is the newest row.
Reviews refer to exceptions by key, without a foreign key; vanished exceptions mean "resolved by data".
CHECK lists keep decision values honest.

lessons.title: JSONB for flexible settings
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can store, query and validate small JSON documents, and decide between JSONB and columns.
lessons.explain:
jsonb stores a JSON document in a column, parsed and indexed. It is right for data whose shape varies and that the database doesn't compute with: a user's saved filter, UI preferences, the raw header of an imported file.

It is wrong for financial facts. Amounts, dates and keys belong in typed columns with constraints, because the database must check, join and sum them.

Operator Means Example
-> get a field as jsonb filters -> 'kinds'
->> get a field as text filters ->> 'insurer_id'
@> contains filters @> '{"insurer_id": 4}'
? has key filters ? 'month'
jsonb_build_object(…) build an object jsonb_build_object('insurer_id', 4)
jsonb_array_elements_text(…) array to rows jsonb_array_elements_text(filters -> 'kinds')

->> always gives text: cast it ((filters ->> 'insurer_id')::int) before comparing with numbers.

saved_views is the app's personal feature: each staff member saves named filters for the exception list. Every row has an owner; in Module 12 RLS makes sure people only see their own.

examples.note: Saved views with a JSONB filter. The CHECK keeps the document an object.
Applying a saved view to the report: each filter only applies when the key is present.
examples.sql:
SELECT e.exception_key, e.kind
FROM saved_views v
JOIN recon_exceptions e
  ON (NOT v.filters ? 'insurer_id' OR e.insurer_id = (v.filters ->> 'insurer_id')::int)
 AND (NOT v.filters ? 'month'      OR e.month = (v.filters ->> 'month')::date)
 AND (NOT v.filters ? 'kinds'      OR e.kind IN (SELECT jsonb_array_elements_text(v.filters -> 'kinds')))
WHERE v.view_id = 1
ORDER BY e.exception_key;

mistakes.text: Comparing the text from ->> with a number fails: there's no text = integer operator. Cast first.
mistakes.sql: SELECT name FROM saved_views WHERE filters ->> 'insurer_id' = 4;
mistakes.error: operator does not exist: text = integer

exercises.prompt: The names of all saved views that filter on insurer 1, using @>.
exercises.solution: SELECT name FROM saved_views WHERE filters @> '{"insurer_id": 1}';

exercises.prompt: Every kind mentioned in any saved view, with how many views mention it: kind, views. Order by kind.
exercises.solution: SELECT k AS kind, count(*) AS views FROM saved_views, jsonb_array_elements_text(filters -> 'kinds') AS k GROUP BY k ORDER BY k;

exercises.prompt: Bas saves a view Ambiguous only with filter kinds ["ambiguous"], built with jsonb_build_object and jsonb_build_array. Insert it and return name and filters.
Apply Anna's view Needs a person (view 2) to the report and count the matching exceptions per kind: kind, exceptions, ordered by kind.
exercises.solution:
SELECT e.kind, count(*) AS exceptions FROM saved_views v JOIN recon_exceptions e
  ON (NOT v.filters ? 'insurer_id' OR e.insurer_id = (v.filters ->> 'insurer_id')::int)
 AND (NOT v.filters ? 'month' OR e.month = (v.filters ->> 'month')::date)
 AND (NOT v.filters ? 'kinds' OR e.kind IN (SELECT jsonb_array_elements_text(v.filters -> 'kinds')))
WHERE v.view_id = 2 GROUP BY e.kind ORDER BY e.kind;

exercises.prompt: Review the AI. An AI proposes storing each imported statement line as one JSONB document (statement_lines(line_id, data jsonb)) "for flexibility". In SQL comments, give two concrete things that break or get harder, and when JSONB would be right in the import.
exercises.solution:
-- 1. No types or constraints: an amount "12,50" or a missing booking date is accepted silently;
--    numeric(12,2), NOT NULL and the line_type CHECK are gone.
-- 2. Every query must cast: sum((data->>'amount')::numeric) everywhere; the generated policy_key and
--    UNIQUE (batch_id, source_row) can't be declared the normal way, and mistakes in keys go unnoticed.
-- Right use: keep the original raw row as an extra jsonb column (raw_row) next to the typed columns,
-- as evidence of exactly what the file said.

lessons.project: Add saved_views to 0003_reviews.sql (or a new 0004_saved_views.sql if 0003 is already applied: never edit an applied migration). Store your first view from the Supabase SQL editor.
recap: JSONB fits flexible, non-financial settings; facts you compute with get typed columns.
->> returns text: cast before comparing.
Validate JSONB shape with a CHECK where it matters.

lessons.title: Migrations on a live schema
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can change tables that already hold data without breaking them, and record which changes ran.
lessons.explain:
A migration is a numbered SQL file that moves the schema one step forward. The rules that keep a team (and future you) out of trouble:

  1. Numbered and ordered: 0001_imports.sql, 0002_recon_views.sql, …
  2. Never edit a migration that has run anywhere. Fix it with a new one.
  3. One transaction per file (BEGIN; … COMMIT;): all or nothing. PostgreSQL can run almost all DDL inside a transaction.
  4. Record what ran in a small schema_migrations table, so you can see a database's state.
  5. End with a check query that proves the result.

Changing tables with data in them:

Change Safe way
add a column ADD COLUMN x type (nullable, or with a DEFAULT)
make it required fill it first (UPDATE), then SET NOT NULL
add a rule old rows break ADD CONSTRAINT … NOT VALID (new rows only), clean up, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT
drop a column a view uses refused; change the view in the same migration

examples.note: Recording migrations.
A rule for the future only. A needs_info decision must carry a note; old rows are checked later.
The body of a migration file: change, record, check. In the file you wrap the change and the record in BEGIN; … COMMIT;; here the course runs it in a rollback for you, so the lines are left out.

mistakes.text: Dropping a column a view depends on is refused. That protects recon_exceptions; change the views in the same migration instead of reaching for CASCADE, which would silently drop them.
mistakes.sql: ALTER TABLE statement_lines DROP COLUMN commission;
mistakes.error: cannot drop column commission of table statement_lines because other objects depend on it

exercises.prompt: Add a nullable column team (text) to staff, fill it with 'reconciliation' for everyone, then make it NOT NULL with a default of 'reconciliation'. Return full_name and team ordered by staff_id.
Validate needs_info_has_note (it should succeed, since every needs_info review has a note) and show conname and convalidated from pg_constraint.
exercises.solution:
ALTER TABLE exception_reviews VALIDATE CONSTRAINT needs_info_has_note;
SELECT conname, convalidated FROM pg_constraint WHERE conname = 'needs_info_has_note';

exercises.prompt: Make a saved view's name unique per owner case-insensitively: Anna must not have both "Needs a person" and "needs a person". Create a unique index on (owner_id, lower(name)) named saved_views_owner_lower_name, and show the index name from pg_indexes.
exercises.solution:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX saved_views_owner_lower_name ON saved_views (owner_id, lower(name));
SELECT indexname FROM pg_indexes WHERE indexname = 'saved_views_owner_lower_name';

exercises.prompt: Which migrations does this database not have, compared with the list 0001_imports, 0002_recon_views, 0003_reviews, 0004_saved_views? Use a VALUES list and NOT EXISTS. Return version.
exercises.solution:
SELECT v.version FROM (VALUES ('0001_imports'), ('0002_recon_views'), ('0003_reviews'), ('0004_saved_views')) AS v (version)
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM schema_migrations m WHERE m.version = v.version);

exercises.prompt: Transfer: a design in an unfamiliar domain. A bike-rental shop wants a database: bikes (frame number, type, daily price), customers, rentals (which bike, which customer, start, planned end, actual return) and damage reports made at return, with a photo link and a repair cost decided later by the mechanic. Write the CREATE TABLE statements. Then, in comments, say which facts are recorded decisions and which are calculated, and which constraint stops a bike being rented twice at the same time. Compare with the solution yourself.

lessons.project: Add schema_migrations to harbourline-recon and insert a row for every migration you've applied. From now on, every migration file ends with its own INSERT INTO schema_migrations and a check query.
recap: Migrations are numbered, forward-only, one transaction each, and recorded.
Add, fill, then require; use NOT VALID + VALIDATE for rules old rows might break.
Views protect the columns they use; change them in the same migration.

quiz.text: Why does exception_reviews have no foreign key to the exceptions?

options.text: Exceptions are a calculated view, not a table; a review must survive when its exception disappears

quiz.explain: The review is history. Its exception may later be resolved by new data.

quiz.text: Two reviews exist for missing:82:-. Which is the current decision?

options.text: The one with the latest reviewed_at (then highest review_id)
The one by the team lead

quiz.explain: Append-only history: the newest row is the current state.

quiz.text: Where does a staff member's email belong?
quiz.explain: It describes the person, not the review.

quiz.text:
Predict the result.

SELECT filters ->> 'insurer_id' AS a, pg_typeof(filters ->> 'insurer_id') AS t FROM saved_views WHERE view_id = 1;
quiz.explain: Cast before comparing with numbers.
quiz.predictSql: SELECT filters ->> 'insurer_id' AS a, pg_typeof(filters ->> 'insurer_id') AS t FROM saved_views WHERE view_id = 1;

quiz.text: Migration 0003 has run on Supabase and contains a mistake. What do you do?
quiz.explain: Applied migrations are history; databases that ran the old 0003 would never get the change.

quiz.text: Per staff member, the number of reviews they recorded, including staff with none: full_name, reviews, ordered by full_name.
quiz.solution: SELECT s.full_name, count(r.review_id) AS reviews FROM staff s LEFT JOIN exception_reviews r ON r.reviewed_by = s.staff_id GROUP BY s.full_name ORDER BY s.full_name;

practical.prompt: The team wants to assign exceptions to a person before reviewing. Write migration 0005_assignments: an append-only table exception_assignments (assignment_id identity PK, exception_key required, assigned_to FK to staff, required, assigned_by FK to staff, required, assigned_at timestamptz default now()), and a view exception_current_assignment with the newest assignment per key. Record the migration in schema_migrations. (The checker runs your answer in a rollback, so leave out BEGIN/COMMIT here; put them in the real file.) Then assign ambiguous:-:125 to Bas (by Anna), and afterwards to Anna (by Anna), and end with the check query: the current assignment of ambiguous:-:125 as exception_key, full_name.

modules.intro:
From this module on, the practice database matches the app. Next to the Harbourline tables it has import_batches, statement_lines (the statements as imported batches) and the reconciliation views from Module 8 (recon_ours, recon_theirs, recon_candidates, recon_exceptions, recon_summary), built on the app's tables. A small stand-in for Supabase's auth.users holds four test users: Anna, Bas, Chris and Dana.

The design rule of this module: exceptions are calculated, decisions are recorded. The views recompute exceptions from the data every time. What a person decided about an exception is a fact of a different kind: it happened at a moment, by someone, for a reason, and it must never be recalculated away.

modules.title: Transactions and concurrency
modules.summary: All-or-nothing changes, what happens when two people work at once, and a local PostgreSQL with psql to see it with your own eyes.
objectives: Group changes into a transaction and recover from mistakes with savepoints.
Explain a lost update and prevent it with an atomic statement, a lock, a version check or an append-only design.
Use a UNIQUE constraint as a guard so something happens only once, even under concurrency.
Run PostgreSQL locally, use psql, and run migrations with ON_ERROR_STOP.
Reproduce lock waiting with two sessions.

lessons.title: All or nothing
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can make several changes succeed or fail together, and undo part of a transaction.
lessons.explain:
A transaction groups statements so they take effect together (atomicity):

BEGIN;
  -- statements
COMMIT;     -- make everything permanent
-- or ROLLBACK;  -- undo everything since BEGIN
  • Without BEGIN, every statement is its own transaction (autocommit). A single INSERT … SELECT of 14 lines is already all or nothing.
  • After an error, the transaction is aborted: every further statement is refused until you ROLLBACK. Nothing half-done gets committed.
  • SAVEPOINT name marks a point; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name undoes back to it and keeps the transaction alive.
  • Other sessions don't see your uncommitted changes.

Where the app needs this: an import is a batch header plus its lines. A batch with half its lines is worse than no batch, because the reconciliation would report fake "missing" invoices. In Module 11 the import becomes one SQL function, so it runs in one transaction even when called from the browser.

examples.note: Two changes, then a savepoint, then a third change that you undo. (The course already opened the transaction.)
One statement is one transaction. This accepts all rounding exceptions that have no decision yet, or none at all if anything fails.
examples.sql:
INSERT INTO exception_reviews (exception_key, decision, note, reviewed_by)
SELECT e.exception_key, 'accepted', 'Rounding within 0.01', 1
FROM recon_exceptions e
WHERE e.kind = 'rounding'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM exception_current_review cr WHERE cr.exception_key = e.exception_key)
RETURNING exception_key;

mistakes.text: After an error, the transaction refuses everything else. In psql you'd see current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block. Here the first statement fails (the decision isn't allowed), so the whole run stops and nothing is kept.
mistakes.sql:
INSERT INTO exception_reviews (exception_key, decision, reviewed_by) VALUES ('missing:89:-', 'done', 2);
SELECT count(*) FROM exception_reviews;
mistakes.error: new row for relation "exception_reviews" violates check constraint "exception_reviews_decision_check"

exercises.prompt: Record reviews for missing:89:- and missing:96:- (both to_insurer, note Mailed insurer, by Bas, staff 2). Set a savepoint extra, record a third review for missing:204:-, then roll back to extra. End with the keys reviewed by Bas today: SELECT exception_key FROM exception_reviews WHERE reviewed_by = 2 AND reviewed_at >= current_date ORDER BY exception_key.

Anna accepts every timing difference that has no current review, in one statement, with note Booked a month later. Return the number of reviews inserted using a CTE: WITH ins AS (INSERT … RETURNING 1) SELECT count(*) AS accepted FROM ins.
exercises.solution:
WITH ins AS (
  INSERT INTO exception_reviews (exception_key, decision, note, reviewed_by)
  SELECT e.exception_key, 'accepted', 'Booked a month later', 1 FROM recon_exceptions e
  WHERE e.kind = 'timing_difference' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM exception_current_review cr WHERE cr.exception_key = e.exception_key)
  RETURNING 1)
SELECT count(*) AS accepted FROM ins;

exercises.prompt: Predict, then check. Inside one transaction: insert a saved view Test A for Chris, savepoint s1, insert Test B, savepoint s2, insert Test C, roll back to s1, insert Test D. Which of Chris's views exist at the end? Write the statements and end with SELECT name FROM saved_views WHERE owner_id = 'c0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000003' ORDER BY name.

Review the AI. An AI wrote this browser code for the import. In SQL comments, say what goes wrong if the network drops after the first call, what the reconciliation would then show, and where the fix belongs.

const { data: batch } = await supabase.from('import_batches').insert(header).select().single();
await supabase.from('statement_lines').insert(lines.map(l => ({ ...l, batch_id: batch.batch_id })));
exercises.solution:
-- Two calls = two separate transactions. If the second fails, the batch exists with no lines (or some).
-- The file's hash is now taken, so re-importing is refused by UNIQUE(file_sha256): the batch is stuck half-done.
-- Reconciliation then reports the month's invoices as missing_on_statement: fake exceptions.
-- Fix: one SQL function that inserts header + lines in one transaction, called once with rpc (Module 11).
-- Plus: check row_count against the number of lines inserted, and fail the function if they differ.

lessons.project: In app/notes.md, list which app actions change more than one row or table (import; bulk accept; later: claim + review). Each one must be a single statement or a single SQL function.
recap: A transaction is all or nothing; an error aborts it until ROLLBACK.
One statement is already atomic; several need BEGIN … COMMIT or a function.
SAVEPOINT lets you undo part of a transaction.

lessons.title: Two people at once
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can recognize a lost update and choose the right protection for it.
lessons.explain:
PostgreSQL's default isolation level is Read Committed: each statement sees the data committed before that statement started. Two sessions can therefore read the same row, both decide something, and both write.

The lost update. Anna and Bas both open saved view 1 (filters {insurer 4, December}). Anna adds a kind filter and saves; Bas changes the month and saves. Bas's save writes the whole filters document he read before Anna's change, so Anna's change is silently gone. Nobody gets an error.

Ways to prevent it:

Protection How Good for
atomic statement compute in SQL: SET n = n + 1, filters = filters || '{"kinds":[…]}' counters, merges
pessimistic lock SELECT … FOR UPDATE in a transaction; the other waits short read-decide-write in SQL
optimistic check a version column; UPDATE … WHERE version = 3; 0 rows means "someone changed it, reload" edits in a browser, where you can't hold a lock
append-only never update; insert a new row decisions and history: exception_reviews
unique constraint let the database refuse the second one "only once": imports, claims

The app uses append-only for decisions, optimistic checks for saved views, and unique constraints for imports and claims. Browsers can't hold database locks between clicks, so FOR UPDATE only appears inside SQL functions.

examples.note: The lost update, played in one session. Both "people" read version 1; both write the document they read plus their change.
examples.sql:
-- Anna and Bas both read: {"insurer_id": 4, "month": "2025-12-01"}
UPDATE saved_views SET filters = '{"insurer_id": 4, "month": "2025-12-01", "kinds": ["ambiguous"]}' WHERE view_id = 1;  -- Anna saves
UPDATE saved_views SET filters = '{"insurer_id": 4, "month": "2026-01-01"}' WHERE view_id = 1;                         -- Bas saves
SELECT filters FROM saved_views WHERE view_id = 1;  -- Anna's "kinds" is gone

examples.note: An optimistic check. A version column that every update increases.
examples.sql:
ALTER TABLE saved_views ADD COLUMN version integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1;
SELECT view_id, name, version FROM saved_views ORDER BY view_id;

examples.note: Anna saves first and wins; Bas's save, still based on version 1, changes nothing, and the app tells him to reload.
A pessimistic lock: FOR UPDATE marks the row as locked until the transaction ends. A second session's FOR UPDATE (or UPDATE) on the same row would wait.
examples.sql:
SELECT view_id, name FROM saved_views WHERE view_id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
SELECT locktype, mode, granted FROM pg_locks WHERE relation = 'saved_views'::regclass;

mistakes.text: Read-modify-write in the application: reading a value, adding in JavaScript, and writing the sum back. Under concurrency two runs both read 1 and both write 2. Played in one session it "works", which is why this bug survives testing.
mistakes.sql:
SELECT version FROM saved_views WHERE view_id = 2;                -- app reads 1, computes 1 + 1
UPDATE saved_views SET version = 2 WHERE view_id = 2;               -- first writer
UPDATE saved_views SET version = 2 WHERE view_id = 2;               -- second writer, also computed 1 + 1
SELECT version FROM saved_views WHERE view_id = 2;

exercises.prompt: Bas renames his view 3 to NHV open work, with an optimistic check: only if version is still 1, increasing the version. Return name and version.
exercises.solution: UPDATE saved_views SET name = 'NHV open work', version = version + 1 WHERE view_id = 3 AND version = 1 RETURNING name, version;

exercises.prompt: Now play the second browser tab: it still thinks view 3 has version 1. First do the rename from the previous exercise, then run the same update again with a different name, NHV everything. The second update must change 0 rows. End with that second UPDATE … RETURNING name, version.
exercises.solution:
UPDATE saved_views SET name = 'NHV open work', version = version + 1 WHERE view_id = 3 AND version = 1;
UPDATE saved_views SET name = 'NHV everything', version = version + 1 WHERE view_id = 3 AND version = 1 RETURNING name, version;

exercises.prompt: Add the kind not_in_our_books to Anna's view 2 atomically, without reading the document first: append to the kinds array inside SQL with jsonb_set(filters, '{kinds}', (filters -> 'kinds') || '"not_in_our_books"'). Return the new filters -> 'kinds' as kinds.
exercises.solution:
UPDATE saved_views SET filters = jsonb_set(filters, '{kinds}', (filters -> 'kinds') || '"not_in_our_books"'), version = version + 1
WHERE view_id = 2 RETURNING filters -> 'kinds' AS kinds;

exercises.prompt: Why is exception_reviews immune to lost updates? Show it: Anna and Bas both review ambiguous:-:136 "at the same time" (two inserts: Anna to_insurer with note Called NHV, Bas needs_info with note Which month?). Then show the full history for that key: full_name, decision, ordered by review_id. Both decisions survive; the team sees the disagreement.

Review the AI. To "fix" the lost update, an AI suggests SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE for every request from the browser. In comments: what does the second writer now get, what must the app do then, and why is the version column still the clearer design for saved views?
exercises.solution:
-- SERIALIZABLE makes PostgreSQL detect the conflict: the second transaction fails with
-- "could not serialize access due to concurrent update" (SQLSTATE 40001).
-- The app must catch that and retry or ask the user to reload, so it needs the same handling as a version check.
-- But: each browser request is its own short transaction, and the two saves are seconds or minutes apart.
-- By then the first transaction has long committed, so there is no overlap to detect: Bas's stale document
-- still overwrites Anna's change. Only a version (or updated_at) check compares against what the user READ.

lessons.project: Add migration 0006_saved_view_versions.sql to harbourline-recon with the version column, recorded in schema_migrations. In app/notes.md, note the rule: every update of a saved view includes WHERE version = :version_read.
recap: Read Committed: each statement sees what was committed before it began.
Lost updates come from read-modify-write; fix them in SQL, with a version check, or by appending.
Browsers can't hold locks between clicks; use version checks and constraints.

lessons.title: Local PostgreSQL and two real sessions
lessons.goal: Afterwards you have PostgreSQL 18 on your computer, can work in psql, and have watched one session wait for another.
lessons.explain:
The course database runs in your browser and has one connection. To see concurrency for real you need a server with two connections. Choose one:

Option Steps
Docker (any OS) docker run --name pg18 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=dev -p 5432:5432 -d postgres:18 then docker exec -it pg18 psql -U postgres
macOS install Postgres.app (PostgreSQL 18), click Initialize, open psql from the menu
Windows / Linux the installer from postgresql.org, or your package manager; then psql -U postgres

Create a practice database and load Harbourline: createdb harbourline (or CREATE DATABASE harbourline; in psql), then psql -d harbourline -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f harbourline_v1.sql. Use Copy dataset script at the top of the course to get the file.

psql essentials:

Command Does
\l, \c name list databases, connect
\dt, \dv, \d name, \d+ name tables, views, describe
\i file.sql run a file
\x expanded output for wide rows
\timing show how long each statement takes
\q quit

-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 makes psql stop at the first error. Without it psql keeps going after a failed statement, and a migration can end up half-applied.

Lock waits. If session A holds a row lock and session B wants it, B waits until A commits or rolls back. SET lock_timeout = '5s' makes B give up with an error instead of waiting forever. If A waits for B while B waits for A, PostgreSQL detects a deadlock after about a second and cancels one of them.

examples.note: The settings you'll change locally, shown here. SET LOCAL only lasts until the end of the transaction.
examples.sql:
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '5s';
SELECT current_setting('lock_timeout') AS lock_timeout, current_setting('transaction_isolation') AS isolation, current_setting('TimeZone') AS tz;

examples.note: The lock-wait lab, to run in two terminals against your local database (with 0003/0004 applied, or the course's saved_views recreated).

exercises.prompt: Write the shell command that runs app/migrations/0003_reviews.sql against the local database harbourline_recon, stopping at the first error. Write it as a SQL comment, then check against the solution.
exercises.solution:
-- psql -d harbourline_recon -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f app/migrations/0003_reviews.sql
-- (with Docker: docker exec -i pg18 psql -U postgres -d harbourline_recon -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 < app/migrations/0003_reviews.sql)

exercises.prompt: Locally, in two terminals: reproduce the lost update from 10.2 with saved_views (A and B both read view 1, A saves, B saves the document it read). Then repeat with the version check and note what B's UPDATE reports (UPDATE 0). Finally run A's SELECT … FOR UPDATE and see B wait; in B, set SET lock_timeout = '3s' first and read the error. Write down the three outcomes as comments.
exercises.solution:
-- 1. Without protection: both UPDATEs report UPDATE 1; the final filters are B's; A's change is lost silently.
-- 2. With WHERE version = 1: A gets UPDATE 1 (version becomes 2); B gets UPDATE 0 -> the app must reload.
-- 3. A: BEGIN; SELECT ... FOR UPDATE;  B: SET lock_timeout = '3s'; UPDATE ... -> after 3 s:
--    ERROR: canceling statement due to lock timeout. (Without the timeout B simply waits until A commits.)

exercises.prompt: Locally, provoke a deadlock: A updates view 1 then view 2, B updates view 2 then view 1, interleaved (A1, B2, A2, B1). Note which session gets the error and what the message says. Then say in one comment how a consistent order prevents it.

Back in the course: the settings that protect a session. In one transaction, set lock_timeout to 3s and statement_timeout to 30s with SET LOCAL, then show both with current_setting, as lock_timeout and statement_timeout.

lessons.project: Create a local database harbourline_recon, run app_starter.sql and every migration from app/migrations in order with ON_ERROR_STOP, and write a small script app/migrate.sh that does this. Run it twice: the second run must fail on the first migration (the tables exist), which proves the migrations aren't silently re-applied.
recap: Run PostgreSQL locally with Docker, Postgres.app or the installer; work in psql.
Always run migration files with -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1.
Lock waits are normal; set lock_timeout, and lock in a consistent order to avoid deadlocks.

quiz.text: The import inserts a batch, then its lines in a second request. The second request fails. What's the result?

options.text: A batch without (all) its lines, and fake missing-invoice exceptions
An error in the reconciliation views

quiz.explain: Two requests are two transactions. Only one transaction (one function) makes it all or nothing.

quiz.text: In a transaction, a statement fails. What happens to the next statement?

options.text: It's refused until you ROLLBACK (or roll back to a savepoint)

quiz.explain: An aborted transaction ignores commands until it ends.

quiz.text: Which protection fits saved views edited in a browser?

options.text: SELECT … FOR UPDATE held between clicks
A version column checked in the UPDATE

quiz.explain: Browsers can't hold locks between requests; a version compares with what the user read.

quiz.text:
Predict the number of rows returned by the second UPDATE.

UPDATE saved_views SET version = version + 1 WHERE view_id = 1 AND version = 1;
UPDATE saved_views SET version = version + 1 WHERE view_id = 1 AND version = 1 RETURNING view_id;
quiz.answer: 0 rows. The first update raised the version to 2, so the second finds no row with version 1.
quiz.explain: That's the optimistic check working.
quiz.predictSql:
UPDATE saved_views SET version = version + 1 WHERE view_id = 1 AND version = 1;
UPDATE saved_views SET version = version + 1 WHERE view_id = 1 AND version = 1 RETURNING view_id;

quiz.text: Why does exception_reviews need no lock or version column?

options.text: Nothing is ever updated; each decision is a new row
Reviews never happen at the same time

quiz.explain: Append-only designs have no read-modify-write to lose.

quiz.text: Show the version of every saved view of Anna (a0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001): name, version, ordered by name.
quiz.solution: SELECT name, version FROM saved_views WHERE owner_id = 'a0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001' ORDER BY name;

practical.prompt: Before reviewing, a reconciler claims an exception so two people don't phone the same insurer. Exactly one person may hold a claim on an exception; the second claimer must get "already claimed", not an error and not a silent overwrite. Create exception_claims (exception_key text primary key, claimed_by FK to staff, required, claimed_at timestamptz default now()). Bas claims missing:204:-. Then Anna tries to claim the same key with INSERT … ON CONFLICT (exception_key) DO NOTHING RETURNING claimed_by: it must return 0 rows. End with SELECT exception_key, s.full_name FROM exception_claims c JOIN staff s ON s.staff_id = c.claimed_by.

modules.intro:
The practice database now also has the team tables from Module 9: staff (Anna, Bas, Chris), exception_reviews with six reviews, the exception_current_review view, saved_views and schema_migrations.

How the course runs your answers. Every exercise runs inside a transaction that the course rolls back afterwards. So in exercises you use SAVEPOINT instead of BEGIN/COMMIT. Real two-person experiments need two real connections; lesson 10.3 sets up PostgreSQL on your computer for that.

modules.title: JavaScript you need for the app
modules.prereq: Module 10, and your score on the JavaScript reading check of Module 0
modules.summary: Just enough JavaScript to read, run and change the app's code yourself: values and arrays, functions and await, the { data, error } pattern, money and dates, and changes made cold.
objectives: Read and write objects, arrays and template strings, and transform lists with map, filter and reduce.
Write functions and async functions, and call the database with the { data, error } pattern, always checking the error.
Avoid floating-point money errors and time-zone surprises by computing in SQL or in cents.
Change code you did not write, one step at a time, and verify each step by running it.

lessons.title: Values, objects and arrays
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can build and read objects and arrays, and transform a list of rows.
lessons.explain:
Kind Example Notes
text (string) 'NHV', `Line ${n}` backticks allow ${…} inside
number 12.5, 40 one number type, with decimals
boolean true, false
nothing null, undefined the database's NULL arrives as null
object { code: 'NHV', active: true } named fields: obj.code
array [12.5, 40, 7.25] ordered list: arr[0], arr.length

const names a value you won't reassign; let one you will. Compare with === (strict): 1 === '1' is false, which is what you want.

Rows from the database arrive as an array of objects: [{ insurer_id: 1, exceptions: 9 }, …]. Most app code transforms such arrays:

Method Returns Example
map(f) a new array, f applied to each item rows.map(r => r.code)
filter(f) the items where f is true rows.filter(r => r.amount > 100)
find(f) the first match, or undefined rows.find(r => r.code === 'NHV')
reduce(f, start) one value built up from all items rows.reduce((sum, r) => sum + r.n, 0)
sort(f) sorts in place; f(a, b) negative means a first rows.sort((a, b) => b.n - a.n)
join(sep) text codes.join(', ')

r => r.code is a short function: take r, give back r.code.

examples.note: Values, an object and an array, printed.
Transforming an array of rows like the database returns.

mistakes.text:
= assigns, === compares. Inside a condition, = silently assigns and the condition is always true for non-empty text. In strict mode, reassigning a const throws an error, which is the useful kind of mistake:

const code = 'NHV';
code = 'ATL';   // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

exercises.prompt: Print the insurer codes of rows as one line, separated by /, in the order given.
exercises.jsSolution:
const rows = [{ code: 'NHV' }, { code: 'ATL' }, { code: 'POL' }];
console.log(rows.map(r => r.code).join(' / '));
exercises.jsStarter:
const rows = [{ code: 'NHV' }, { code: 'ATL' }, { code: 'POL' }];
// your code

exercises.prompt: Print how many lines have an amount above 100, then the line ids of those lines as an array.
Count the exceptions per insurer with reduce, into an object like {"1":2,"2":1}, and print it.
exercises.jsStarter: const rows = [{ insurer_id: 1 }, { insurer_id: 2 }, { insurer_id: 1 }, { insurer_id: 3 }, { insurer_id: 1 }];

exercises.prompt: Sort the summary rows by exceptions, highest first, and print one line per row in the form ATL: 12.
exercises.jsStarter: const summary = [{ code: 'NHV', exceptions: 9 }, { code: 'ATL', exceptions: 12 }, { code: 'KST', exceptions: 4 }];

exercises.prompt: Print the note of each review, or (no note) when it's null. Use ??.
exercises.jsSolution:
const reviews = [{ note: 'Cent rounding' }, { note: null }, { note: 'Ask account manager' }];
for (const r of reviews) console.log(r.note ?? '(no note)');
exercises.jsStarter: const reviews = [{ note: 'Cent rounding' }, { note: null }, { note: 'Ask account manager' }];

lessons.project: Nothing to build yet. Write in app/notes.md which of map, filter, reduce, find you'd need to show "the number of open exceptions per insurer" if the database gave you all exceptions, and then why you'll ask the database for the counts instead (Module 11).
recap: Rows arrive as an array of objects; null is the database's NULL.
map, filter, find, reduce, sort and join cover most transformations.
Use const, === and ??.

lessons.title: Functions, await and the database
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can write async functions that query the database and handle errors properly.
lessons.explain:
A function takes inputs and returns a result:

function label(code, n) { return `${code}: ${n}`; }
const label2 = (code, n) => `${code}: ${n}`;   // the same, as an arrow function

Talking to a database takes time, so the call returns a promise: a result that arrives later. Inside an async function, await waits for it. (The code you type here already runs inside an async function, so you can use await directly.)

Every Supabase call gives back an object with two fields:

const { data, error } = await supabase.from('recon_summary').select('insurer_id, month, exceptions').eq('insurer_id', 4).order('month');
  • error is null when it worked. Otherwise it has a message (and a code, the PostgreSQL error code).
  • data is the rows (an array), or one object with .single(), or null on error.

Always check error first. Code that only looks at data turns every failure into "no rows", which in a reconciliation app looks exactly like "nothing to do".

The calls you'll use:

Call SQL it stands for
.from('t').select('a, b') SELECT a, b FROM t
.eq('a', 1), .neq, .gt, .gte, .lt, .lte, .in('a', [1, 2]), .is('a', null) WHERE … (all combined with AND)
.order('a', { ascending: false }), .limit(5) ORDER BY a DESC LIMIT 5
.single() exactly one row expected, else an error
.insert({ … }).select() INSERT … RETURNING *
.update({ … }).eq(…) UPDATE … WHERE … (refused without a filter)
.rpc('fn', { arg: 1 }) SELECT * FROM fn(arg => 1)

numeric values arrive as JavaScript numbers, and bigint counts too.

examples.note: A query, with the error checked.
A function that returns a value, and a failure handled. The insert is refused by the CHECK on decision.
logs: {"ok":false,"message":"new row for relation \"exception_reviews\" violates check constraint \"exception_reviews_decision_check\""}

mistakes.text:
Forgetting await gives you the promise, not the result. Nothing fails; you just get the wrong thing:

const result = supabase.from('staff').select('full_name');   // no await
console.log(result.data);   // undefined

exercises.prompt: Print the full_name of every staff member, ordered by staff_id, one per line. Check the error.

Fetch all exceptions of insurer 2 with kind missing_on_statement from recon_exceptions (columns exception_key, difference, ordered by exception_key). Print the number of rows, then each row as key difference.

Write async function currentDecision(key) that returns the decision from exception_current_review for that key, or 'none' if there is no review. Use .maybeSingle() (one row or null, no error when there's none). Print the result for missing:82:- and for missing:89:-.

Bas renames his saved view 3 to NHV open work. Update it and print the returned name. Then try the same update without a filter and print the error message, to see the guard that protects you from updating every row.
Use .in() to fetch the staff members with id 1 and 3 (full_name, role, ordered by staff_id) and print the array.
exercises.jsSolution:
const { data, error } = await supabase.from('staff').select('full_name, role').in('staff_id', [1, 3]).order('staff_id');
console.log(error ? error.message : data);

lessons.project: Write in app/notes.md the three lines you'll repeat in every data call: the await, the destructuring of { data, error }, and the if (error) branch. Decide now what the app shows the user when error is set (a visible message, never an empty list).
recap: await the call; the result is { data, error }.
Check error before using data, every time.
.single() and .maybeSingle() for one row; updates and deletes need a filter.

lessons.title: Money and dates in JavaScript
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can avoid the two classic JavaScript errors in a finance app: floating-point sums and shifting dates.
lessons.explain:
Money. JavaScript numbers are binary floating point. 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. Summing hundreds of amounts drifts by cents, and then the app's total disagrees with the database's numeric total, so a tie-out fails for no real reason. Rules:

  1. Let SQL compute totals (sum on numeric is exact). The app reads finished numbers from views like recon_summary, or from a function.
  2. If you must add in JavaScript, work in cents: Math.round(amount * 100), add integers, divide by 100 only to display.
  3. Format for display only, with Intl.NumberFormat('nl-NL', { style: 'currency', currency: 'EUR' }). Never compute with the formatted text.

Dates. A date arrives as text '2026-01-01'; keep it as text. new Date('2026-01-01') means midnight UTC, and showing it in Amsterdam or New York can move it to another day or month. Month logic (which statement month, "a month later") belongs in SQL, where Module 3 made it explicit. Comparing 'YYYY-MM-DD' text works correctly because it sorts like the dates do.

Timestamps (timestamptz) arrive as ISO text with an offset, like 2026-02-03T08:15:00+00:00. To show them in Amsterdam time use Intl.DateTimeFormat with timeZone: 'Europe/Amsterdam'.

examples.note: The float problem, and the two fixes.
Let the database do the sum: the totals per kind from recon_exceptions, computed by a view in SQL. The app only displays them.
A date shifting when treated as a moment, and a timestamp shown in Amsterdam time.

mistakes.text: toFixed(2) returns text and rounds the binary value, not the decimal you meant: (1.005).toFixed(2) is '1.00'. Adding text joins it: '1.00' + 2 is '1.002'. Use it only at the very end, for display.

exercises.prompt: Add these amounts exactly, by working in cents, and print the total with two decimals (toFixed(2) at the end is fine).
Fetch the amount_difference exceptions of insurer 1 (difference only) and print the sum of their differences, computed in cents, as a number.
Format 1234.5 and -35.4 as euros in Dutch notation, one per line.

Format at the end, for display only.

lessons.title: Changing code you didn't write
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can make a small, correct change to unfamiliar code on your own, and prove it works.
lessons.explain:
In Module 11 you get a working app that you didn't write. Your job is to change it safely. The routine:

  1. Read it top to bottom once. For each line, say what it gives back: a promise, an array, an object, nothing.
  2. Run it unchanged and look at the output. Now you know what "working" looks like.
  3. Make one change. Run again. Compare.
  4. Print in between (console.log) when you don't know what a value holds. Remove the prints afterwards.
  5. Stop when the output is right and you can say why. Code that works for a reason you can't explain will break later for a reason you can't find.

The exercises below are cold changes: do them without hints, AI or the solution. Each starts from the same small function, loadOpenWork, that lists exceptions needing a person.

examples.note: The starting function. Run it and read the output before the exercises.

exercises.prompt: Cold change 1. Give loadOpenWork a second parameter month and only return exceptions of that month when it's given (when it's undefined, return all months, as now). Print the number of rows for insurer 3 with no month, then for insurer 3 in 2026-01-01.

Cold change 2. The team only wants work without a current decision. Fetch the keys that have a current review from exception_current_review (one extra call), and leave those out. Print the remaining number of rows for insurer 1, then the first key.

Cold change 3: find and fix the bug. This version is supposed to print the total absolute amount difference of insurer 1, but it prints something absurd. Run it, find out why with a console.log, and fix it so it prints the right number (computed in cents).

Cold change 4. Reviewing needs the reviewer's name, not their id. Print the history of missing:82:- from exception_reviews (reviewed_at, decision, reviewed_by, oldest first) as lines decision by Name, looking the names up from one staff query and a map from id to name.

lessons.project: Keep a list in app/notes.md of each cold change you did, with how long it took and whether you needed the solution. Module 11 repeats this on the real app; the list shows your progress.
recap: Read, run unchanged, change one thing, run again.
Print values you aren't sure about.
Done means: right output, and you can explain why.
