modules.title: Connecting the app
modules.summary: Put the reconciliation behind a real web app: Supabase keys and grants, a working starter app, the import as one SQL function called with rpc, decisions and saved views from the screen, and the Supabase CLI.
objectives: Explain the publishable and secret keys, and expose exactly the tables and views the app needs with GRANT.
Run the starter app against your Supabase project and find where each screen gets its data.
Move multi-step work into one SQL function and call it with rpc, so it is one transaction.
Record decisions and update saved views from the app with the protections of Modules 9 and 10.
Use the Supabase CLI for migrations and generated types, and make cold changes to the app on your own.

lessons.title: Keys, roles and grants
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can say what each Supabase key may do, and grant the app exactly the access it needs.
lessons.explain:
Supabase puts an HTTP API (the Data API, PostgREST) in front of your database. The browser sends requests with a key; the API runs each request as a database role:

Key Who has it Runs as Respects RLS
publishable key (sb_publishable_…) the browser, public by design anon, or authenticated after sign-in yes
secret key (sb_secret_…) servers and your own scripts only service_role no: bypasses RLS

So the publishable key is not a secret: anyone can read it from your page. What protects the data is what the roles anon and authenticated are allowed to do, and that's ordinary PostgreSQL: GRANT and (Module 12) RLS. The secret key bypasses both and never goes into a browser, a repository or a chat.

On new Supabase projects, tables you create aren't automatically visible to the Data API roles: you grant them. Grant the least you need:

  • anon (not signed in): nothing. Harbourline Recon has no public pages.
  • authenticated: read the views and lookup tables; insert (only) into exception_reviews, so the review history stays append-only even if someone calls the API by hand; read and change their saved views.

A privilege is checked per role, table and action. Test it by switching role inside a transaction: SET LOCAL ROLE authenticated.

examples.note: Who may do what right now. Nothing is granted yet.
The grants of the app, as migration 0008_api_grants.

Acting as a signed-in user. Reading the views works; the base tables behind them weren't granted, yet the view still returns rows. That's how views work by default: they read with their owner's rights. Module 12 comes back to this, because it also means a view can bypass row level security.
examples.sql:
SET LOCAL ROLE authenticated;
SELECT count(*) AS exceptions_visible FROM recon_exceptions;

mistakes.text: authenticated may insert reviews but not change them. An UPDATE is refused, which is the append-only rule enforced by the database instead of by good intentions.
mistakes.sql:
SET LOCAL ROLE authenticated;
UPDATE exception_reviews SET decision = 'accepted' WHERE exception_key = 'missing:82:-';
mistakes.error: permission denied for table exception_reviews

exercises.prompt: Acting as anon, try to count the rows of recon_summary. The check expects the error, so instead of running that, show the privilege with has_table_privilege for anon and for authenticated on recon_summary: columns anon_select, authenticated_select.
exercises.solution: SELECT has_table_privilege('anon', 'recon_summary', 'SELECT') AS anon_select, has_table_privilege('authenticated', 'recon_summary', 'SELECT') AS authenticated_select;

exercises.prompt: As authenticated (with SET LOCAL ROLE), record a review for missing:204:- (decision to_insurer, note Asked KST, by staff 2) and return its exception_key and decision.
exercises.solution:
SET LOCAL ROLE authenticated;
INSERT INTO exception_reviews (exception_key, decision, note, reviewed_by) VALUES ('missing:204:-', 'to_insurer', 'Asked KST', 2) RETURNING exception_key, decision;

exercises.prompt: Which privileges does authenticated have on exception_reviews, and which does it not have? Show privilege_type for every privilege of authenticated on that table from information_schema.role_table_grants, ordered.
exercises.solution: SELECT privilege_type FROM information_schema.role_table_grants WHERE grantee = 'authenticated' AND table_name = 'exception_reviews' ORDER BY privilege_type;

exercises.prompt: The app's import screen will call a function, and the team lead wants a list of batches. Grant authenticated nothing new, but write the query the app would run as that role to list the last 3 batches (batch_id, file_name, row_count, newest batch_id first). Use SET LOCAL ROLE authenticated first to prove it's allowed.
exercises.solution:
SET LOCAL ROLE authenticated;
SELECT batch_id, file_name, row_count FROM import_batches ORDER BY batch_id DESC LIMIT 3;

exercises.prompt: Review the AI. An AI says: "To make the app work quickly, run GRANT ALL ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO anon, authenticated; and use the secret key in .env so you don't hit permission errors." In comments, name what each half exposes and what you do instead.
exercises.solution:
-- GRANT ALL ... TO anon: anyone with the (public) publishable key can read AND change AND delete every
-- table, without signing in. Including staff, reviews and statements. TO authenticated: every signed-in
-- user can UPDATE/DELETE reviews, which breaks the append-only history.
-- Secret key in a VITE_ env file: Vite puts VITE_* values into the JavaScript bundle; the key is then
-- public, and it bypasses RLS completely. Rotate it immediately if that ever happens.
-- Instead: grant per table and action, nothing to anon, INSERT-only on exception_reviews;
-- publishable key in the browser; permission errors are information: read them, grant what's missing.

lessons.project: In harbourline-recon (Supabase SQL editor), run the grants of example 2 as migration 0008_api_grants.sql. Then in Project Settings → API Keys, find the publishable key and note where the secret key is, without copying it anywhere.
recap: The publishable key is public; protection comes from grants and RLS. The secret key bypasses both.
Grant nothing to anon; grant authenticated exactly the actions the app needs.
INSERT-only on reviews makes append-only a database rule.

lessons.title: The starter app
lessons.goal: Afterwards you have the app running against your project and can say which function feeds which screen.
lessons.explain:
Get it running:

  1. Install Node.js 22 or newer.
  2. Make a folder harbourline-recon-app with this layout and copy the files below into it:
harbourline-recon-app/
  package.json
  tsconfig.json
  index.html
  .env.local          (from .env.example)
  src/
    main.ts           screens: sign-in, summary, exceptions, decision, import
    db.ts             every database call
    csv.ts            reads the CSV file into text fields

  1. Fill in .env.local with your project URL and publishable key.
  2. In Supabase, Authentication → Users → Add user: create yourself with a password. Then insert your staff row with your user id (SQL editor): INSERT INTO staff (user_id, full_name, role) VALUES ('<your id>', '<your name>', 'team_lead');
  3. In the folder: npm install, then npm run dev, and open the address it prints.

How the code is organised. main.ts never talks to the database. It calls functions in db.ts, which return data or throw an Error with a readable message. That single rule makes the app testable and keeps every query in one file you can read in ten minutes.

Screen db.ts function Reads from
who am I getMe staff (by auth user id)
summary getSummary(month) recon_summary
exception list getExceptions(filters), getCurrentReviews(keys) recon_exceptions, exception_current_review
decision panel getHistory(key), addReview(…) exception_reviews
saved views getSavedViews, saveView, updateView saved_views
import importStatement(…) import_statement function (lesson 11.3)

The exercises in this lesson run the same calls in the page's stand-in client, so you can try them before your own app runs. The stand-in has no sign-in: where the real app uses the signed-in user, the exercises use a fixed one.

examples.note: getSummary from db.ts, as it runs here.
getExceptions and getCurrentReviews together: the exception list with the decision column, like the screen.

mistakes.text: Putting the secret key in .env.local as VITE_SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY. Vite copies every VITE_-prefixed value into the JavaScript it sends to the browser. The app works, nothing warns you, and the key that bypasses all security is now public. If it ever happens: rotate the key in the dashboard immediately.

exercises.prompt: Write getSummary(month) yourself (without looking at the example) and print, for 2025-12-01, one line per row: insurer_id exceptions.

Write getExceptions(f) as in db.ts, where f may have insurer_id, month and kinds (an array). Call it with { insurer_id: 3, kinds: ['ambiguous', 'amount_difference'] } and print the number of rows, then the keys joined with , .
expectedLogs: ambiguous:-:136, ambiguous:-:237, amount:167:345, amount:220:129, amount:222:135, amount:268:206, amount:290:372, amount:328:278, amount:33:180, amount:36:341

exercises.prompt: getMe in the real app looks up the staff row of the signed-in user. Here, write it with a parameter userId and .maybeSingle(), returning null when there's no staff row. Print the result for Bas (b0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000002) and for Dana (d0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000004).

In the real app: sign in, choose January 2026, and compare the summary on screen with SELECT * FROM recon_summary WHERE month = '2026-01-01' in the SQL editor. Write down in comments whether they match and, if your project has fewer statements than the course database, why the numbers differ.
exercises.solution:
-- They should match row for row: the screen shows recon_summary unchanged.
-- Your project only has the statements you imported yourself (nhv_2026-02.csv in Module 7),
-- so most insurer-months show every invoice as missing_on_statement. That's correct for your data.

lessons.project: Get the app running (steps 1–5). Sign in, open an exception, and record a decision. Then check in the SQL editor that the new row is in exception_reviews with your staff id. Commit the app folder to git without .env.local (add it to .gitignore).
recap: The publishable key and URL go in .env.local; never the secret key.
Screens call db.ts; db.ts returns data or throws a readable error.
The stand-in client runs the same calls, so you can try changes here first.

lessons.title: The import as one function
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can turn a multi-step change into one SQL function and call it from the app with rpc.
lessons.explain:
Each Data API request is one transaction. Two requests (batch, then lines) can't be all-or-nothing together; Module 10 showed what goes wrong. The fix: put the whole import in one SQL function and call it once:

const { data, error } = await supabase.rpc('import_statement', { p_insurer_id: 5, p_statement_month: '2026-04-01', p_file_name: 'kst_2026-04.csv', p_rows: rows });

import_statement takes the CSV rows as text (a JSON array), and does everything inside one transaction:

  1. checks the input and names the first bad row before inserting anything
  2. computes the content hash (same rule as Module 7)
  3. inserts the batch with ON CONFLICT (file_sha256) DO NOTHING: a re-import changes nothing and says so
  4. converts Dutch dates and decimal commas in SQL and inserts the lines
  5. checks the number of inserted lines and returns a small JSON result

Any error anywhere rolls back the whole call. The function is written in PL/pgSQL, PostgreSQL's procedural language: DECLARE variables, SELECT … INTO, IF … THEN, RAISE EXCEPTION, RETURN. You'll read it more than write it; the shape is what matters.

Grants: functions are executable by everyone by default, so the migration revokes that and grants it to authenticated only. It runs with the caller's rights (SECURITY INVOKER, the default), so the caller needs INSERT on the import tables: grant that in the same migration.

examples.note: The function, as in migration 0007.

rows: p_insurer_id integer, p_statement_month date, p_file_name text, p_rows jsonb

examples.note: A supplementary KST statement for April 2026, imported twice. The second call changes nothing.
The same call from JavaScript, as db.ts does it.

mistakes.text: A row with an ISO date (2026-04-02) instead of the insurer's dd-mm-yyyy. The function refuses the whole file and names the row, and nothing was inserted.
mistakes.error: Row 2: unexpected value in {"amount": "670,40", "line_type": "premium", "commission": "134,08", "booking_date": "2026-04-03", "policy_number": "KST-177395", "invoice_reference": "INV-2026-00090"}

exercises.prompt: Import the three KST lines (as in example 2, file name kst_2026-04.csv), then show what happened to the two invoices: the exceptions of insurer 5 whose invoice_id is 154 or 178, as exception_key and kind, ordered by key. They were missing; now they're timing differences.

The third line (KST 751199, no reference, booked in April) didn't resolve missing:211:- (a November invoice). Import the file again as above, then show both exceptions involved: the key of the new line's exception and of invoice 211, with kind and evidence, ordered by key. In one comment, say which rule kept them apart.

From JavaScript: import the same three lines with supabase.rpc, then call it again. Print the status of both results, then the batch_id of the first and the existing_batch_id of the second (they must be equal).

From JavaScript: a file with a bad amount, three decimals: '12,505'. Call import_statement with one such row and print error.message. Then check with a second call that no batch with file name bad.csv exists: print the number of rows import_batches returns for that name.

Review the AI. The function converts '1.234,50' by removing dots and then turning the comma into a dot. An AI suggests replace(amount, ',', '.')::numeric only, "because it's simpler". Show in SQL what each gives for '1.234,50', as columns ours and ai, and explain the AI's result in a comment.
exercises.solution:
-- The AI version turns '1.234,50' into '1.234.50', which is not a number: the cast fails.
-- For '1.234' (one thousand two hundred thirty-four in Dutch notation) it would silently give 1.234.
SELECT replace(replace('1.234,50', '.', ''), ',', '.')::numeric AS ours,
       (SELECT CASE WHEN replace('1.234,50', ',', '.') ~ '^-?[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?$' THEN replace('1.234,50', ',', '.') ELSE 'not a number' END) AS ai;

lessons.project: Run migration 0007 and the import-table grant in harbourline-recon. In the app, import kst_2026-04.csv for KST (create the KST insurer data first if your project lacks it: the starter script has all six insurers), then import it again and read the "already imported" message.
recap: One API request is one transaction; multi-step work goes into one SQL function, called with rpc.
Validate everything first, name the bad row, then insert.
Parsing rules live in SQL, in one place; the content hash makes imports idempotent.

lessons.title: Decisions and saved views from the screen
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can write the app's changes with the protections from Modules 9 and 10, and show failures to the user.
lessons.explain:
Two kinds of change leave the app:

Decisions are inserts into exception_reviews. There's nothing to overwrite, so two people deciding at once is safe; both rows are kept. The app sends reviewed_by = the user's own staff id. (Until Module 12, the database doesn't check that. A user could send someone else's id. RLS will close that.)

Saved views are updates, so they use the version check: update({ …, version: v + 1 }).eq('view_id', id).eq('version', v). Zero rows back means someone else changed it: show "changed elsewhere, reload" instead of silently overwriting.

Showing failures. Every db.ts function throws an Error with a readable message; the screen catches it and shows it next to the button the user pressed. A CHECK violation, a missing grant or a network error all reach the user as text, never as a silently empty list.

examples.note: addReview and the history, as in db.ts.
updateView with the version check: the first save wins, the second is told to reload.

mistakes.text: Swallowing the error: catch (e) {} or if (error) return []. The screen then shows "No exceptions match these filters" when in fact the request was refused. In a reconciliation app that reads as "all clear".

exercises.prompt: Write addReview(staffId, key, decision, note) so that an empty or whitespace-only note is stored as null. Record accepted with note ' ' for rounding:6:343 by staff 1, then print the stored note of the newest review for that key (it must print null).

A needs_info decision must have a note (the constraint from Module 9). Try to record one without a note and print the user-facing message your addReview throws, by catching the error and printing e.message.
expectedLogs: Saving the decision: new row for relation "exception_reviews" violates check constraint "needs_info_has_note"

exercises.prompt: Write renameView(v, newName) with the version check, returning 'saved' or 'changed elsewhere'. Load view 3, rename it to NHV open work, then try renaming with the same loaded object to NHV all. Print both results, then the final name and version from the database.

Review the AI. An AI "simplified" getExceptions like this. Run it with a typo in the view name to see what the screen would show, then write in a comment what's wrong and fix it so the failure is visible: print the thrown message.
expectedLogs: Loading exceptions: relation "recon_exception" does not exist

lessons.project: In the app, open the same saved view in two browser tabs, change it in both, and see the second tab's "changed elsewhere". Then add a visible "Reload" button next to that message (your first change to main.ts; keep it small).
recap: Decisions are inserts; saved views are updates with a version check.
Every failure reaches the user as text.
Until Module 12, the database trusts the reviewed_by the app sends.

lessons.title: The CLI, types and cold changes
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can manage migrations with the Supabase CLI and change the app independently.
lessons.explain:
So far you've pasted migrations into the SQL editor. The Supabase CLI keeps them as files in your repository and applies them in order:

Command Does
npx supabase init creates supabase/ in your app folder
npx supabase login, npx supabase link --project-ref <ref> connects the folder to your project
npx supabase migration new reviews_index creates supabase/migrations/<timestamp>_reviews_index.sql
npx supabase migration list which migrations ran on the linked project
npx supabase db push applies the new ones
npx supabase db dump -f supabase/schema.sql saves the current schema as a file (Module 14 uses this for backups)
npx supabase gen types typescript --linked > src/database.types.ts TypeScript types for your tables and views

Move your existing files 0001…0008 into supabase/migrations/ with timestamp-style names in the same order, then migration list shows which ones the project already has. Mark those as applied with npx supabase migration repair --status applied <version>, so db push doesn't try to run them again.

Generated types let TypeScript check your queries. With createClient<Database>(…), a typo like .from('recon_exception') or .eq('insurer', 1) is a compile error instead of a runtime error. Regenerate after every migration.

Cold changes are the independence check of this module: three changes to the real app, done without AI and without the solutions, timed. Each has a check you can do yourself. Write down the time and whether you needed help.

examples.note: The CLI workflow in a terminal, in your app folder.
examples.sql:
-- npx supabase init
-- npx supabase login
-- npx supabase link --project-ref abcdefghijklmnop
-- npx supabase migration new reviews_by_key_index
--   (edit the new file:)
CREATE INDEX exception_reviews_key_time ON exception_reviews (exception_key, reviewed_at DESC);
-- npx supabase db push
-- npx supabase gen types typescript --linked > src/database.types.ts

exercises.prompt: Write, as comments, the commands to (1) create a new migration called staff_active_index, (2) apply it, (3) regenerate the types, in that order.
exercises.solution:
-- npx supabase migration new staff_active_index
--   (write: CREATE INDEX staff_active ON staff (active);)
-- npx supabase db push
-- npx supabase gen types typescript --linked > src/database.types.ts

exercises.prompt: Cold change 1 (timed, no AI). In the exception list, show the insurer's name instead of its code, and add a column "Reviewed by" with the full name of whoever made the current decision. Check: the list for NHV January shows Noordhaven and your own name on the exception you decided. Compare your diff with the solution afterwards.

Cold change 2 (timed, no AI). Add a checkbox Only open to the filter form. When it's ticked, the list leaves out exceptions whose current decision is anything other than needs_info. Check: tick it, record accepted on a listed exception, and it disappears from the list after the refresh.

Cold change 3 (timed, no AI). The team lead wants the import screen to refuse files larger than 5,000 lines before sending them, with a clear message. Make the change in onImport and also decide whether the function should check it too. Write your answer to that second question as a comment.

lessons.project: Set up the CLI in your app folder, link the project, repair the history of the migrations you already ran, and push a new migration with the index from the example. Generate the types and switch db.ts to createClient<Database>(…); fix any type errors npm run check reports.
recap: Migrations live in supabase/migrations and are applied with db push.
Generated types turn query typos into compile errors.
Cold changes measure what you can do alone; keep your times.

quiz.text: Which key may go in the browser app?

options.text: Both, if the repository is private
Neither; the browser needs no key

quiz.explain: The publishable key is public by design; the secret key bypasses RLS.

quiz.text: Why is the import a SQL function instead of two inserts from JavaScript?

options.text: One rpc call is one transaction: all lines or nothing
supabase-js can't insert into two tables

quiz.explain: Two requests are two transactions; a failure in between leaves half a batch.

quiz.text: authenticated has INSERT but not UPDATE on exception_reviews. What does that guarantee?

options.text: Decisions can't be changed afterwards through the API, so the history stays append-only
Only the team lead can insert

quiz.explain: The database enforces the rule, whatever any client code does.

quiz.text: updateView returns zero rows. What should the screen do?

options.text: Say the view was changed elsewhere and offer a reload

quiz.explain: Zero rows means the version you read is no longer current.

quiz.text:
Predict the status of the result.

SELECT import_statement(5, '2026-04-01', 'x.csv', '[{"policy_number": "KST-354648", "invoice_reference": "", "booking_date": "02-04-2026", "amount": "10,88", "commission": "2,18", "line_type": "premium"}]') ->> 'status' AS status;
quiz.answer: `imported`, with a new batch: no earlier file had exactly this content.
quiz.explain: The duplicate check compares content, not file names.

practical.prompt: No AI. Write async function importAndReport(insurerId, month, fileName, rows) that imports with rpc('import_statement', …) and then prints exactly: on success, imported N lines as batch B, followed by the number of exceptions of that insurer in that month from recon_summary as exceptions now: X (or exceptions now: 0 when the summary has no row); on a duplicate, already imported as batch B; on an error, refused: <message>. Call it three times: the three KST lines for 2026-04-01 (kst_2026-04.csv), the same again, and a single line with booking date 2026-04-02.

modules.intro:
You'll connect three things: your Supabase project (the database you've been building since Module 2), the starter app (given to you, working), and your own SQL. The app is a plain web page built with Vite and TypeScript. You don't need a framework: the screens are in main.ts, and every database call is in db.ts.

The course database here now has everything of migrations 0001 to 0006 (including the version column on saved_views), plus the stand-in roles anon and authenticated that Supabase uses.

Security comes in two steps. This module gives the app access with GRANT, for signed-in users only. Module 12 adds row level security, so each role sees only what it should. Until you've done Module 12, keep the project to test users only.

modules.title: Access control and row level security
modules.summary: Decide in the database who may see and change what: roles and privileges, functions and views that run as someone else, SQL injection, and row level security for the team and for personal saved views.
objectives: Explain how roles, owners, privileges and SECURITY DEFINER functions decide what a query may do.
Find and fix SQL injection in dynamic SQL with format() and USING.
Write RLS policies with USING and WITH CHECK, and test them as different users.
Close the view bypass with security_invoker views.
Produce an access matrix for Anna (team lead), Bas (reconciler), Chris (viewer), Dana (login, not on the team) and anon.

lessons.title: Roles, owners and code that runs as someone else
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can say with whose rights a query, a view and a function run, and why that matters.
lessons.explain:
Every query runs as a role. Whether it may touch a table depends on:

  1. Superuser: may do anything, RLS doesn't apply. The course's own role and Supabase's postgres role are like this; the API roles are not.
  2. Owner: whoever created the table. Owners have all privileges and, by default, bypass RLS on their own tables.
  3. Privileges granted with GRANT (Module 11).
  4. RLS policies (lessons 12.3 and 12.4), checked after privileges.

Two kinds of objects run with someone else's rights:

  • Views, by default, read their tables with the view owner's rights. A signed-in user who may read recon_exceptions therefore reads premium_invoices through it, even without a grant, and RLS on those tables is checked for the owner, so it doesn't restrict anything. With ALTER VIEW … SET (security_invoker = true) the view uses the caller's rights instead.
  • Functions with SECURITY DEFINER run with the function owner's rights. Useful for one carefully limited task (like "what is my role?"), dangerous otherwise. Always add SET search_path = '' and write table names with their schema, so a caller can't slip in a look-alike table.

The policies of this module need to know who is calling. Two small SECURITY DEFINER functions answer that from staff; they must bypass staff's own policies, otherwise every policy would loop back to itself.

examples.note: The API roles: none of them is a superuser, and only service_role (the secret key) bypasses RLS.
examples.sql: SELECT rolname, rolsuper, rolbypassrls, rolcanlogin FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname IN ('anon', 'authenticated', 'service_role') ORDER BY rolname;

examples.note: The view bypass, shown. authenticated has no grant on premium_invoices, yet reads what's computed from every invoice through recon_exceptions.
Who is calling? The two helper functions of migration 0009.
Playing Bas: the functions see his login.

mistakes.text: Without a grant, reading the table directly is refused. That's the privileges working; the problem is only the view path above.
mistakes.sql:
SET LOCAL ROLE authenticated;
SELECT count(*) FROM premium_invoices;
mistakes.error: permission denied for table premium_invoices

exercises.prompt: Play Dana and show auth.uid() as uid, current_staff_role() as staff_role and current_staff_id() as staff_id. Dana has a login but no staff row.
Play anon (no set_config needed) and show whether it may execute current_staff_role(), with has_function_privilege('current_staff_role()', 'EXECUTE'), as anon_may_execute.
exercises.solution:
SET LOCAL ROLE anon;
SELECT has_function_privilege('current_staff_role()', 'EXECUTE') AS anon_may_execute;

exercises.prompt: Make recon_ours use the caller's rights and show its options from pg_class.reloptions (as options). Then, as authenticated, try to count its rows in Run (not in your answer): now the missing grant on premium_invoices shows.
exercises.solution:
ALTER VIEW recon_ours SET (security_invoker = true);
SELECT reloptions AS options FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'recon_ours';

exercises.prompt: Review the AI. An AI wrote this helper "so the app can check roles". In comments, name the two problems and what an attacker with a normal login could do, then write the safe version, named staff_role_of_me(), and show prosecdef and proconfig for it.
exercises.solution:
-- 1. It takes ANY user id: anyone can ask for anyone's role (and, via SECURITY DEFINER, past staff's RLS).
--    The safe version only answers for the caller: auth.uid().
-- 2. No SET search_path: a caller who can create objects could make a schema with their own "staff"
--    table earlier in the search path and have the function read that instead.
CREATE FUNCTION staff_role_of_me() RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql STABLE SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = ''
AS $$ SELECT s.role FROM public.staff s WHERE s.user_id = auth.uid() AND s.active $$;
SELECT prosecdef, proconfig FROM pg_proc WHERE proname = 'staff_role_of_me';
exercises.starter:
CREATE FUNCTION role_of(p_user uuid) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql SECURITY DEFINER
AS $$ SELECT role FROM staff WHERE user_id = p_user $$;

lessons.project: In harbourline-recon, open Database → Roles and compare with the table above. Read the list of functions in Database → Functions and mark which ones are SECURITY DEFINER. You'll add the two helper functions in lesson 12.4.
recap: Superusers and owners bypass RLS; the API roles don't, except service_role.
Views run as their owner unless security_invoker = true.
SECURITY DEFINER functions: answer only for the caller, SET search_path = '', schema-qualified names.

lessons.title: SQL injection
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can spot dynamic SQL that mixes in user input, and fix it.
lessons.explain:
SQL injection happens when text from a user becomes part of the SQL code instead of a value. Then the user can change what the query does.

supabase-js and the stand-in client always send values separately from the SQL, so .eq('kind', userText) is safe. The danger is in your own SQL functions that build a statement as text and run it with EXECUTE, typically for "flexible" search or sorting.

Need Safe tool
a value (WHERE kind = …) EXECUTE '… WHERE kind = $1' USING p_kind
a value inside a built string format('… WHERE kind = %L', p_kind) (%L quotes it as a literal)
a column or table name format('… ORDER BY %I', p_column) (%I quotes it as an identifier), and check it against a list
never '… WHERE kind = ''' || p_kind || ''''

Even with %I, an identifier from a user can name a column you didn't mean to expose; a fixed list of allowed names is the real protection.

examples.note: A vulnerable search function.
The attack: the input closes the quote and adds its own condition.
examples.sql: SELECT count_exceptions_bad($x$nothing' OR '1' = '1$x$) AS injected;

examples.note: The fixed version: the value travels separately with USING.

mistakes.text: Injection can also read other tables. Here the injected text makes PostgreSQL convert a staff name to a number; the conversion fails, and the error message hands over the name. The vulnerable function runs it.
mistakes.sql: SELECT count_exceptions_bad($x$x' OR 1 = (SELECT full_name::int FROM staff ORDER BY staff_id LIMIT 1) OR 'a' = 'b$x$);
mistakes.error: invalid input syntax for type integer: "Anna de Wit"

exercises.prompt: What does format() produce? Show format('WHERE kind = %L', $x$it's$x$) as literal and format('ORDER BY %I', 'Our Amount') as ident.
exercises.solution: SELECT format('WHERE kind = %L', $x$it's$x$) AS literal, format('ORDER BY %I', 'Our Amount') AS ident;

exercises.prompt: Write count_exceptions_for(p_insurer_id integer, p_kind text) with EXECUTE and two USING parameters ($1, $2). Show its result for insurer 1 and kind missing_on_statement, as n.

A sortable list: top_exceptions(p_sort text) returns the 3 exception_keys ordered by the column named in p_sort, which may only be difference, month or exception_key; anything else raises invalid sort column. Use format with %I. Show SELECT * FROM top_exceptions('difference').

Review the AI. An AI fixed the vulnerable function with replace(p_kind, '''', '') ("remove the quotes"). In comments, say why escaping by hand is the wrong fix even if this particular attack stops, then show that count_exceptions (the USING version) handles an input with a quote, $x$o'brien$x$, without error: result as n.
exercises.solution:
-- Hand-made escaping is easy to get subtly wrong (backslashes, other quote styles, identifiers, numbers
-- compared as text) and it changes the data: a real value with a quote can no longer be searched.
-- USING keeps code and value apart, so there's nothing to escape.
SELECT count_exceptions($x$o'brien$x$) AS n;

lessons.project: Search your harbourline-recon functions for EXECUTE (in the SQL editor: SELECT proname FROM pg_proc WHERE prosrc ILIKE '%execute%' AND pronamespace = 'public'::regnamespace). There should be none yet; keep it that way, or use USING.
recap: Injection turns input into code; it lives in dynamic SQL.
Values: USING or %L. Names: %I plus an allow-list.
The client libraries already separate values; your functions must too.

lessons.title: Row level security for saved views
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can enable RLS on a table, write policies for reading and writing, and prove them as different users.
lessons.explain:
Row level security adds a condition to every query on a table, per role and command:

ALTER TABLE saved_views ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY own_views ON saved_views FOR ALL TO authenticated
  USING (owner_id = (SELECT auth.uid()))          -- which existing rows you may see / update / delete
  WITH CHECK (owner_id = (SELECT auth.uid()));    -- which new or changed rows you may write
  • With RLS on and no policy, the API roles see nothing and can write nothing. "Deny by default".
  • USING filters rows for SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE. Rows that fail it are invisible: no error, just fewer rows.
  • WITH CHECK is tested on rows being INSERTed or UPDATEd. Failing it is an error.
  • FOR SELECT | INSERT | UPDATE | DELETE | ALL picks the command; several policies for the same command are combined with OR.
  • Policies come on top of privileges: the role still needs the GRANT.
  • Write function calls in a policy as (SELECT auth.uid()), not auth.uid(). Wrapped like this, PostgreSQL calls the function once per query instead of once per row. On the reconciliation views, that's the difference between instant and many seconds.

Saved views are personal: you see, change and delete only your own. A default of auth.uid() for owner_id means the app doesn't even send it.

examples.note: Turn RLS on: from now on, signed-in users see no saved views at all.
examples.sql:
ALTER TABLE saved_views ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
SELECT relname, relrowsecurity FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'saved_views';

examples.note: Deny by default: Anna has two saved views, but sees none.
The policy, and the default owner.

rows: ((owner_id = ( SELECT auth.uid() AS uid)) AND (( SELECT current_staff_role() AS current_staff_role) IS NOT NULL))

examples.note: Now Anna sees her own two, and Bas his one.

mistakes.text: Bas tries to create a view in Anna's name. WITH CHECK refuses it with an error.
mistakes.error: new row violates row-level security policy for table "saved_views"

exercises.prompt: As Bas, list the names of the saved views he can see.
As Bas, try to rename Anna's view 1 to Hacked. It doesn't fail; it changes 0 rows, because the row is invisible to him. End with the UPDATE … RETURNING view_id.
As Chris, save a new view Everything without sending owner_id, and return name and whether owner_id is his id (owner_id = auth.uid() as mine).

Dana has a login but isn't staff. Prove that the policy stops her from saving a view: as Dana, insert a view Dana's and show the error in Run. For the check, as Dana, return current_staff_role() IS NULL as not_staff and the number of saved views she can see as visible.

Review the AI. An AI wrote CREATE POLICY views_read ON saved_views FOR SELECT TO authenticated USING (true); "so team leads can help people with their views". In comments, say what it does to the personal feature, given that policies for the same command are combined with OR, and write the narrower policy lead_reads_views that lets only a team_lead read everyone's views. Show polname of the policies on saved_views, ordered.

lessons.project: In harbourline-recon, enable RLS on saved_views with the policy and default above (add current_staff_role() from lesson 12.1 first). In the app, sign in as yourself and as a second test user, and check that each sees only their own views.
recap: RLS on + no policy = nothing visible, nothing writable.
USING hides rows silently; WITH CHECK refuses writes with an error.
Policies are OR'ed per command: one broad policy undoes the narrow ones.

lessons.title: RLS for the team
lessons.goal: Afterwards the whole app follows the access model in the database, and you can prove it with a matrix.
lessons.explain:
The access model of Harbourline Recon:

Anna (team_lead) Bas (reconciler) Chris (viewer) Dana (not staff) anon
read exceptions, summary, statements yes yes yes no no
record a decision yes, as herself yes, as himself no no no
change or delete a decision no no no no no
import a statement yes yes no no no
saved views own own own none none

How the pieces fit:

  1. Views use the caller's rights (security_invoker = true), so policies on the base tables apply through every view. The caller then needs SELECT on the base tables and on the views in between.
  2. Base tables get "staff only" SELECT policies: USING ((SELECT current_staff_role()) IS NOT NULL).
  3. Reviews: SELECT for staff; INSERT only for team_lead and reconciler, and only with reviewed_by = current_staff_id(). No UPDATE or DELETE policy, so those are impossible even with a grant.
  4. Imports: INSERT policies on import_batches and statement_lines for the same two roles. import_statement runs with the caller's rights, so the policies apply to it too.

examples.note: Steps 1 and 2: invoker views and staff-only reading.
Steps 3 and 4: decisions and imports.
The view bypass is closed: Dana now sees nothing through the views either.

mistakes.text: Bas records a decision in Anna's name (reviewed_by = 1). The policy refuses it: the app can no longer put words in someone else's mouth.
mistakes.error: new row violates row-level security policy for table "exception_reviews"

exercises.prompt: As Bas, record his own decision on missing:204:- (to_insurer, note Asked KST), using current_staff_id() for reviewed_by, and return exception_key and reviewed_by.

As Chris (viewer), show how many exceptions he can read, as exceptions, and whether he may insert into exception_reviews according to the privileges, as has_grant. (He has the grant, but the policy refuses him; try an insert in Run to see the error.)

As Anna, try to change an existing decision: UPDATE exception_reviews SET note = 'edited' WHERE exception_key = 'missing:82:-'. With RLS on and no UPDATE policy, what happens? Grant UPDATE to authenticated first (as the course's own role, before switching), so you see the policy and not the privilege at work. End with the UPDATE RETURNING review_id.

As Chris, call import_statement for KST (insurer 5, 2026-04-01) with one line. It must be refused by the policy. Show the error in Run. For the check, as Bas, import the same line and return the result's status (->> 'status') as status.

The access matrix. Build a temporary table matrix (who text, exceptions bigint, staff bigint, views bigint) as the course role, grant it to authenticated, then for Anna, Bas, Chris and Dana in turn: set the user, SET LOCAL ROLE authenticated, insert one row with what they see, and RESET ROLE. End with SELECT * FROM matrix ORDER BY who.

lessons.project: Run migration 0009 in harbourline-recon (it contains everything of lessons 12.1, 12.3 and 12.4; skip parts you already ran). Then open Advisors → Security Advisor in the dashboard and resolve what it reports. In the app, sign in as a test user without a staff row: the app must show nothing but its sign-in message.
recap: security_invoker views + staff-only policies on base tables close the view bypass.
Decisions: INSERT policy with reviewed_by = current_staff_id(); no UPDATE or DELETE policy.
Prove the access model with a matrix, per user.

quiz.text: RLS is enabled on a table and there are no policies. What does authenticated see?
quiz.explain: Deny by default.

quiz.text: Why did Dana see all exceptions through recon_exceptions before lesson 12.4?

options.text: The view read the tables with its owner's rights, so the base tables' policies didn't apply to her

quiz.explain: Views run as their owner unless security_invoker = true.

quiz.text: Bas updates Anna's saved view and gets "UPDATE 0", no error. Why?

options.text: The update failed silently because of a bug
USING hides Anna's row from Bas, so there is nothing to update

quiz.explain: USING filters silently; WITH CHECK errors.

quiz.text: Which is a safe way to use a user-supplied kind in dynamic SQL?
quiz.explain: USING passes it as a value. %I is for names, not values.

quiz.text:
Predict the three numbers.

SELECT set_config('request.jwt.claim.sub', 'c0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000003', true);
SET LOCAL ROLE authenticated;
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM saved_views) AS views, (SELECT count(*) FROM staff) AS staff, current_staff_role() AS role;
quiz.answer: `0` views (he owns none, and saved views are personal), `3` staff (the team is visible to the team), role `viewer`.
quiz.explain: Policies apply per user; the viewer reads the team but owns no views.

practical.prompt: The team adds a comment feature: anyone on the team can comment on an exception; only the author may delete their own comment; nobody edits comments. Create exception_comments (comment_id identity PK, exception_key required, body required, author_id integer FK to staff, default current_staff_id(), created_at default now()), grant authenticated SELECT, INSERT and DELETE, enable RLS, and write the policies (read: staff; insert: staff, as themselves; delete: own). Prove it: as Chris add a comment Checked the PDF on ambiguous:-:125; as Bas try to delete it (0 rows); then, as the course role, save the number of comments in a temporary table after_bas; as Chris delete it. End, as the course role (RESET ROLE), with after_bas (must be 1) and after_chris (must be 0).

modules.intro:
The course database now has the grants of migration 0008. Everyone signed in can read the views, insert reviews and change saved views. That's too much: Dana is not on the team, Chris only views, and everyone can see and change everyone's saved views. This module fixes it in the database, where no client can get around it.

Playing a user. Supabase runs each request as the role authenticated with the user's id in a setting that auth.uid() reads. The course does the same, inside the transaction of your exercise:

SELECT set_config('request.jwt.claim.sub', 'b0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000002', true);  -- Bas
SET LOCAL ROLE authenticated;
User Id starts with On the team as
Anna a0000000-…-000000000001 team_lead
Bas b0000000-…-000000000002 reconciler
Chris c0000000-…-000000000003 viewer
Dana d0000000-…-000000000004 not staff (has a login)

RESET ROLE switches back to the course's own (superuser) role.

modules.title: Performance and indexes
modules.summary: Read query plans, add the right indexes (and know their cost), and fix the slow patterns that come from apps: N+1 queries, deep OFFSET paging and recomputing heavy views.
objectives: Read an EXPLAIN plan: scan types, filters, sorts, and what ANALYZE adds.
Choose B-tree, multicolumn, expression and partial indexes for real queries, and say what each costs on writes.
Recognize when an index can't be used.
Replace N+1 queries with one query, OFFSET paging with keyset paging, and decide when a materialized view is worth it.

lessons.title: Reading a query plan
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can tell from a plan how PostgreSQL finds the rows, and spot the expensive step.
lessons.explain:
EXPLAIN query shows the plan: a tree of steps, read from the most indented line upwards. Each step produces rows for the one above it.

Node Means Fast when
Seq Scan read every row of the table the table is small, or you need most rows
Index Scan find rows through an index, then fetch them few rows match
Index Only Scan answer from the index alone all needed columns are in the index
Bitmap Index/Heap Scan collect matches from an index, fetch them in table order a moderate number of rows match
Sort order rows (in memory or on disk) few rows, or avoidable with an index in the right order
Hash Join / Nested Loop / Merge Join the three ways to join depends on sizes and indexes
Filter: a condition checked row by row, after fetching
Index Cond: a condition answered by the index

EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and adds the real time and real row counts per step. When the estimated rows (rows=) and the actual rows differ a lot, PostgreSQL's statistics are off: run ANALYZE table.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE on an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE really changes data. Wrap it in BEGIN; … ROLLBACK;.

examples.note: Finding one line by its primary key: an index scan.
examples.sql: SELECT * FROM plan_of('SELECT * FROM big_lines WHERE line_id = 5');

rows: Index Scan using big_lines_pkey on big_lines

examples.note: Finding a policy's lines: there's no index on policy_key, so every one of the 100,000 rows is read and filtered.
examples.sql: SELECT * FROM plan_of('SELECT * FROM big_lines WHERE policy_key = ''POL001234''');

examples.note: The current review of one key: read everything, filter, then sort. Three steps that an index can replace (next lesson).
examples.sql: SELECT * FROM plan_of('SELECT * FROM big_reviews WHERE exception_key = ''line:5'' ORDER BY reviewed_at DESC LIMIT 1');

examples.note: EXPLAIN ANALYZE with real times. Your times will differ from the ones shown, and the browser is slower than a server; compare steps, not milliseconds.
examples.sql: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT count(*) FROM big_lines WHERE policy_key = 'POL001234';

rows: Aggregate  (cost=2146.01..2146.02 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=12.072..12.074 rows=1.00 loops=1)
->  Seq Scan on big_lines  (cost=0.00..2146.00 rows=3 width=0) (actual time=1.987..12.053 rows=3.00 loops=1)

mistakes.text: Running EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a DELETE without a transaction deletes the rows. Here the course rolls it back for you; in psql, it wouldn't.
mistakes.sql: EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM big_reviews WHERE decision = 'needs_info';

rows: Delete on big_reviews  (cost=0.00..1073.00 rows=0 width=0) (actual time=16.998..16.999 rows=0.00 loops=1)
->  Seq Scan on big_reviews  (cost=0.00..1073.00 rows=9867 width=6) (actual time=0.012..9.371 rows=10000.00 loops=1)

exercises.prompt: Show the plan of SELECT * FROM big_lines WHERE insurer_id = 3 AND month = '2025-01-01' with plan_of.
exercises.solution: SELECT * FROM plan_of('SELECT * FROM big_lines WHERE insurer_id = 3 AND month = ''2025-01-01''');

exercises.prompt: Does the join of big_reviews to big_lines on 'line:' || line_id = exception_key use an index on big_lines? Return plan_uses(…, 'Index') as uses_index and plan_uses(…, 'Hash Join') as hash_join for SELECT count(*) FROM big_reviews r JOIN big_lines l ON 'line:' || l.line_id = r.exception_key.
exercises.solution:
SELECT plan_uses('SELECT count(*) FROM big_reviews r JOIN big_lines l ON ''line:'' || l.line_id = r.exception_key', 'Index') AS uses_index,
       plan_uses('SELECT count(*) FROM big_reviews r JOIN big_lines l ON ''line:'' || l.line_id = r.exception_key', 'Hash Join') AS hash_join;

exercises.prompt: Which reconciliation view is the heaviest to compute? Show the plan of SELECT count(*) FROM recon_exceptions and count its lines: return the number of plan lines as plan_lines and whether it contains a Sort as sorts.
exercises.solution: SELECT count(*) AS plan_lines, bool_or(p LIKE '%Sort%') AS sorts FROM plan_of('SELECT count(*) FROM recon_exceptions') AS p;

exercises.prompt: Review the AI. To "check why the import is slow", an AI ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT import_statement(…) on the production database. In comments, say what that did, and how to measure it safely.
exercises.solution:
-- EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement: the import really happened (a batch and its lines were inserted).
-- Also, a function call shows as one opaque step; the plans inside it aren't shown.
-- Safely: BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT import_statement(...); ROLLBACK;  on a copy or test project,
-- and for the inner statements, EXPLAIN them one by one, or enable auto_explain on a test database.

lessons.project: In the Supabase SQL editor, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM recon_exceptions; on harbourline-recon and note the total time and the slowest step in app/notes.md. You'll compare after this module.
recap: Read plans bottom-up: scans, then joins, sorts and limits.
Filter = checked row by row; Index Cond = answered by an index.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the statement; wrap changes in BEGIN … ROLLBACK.

lessons.title: Choosing indexes
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can pick the index that serves a given query, and explain when an index won't help.
lessons.explain:
An index is a sorted copy of some columns with pointers to the rows. A B-tree (the default) serves =, <, >, BETWEEN, IN, ORDER BY and LIKE 'abc%'.

Kind Example Serves
single column ON big_lines (policy_key) WHERE policy_key = …
multicolumn ON big_reviews (exception_key, reviewed_at DESC) WHERE exception_key = … ORDER BY reviewed_at DESC: filter and order, so no Sort
expression ON statement_lines (upper(invoice_reference)) WHERE upper(invoice_reference) = …
partial ON big_reviews (exception_key) WHERE decision = 'needs_info' the open-work query only; small
unique UNIQUE (batch_id, source_row) a rule and an index

Column order matters in a multicolumn index: it works for the first column alone, or the first and second, but not for the second alone. Put the equality columns first, then the range or sort column.

An index is not used when:

  • the query wraps the column in a function the index doesn't have (WHERE upper(policy_key) = … vs an index on policy_key)
  • LIKE '%abc' (leading wildcard)
  • most rows match anyway: reading the whole table is then cheaper
  • the types differ (WHERE line_id = '5'::text)

Every index costs disk space and time on every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, because it has to be kept up to date. Add indexes for queries you actually run; check pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan later and drop unused ones.

Foreign keys don't get an index automatically. A join or delete on the referencing column (like statement_lines.batch_id) usually wants one.

examples.note: One index, two plans: before and after.
The current review without a Sort: a multicolumn index in the order of the query.

rows: ->  Index Scan using big_reviews_key_time on big_reviews

examples.note: Wrapping the column in a function hides it from the index.
examples.sql:
SELECT plan_uses('SELECT * FROM big_lines WHERE policy_key = ''POL001234''', 'big_lines_policy_key') AS plain,
       plan_uses('SELECT * FROM big_lines WHERE lower(policy_key) = ''pol001234''', 'big_lines_policy_key') AS wrapped;

examples.note: What the indexes cost in space, next to the table itself.

mistakes.text: An index on the wrong column order. The query filters on reviewed_at alone; an index that starts with exception_key can't serve it.
mistakes.sql:
CREATE INDEX wrong_order ON big_reviews (exception_key, reviewed_at);
SELECT plan_uses('SELECT * FROM big_reviews WHERE reviewed_at >= ''2025-01-20'' AND reviewed_at < ''2025-01-21''', 'wrong_order') AS uses_it;

exercises.prompt: Make SELECT * FROM big_lines WHERE upper(invoice_reference) = 'INV-000005' use an index. Create it as big_lines_ref_upper, run ANALYZE big_lines, and return plan_uses(…, 'big_lines_ref_upper') as uses_index.

The open-work query is SELECT exception_key FROM big_reviews WHERE decision = 'needs_info' AND reviewed_by = 2. Create a partial index big_reviews_open on (reviewed_by) for needs_info rows only, analyze, and return whether the plan uses it, as uses_index, and the index size in bytes compared with a full index on (reviewed_by), as partial_is_smaller (create the full one as big_reviews_by to compare).

Review the AI. "To make everything fast", an AI created an index on every column of big_lines. In comments, give two costs, then write the query that lists the indexes on big_lines with their size, from pg_indexes joined to pg_class (indexname, pg_relation_size(…) as bytes), ordered by name. (With only the primary key, that's one row.)
exercises.solution:
-- Costs: every INSERT/UPDATE of a line now updates 6 indexes (imports get slower), and the indexes
-- can be larger than the table. Most of them will never be used: low-selectivity columns like
-- insurer_id are read faster by a scan. Index the queries you run, then check idx_scan.
SELECT i.indexname, pg_relation_size(c.oid) AS bytes
FROM pg_indexes i JOIN pg_class c ON c.relname = i.indexname
WHERE i.tablename = 'big_lines' ORDER BY i.indexname;

lessons.title: Slow patterns from apps
lessons.goal: Afterwards you can recognize and fix N+1 queries, deep OFFSET paging and needless recomputation.
lessons.explain:
N+1 queries. The screen loads 50 exceptions, then asks the database for each one's current decision: 51 requests. Every request has network latency (often 20–100 ms to Supabase), so the screen takes seconds. Fix: one query for all of them, with IN (.in('exception_key', keys)) or a join in a view. The starter app's getCurrentReviews(keys) already does this.

OFFSET paging. ORDER BY … LIMIT 50 OFFSET 5000 still produces and throws away 5,000 rows, and rows shift between pages when data changes. Keyset paging remembers where the last page ended: WHERE (reviewed_at, review_id) < (:last_time, :last_id) ORDER BY reviewed_at DESC, review_id DESC LIMIT 50. With an index on those columns it is fast on any page.

Recomputing a heavy view. recon_exceptions recomputes everything on every request. That's what you want for correctness, and fine at Harbourline's size. If it ever gets slow, a materialized view stores the result: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW … AS …, refreshed with REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW after each import. The trade-off: between refreshes, the numbers are stale. For a reconciliation, stale numbers are dangerous, so measure first and refresh inside the import function if you do it.

examples.note: N+1 versus one query, from JavaScript. Both print the same; count the calls.
Keyset paging: page 2 of the review history, starting after the last row of page 1.
The plans of both paging styles, for a page deep in the history.
examples.sql:
SELECT plan_uses('SELECT review_id FROM big_reviews ORDER BY reviewed_at DESC, review_id DESC LIMIT 50 OFFSET 40000', 'Seq Scan') AS offset_scans_table,
       plan_uses('SELECT review_id FROM big_reviews WHERE (reviewed_at, review_id) < (''2025-01-08 10:40:00+00'', 10000) ORDER BY reviewed_at DESC, review_id DESC LIMIT 50', 'Index') AS keyset_uses_index;

examples.note: A materialized summary, and why it needs refreshing. A new review doesn't show until the refresh.

mistakes.text: OFFSET paging while new rows arrive: a row inserted at the top pushes everything down one place, so the first row of page 2 is the last row of page 1 again. The user sees a duplicate (or misses one, when rows are removed).
mistakes.sql:
WITH page1 AS (SELECT review_id FROM big_reviews ORDER BY reviewed_at DESC, review_id DESC LIMIT 3)
SELECT 'page 1 ended at' AS what, min(review_id) AS review_id FROM page1
UNION ALL
SELECT 'page 2 after one new review starts at', review_id FROM (
  SELECT review_id FROM (SELECT review_id, reviewed_at FROM big_reviews UNION ALL SELECT 99999, now()) AS t
  ORDER BY reviewed_at DESC, review_id DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 3) AS p2;

Keyset paging: WHERE (sort, id) < (last_sort, last_id), stable and fast.
Materialized views trade freshness for speed; refresh after each import.

modules.intro:
Performance problems only show with data. Next to the Harbourline tables, this module's database has two larger generated tables:

Table Rows Columns
big_lines 100,000 line_id (PK), insurer_id, policy_key, month, amount, invoice_reference
big_reviews 50,000 review_id (PK), exception_key, reviewed_at, decision, reviewed_by

Two course helpers show plans without the cost numbers, so your output matches the examples exactly: SELECT * FROM plan_of('your query') lists the plan lines, and plan_uses('your query', 'Index Scan') says whether a plan contains a node. Inside the quoted query, double every single quote: '… WHERE policy_key = ''POL001234'''.

In your own psql or the Supabase SQL editor, you write EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE in front of the query instead.
